spine: Experiment, one change at a time
ml-dl-q1.testing: whether you investigate before you optimise, and whether you know one symptom can have several root causes.
ml-dl-q1.trap: opening with "I'd add dropout and regularization." It sounds right and skips the diagnosis.
ml-dl-q1.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Name it "A 27-point gap between train and test tells me the model isn't generalising. My first hypothesis is overfitting, but I wouldn't reach for regularization yet."
2 · Rule out the fakes "First I'd make sure the gap is real. I'd check the split for leakage: duplicates across train and test, a feature derived from the label, preprocessing fitted on the full dataset, or the same customer on both sides. I'd also check the test set is big enough and from the same distribution."
3 · Confirm with evidence "Then I'd confirm it: train and validation loss over epochs, and a learning curve over training-set size. Training loss falling while validation loss rises is overfitting. I'd look past accuracy to per-class recall and a baseline, because on imbalanced data 99% can mean nothing."
4 · Experiment "Once it's confirmed, I'd run controlled experiments, one change at a time: early stopping, then weight decay or dropout, then a smaller model, then better or more representative data, each tracked against validation."
5 · Interpret "I'd read each result before choosing the next lever, because the same gap can come from different causes."
6 · Validate, monitor "Finally I'd pick the winner on validation, evaluate once on the untouched test set against the baseline, and ship with drift monitoring."
Close "The goal isn't a smaller gap for its own sake. It's reliable performance on real, unseen data."

stages.name: Name it
stages.claim: a generalisation gap, hypothesis: high variance
stages.html:
"Twenty-seven points is a generalisation gap. My working hypothesis is overfitting, but it's a hypothesis, not a diagnosis."

The same two numbers have four explanations:

Explanation What is actually happening First clue
Overfitting (working hypothesis) the model memorised the training set, noise included validation loss rises while training loss falls
Data leakage training saw information it won't have in production validation is high too; only the truly held-out set is low
Distribution shift test data differs from training data feature or label distributions differ between the two sets
Unreliable test set too small or unrepresentative a wide confidence interval; odd slices

Why this matters: naming the rivals up front is what earns you the right to investigate before fixing.

stages.name: Rule out the fakes
stages.claim: audit the split before the model
stages.html:
"Before I touch the model, I validate the pipeline. A flawed split can't be fixed by architecture."

Check The question If it fails
Independence any duplicates or near-duplicates across train and test? de-duplicate, then re-split
Label leakage is any feature computed from, or after, the outcome? drop or re-time the feature
Preprocessing were the scaler, encoder and imputer fitted on train only? move them inside a pipeline fitted per fold
Split structure time-ordered data, or repeated users or devices? chronological split; group split
Test size is the test set big and representative enough? 72% on 200 rows is a wide interval: get more, or bootstrap it

Example: in fraud detection, if one customer's transactions sit in both train and test, the model learns that customer, not fraud. Use a group split.

Why this matters: leakage usually inflates both scores. If validation is high and only test is low, suspect the split or the test set before variance.

stages.name: Confirm with evidence
stages.claim: curves, data and the right metric
stages.html:
"I don't diagnose from two final numbers. I read the curves."

Evidence What I look for What it tells me
Loss over epochs train loss falling while validation loss rises overfitting; loss shows confidence problems accuracy hides
Learning curve over data size does the gap narrow as data grows? narrowing: more data helps · flat: it's capacity, not data
Class balance, train vs test different class mix imbalance or label shift
Feature distributions clear train images, blurry test images covariate shift
Label quality noisy or inconsistent labels the model memorised noise
Per-class metrics vs a baseline precision, recall, PR-AUC for rare classes in fraud, "always legitimate" can score 99%

Why this matters: overfitting and distribution shift are different problems with different fixes, and they can co-exist.

stages.name: Experiment, one change at a time
stages.html:
"Once overfitting is confirmed, I run controlled experiments, changing one factor at a time."

# Change Why it should help Best suited when
1 Early stopping on validation loss the model learns general patterns early and noise later validation peaks before training ends
2 Regularization: weight decay, dropout; for trees max_depth, min_samples_leaf, subsampling lowers sensitivity to training-specific patterns capacity is fine but the fit is too sharp
3 Smaller model: fewer layers, units or features less room to memorise the model is large relative to the data
4 Better data: targeted collection, relabelling, valid augmentation more diverse examples generalise the learning curve says more data helps
5 Tune hyperparameters on validation the settings interact last, once the bigger levers are in place

Each run is logged against the same baseline, with real numbers:

Experiment Train acc Val acc
Baseline 99% 72%
Early stopping measure measure
Weight decay or dropout measure measure
Smaller model measure measure
More representative data measure measure

Why this matters: the goal isn't to drag train accuracy down to 72%. It's to raise validation while keeping what the model genuinely learned.

stages.name: Interpret the result
stages.html:
"This is where I show judgement: not every train–test gap has the same cause."

Observation Likely cause Next action
Train 99%, val 72%, val loss rising overfitting regularise, early stop, reduce capacity
Train 75%, val 72% underfitting more capacity, better features
Train and val high, test low leakage or split mismatch audit pipeline and split strategy
Val fine, test distribution differs distribution shift fix representativeness, reweight, collect data
Accuracy high, minority recall low class imbalance per-class metrics, weighting, resampling

If early stopping lifts validation from 72% to 80% (illustrative), I'd then test whether regularization or data closes more of the gap. Real validation numbers drive the next step.

stages.name: Validate once, then monitor
stages.html:
"The test set gets looked at once. Otherwise it quietly becomes a second validation set."

Why this matters: "fixed" means reliable on real traffic, not a nicer number on a test set you've tuned against.

followUps.question: Why not just reduce the number of epochs?
followUps.html:
That's early stopping, and it's my first experiment, but only after I've shown overfitting is the cause.

If the gap comes from Fewer epochs gives
Overfitting a smaller gap; the validation-loss curve picks the stopping point
Leakage, a bad split, shift a weaker model with the same gap

I let the curve choose the epoch; I don't guess a number.

followUps.question: Would you always add dropout?
followUps.html:
No. Every technique is tested against the baseline, not assumed.

Model Dropout? Regularise with
Large neural net often helps dropout, weight decay
Small net, or one with batch norm can hurt weight decay, early stopping
Gradient-boosted trees doesn't apply depth, leaf size, subsampling

followUps.question: The learning curve is flat and you can't get more data. Now what?
followUps.html:
A flat gap means data volume isn't the constraint, so I attack capacity and signal.

  • Capacity: stronger regularisation, or a simpler model.
  • Signal: fewer, better-engineered features.
  • Variance: an ensemble such as bagging to average it away.
  • Labels: check for noise; a model can't generalise past inconsistent labels.

Then I sanity-check whether 72% is actually poor, against a baseline or human performance.

followUps.question: Can you get 99% / 72% without overfitting?
followUps.html:
Yes. The gap is a symptom, not a diagnosis.

Cause Why it gives 99 / 72
Distribution shift test rows come from a different population
Small or unrepresentative test set 72% is a noisy estimate
Evaluation-pipeline bug different preprocessing at test time

That's why I audit the split and read the curves first.

followUps.question: How do you know an improvement is statistically meaningful?
followUps.html:
Size the noise first, then compare the two models on the same examples.

SE = √( p(1−p) / n )      ← standard error of accuracy on n test rows
p = 0.72, n = 1,000  →  95% interval ≈ ±2.8 points
Then:same test rowsMcNemar's test, or bootstrap the differencerepeat across folds or seeds on small data

One lucky split shouldn't decide it.

followUps.question: It's a gradient-boosted model, not a neural net. What changes?
followUps.html:
The diagnosis is identical; the levers change.

Neural net Gradient boosting
dropout row and column subsampling
weight decay L1/L2 on leaf weights
smaller network max_depth, min_child_weight / min_samples_leaf
lower learning rate lower learning rate with more trees
early stopping on validation loss the same, per boosting round

followUps.question: How would you catch this before it reaches production?
followUps.html:
Make it structural, so it doesn't depend on anyone remembering.

Gates:transforms in a pipeline fitted per foldgroup or time splits by defaultleakage checklist in reviewfinal test set nobody tunes onshadow-score live traffic

The checklist question is "would I know this feature at prediction time?". Shadow scoring shows drift against real inputs, not a static file.

dontSay: "I'd add dropout and regularization." (as the opening) — fixing before diagnosing is the trap this question sets.
"The model is 99% accurate on training, so it's learned well." — it may have memorised, and accuracy may hide imbalance.
"I'll keep tuning until test accuracy goes up." — that turns the test set into a validation set.
"Overfitting, definitely." — the gap alone doesn't prove it; leakage and shift look the same.

ml-dl-q2.testing: whether you know the ways an offline number can be optimistic, and check them in the right order.
ml-dl-q2.trap: "It's data drift, retrain on fresh data." Drift doesn't arrive pre-installed on day one.
ml-dl-q2.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the gap "A drop from 0.94 to 0.71 with no code change tells me the offline number was probably never real, so I'd treat it as an evaluation problem before a model problem."
2 · Leakage first "I'd check leakage first, because it's the most common cause of a gap this size. Is any top feature computed from or after the label? Was the scaler or encoder fitted on the full dataset before the split? Is the same customer, or future data, on both sides of the split?"
3 · Then train–serve skew "Next, train–serve skew. Training features usually come from warehouse SQL, serving features from application code, and two implementations of 'the same' feature quietly disagree on nulls, time zones or windows."
4 · Drift last "Only then would I call it drift, by comparing production feature distributions against training with PSI or KS."
5 · Prove it by replay "To prove which one it is, I'd log the features actually served, replay them through the offline pipeline, and compare scores row by row."
6 · Make it structural "Finally I'd make the fix structural: every transform inside a pipeline fitted per fold, group or time-based splits, and one shared feature definition for training and serving, so the next model can't repeat this."

stages.name: Frame the gap
stages.claim: an optimistic offline number, not a broken model
stages.html:
"Twenty-three points on day one is too big and too sudden for drift. I assume the 0.94 was inflated until proven otherwise."

  • Ask when it dropped: from the first production day (evaluation problem) or gradually (drift).
  • Ask what 0.71 is measured on: same metric, same label definition, same population as offline?
  • Ask whether production labels are complete; a label delay makes recent rows look worse or better than they are.

Why this matters: the timing alone reorders the suspects. Day-one gaps are leakage or skew; slow decay is drift.

stages.name: Leakage first
stages.html:
"Leakage is the most common cause, so I go through its families one by one."

Family What it looks like How I check
Target leakage feature computed from or after the outcome (refund flag, "days since cancellation") for the top features: "would I know this at prediction time?"
Preprocessing contamination scaler, imputer or encoder fitted on all data before splitting is every transform inside the per-fold pipeline?
Temporal leakage random split on time-ordered data trains on the future re-score on a strict time holdout
Group leakage same user or device in train and validation re-score with GroupKFold on the entity id

Example: a churn model with "number of support tickets in the last 30 days" computed at the end of the label window looks brilliant offline and has nothing to use at serving time.

Why this matters: re-scoring on an honest split is cheap. If CV drops toward 0.71, you've found it without touching production.

stages.name: Then train–serve skew
stages.html:
"If the offline evaluation is honest, the next suspect is that production computes different features."

  • Training features from warehouse SQL; serving features from service code. Two code paths drift apart.
  • Typical differences: null defaults, time zones, aggregation windows, unit changes, categorical levels unseen offline.
  • A feature that exists in the warehouse but is not available at request time gets silently defaulted at serving.
  • Check per-feature null rates and distributions: served vs training.

Example: training uses avg_spend_30d from a nightly batch; the service computes it from a cache that resets on deploy, so half of production sees zero.

Why this matters: skew looks exactly like drift on a dashboard, but retraining won't fix it. It just trains on the bug.

stages.name: Drift last
stages.html:
"Only after leakage and skew are ruled out do I call it drift."

Point What it means
Covariate shift input distributions moved. Detect with PSI or KS per feature, and prediction-distribution drift.
Label shift the base rate changed. Compare predicted vs observed positive rate.
Concept drift the relationship changed. Needs labels; watch rolling metrics per segment.

On day one, genuine drift is unlikely unless the launch population differs from the training population (a new market, a new client). That's worth asking.

stages.name: Prove it by replay
stages.html:
"I don't argue about which cause it is. I replay."

  1. Log the exact feature vectors served in production, plus the model version.
  2. Recompute the same rows through the offline feature pipeline.
  3. Compare feature by feature, and compare model scores row by row.
Result Diagnosis
Offline and served features match, scores match, metric still low leakage inflated the offline number
Features differ for some columns train–serve skew in those columns
Features match, distributions differ from training drift or a population change

Why this matters: it turns a debate into a diff, and it tells you which team owns the fix.

stages.name: Make it structural
stages.claim: so the next model can't do this
stages.html:
"The fix isn't this model. It's the process that let a fake 0.94 ship."

  • Every transform inside a Pipeline / ColumnTransformer, fitted per fold.
  • Group- or time-based splits by default; a final time-ordered holdout nobody tunes on.
  • One feature definition shared by training and serving (feature store or a shared library).
  • A leakage checklist in model review; shadow-score live traffic before cut-over.
  • Monitoring: feature nulls and PSI against the training profile, plus delayed-label metrics.

followUps.question: How would you find target leakage fast in a model with 300 features?
followUps.html:
Interrogate the top ten features by importance: guilty until proven innocent.

Audit:sort by importanceask "known at prediction time? when is it written?"drop the suspectsre-score on a time holdout
  • Red flag: implausibly high importance, or SHAP values that separate the classes almost perfectly.
  • Confirmation: a large drop in the re-scored metric.

followUps.question: Why not just retrain on recent production data?
followUps.html:
Because retraining only fixes drift. It's the last step, after the diagnosis says drift.

Real cause What retraining on production data does
Leakage leaks the same way; the offline number stays fake
Train-serve skew trains on production's broken features and bakes the bug in
Covariate or label drift fixes it

followUps.question: CV is honest, replay shows features match, and it's still 0.71. Now what?
followUps.html:
Then the population or the label differs.

Check Question
Population new market, new client, new acquisition channel?
Label definition same definition and same horizon as training?
Label maturity fully observed? A 30-day churn label read after 10 days looks like a model failure

Then slice the metric by segment to find where the loss concentrates.

followUps.question: You don't have a feature store. How do you prevent skew?
followUps.html:
One definition of each feature, and proof every night that it still holds.

  • Shared code: one computation library or dbt layer used by both the training job and the service.
  • Log and wait: log the features the service actually computes and train on those logs, so training and serving are identical by construction.
  • Nightly check: served-feature distributions against the training profile.

followUps.question: How do you tell drift from a pipeline break on a dashboard?
followUps.html:
A break is abrupt and local; drift is gradual and spread.

Pipeline break Drift
Shape step change slow slope
Scope one or two features many correlated features
Signature nulls, a unit change shifted distributions
Lines up with a deploy or an upstream schema change nothing in the deploy log

Null rates, value ranges and the deploy log come first; PSI after.

followUps.question: How do you catch this before shipping next time?
followUps.html:
Evaluate the way you'll serve, and make the comparison a launch gate.

Gate:time-ordered final holdoutfeatures computed by the serving pathshadow-score live traffic for a weekcut over

If the shadow score doesn't match offline within the tolerance, the launch stops. That turns this incident into a check.

dontSay: "It's data drift." (as the first answer) — drift doesn't explain a day-one gap.
"Let's retrain with more data." — retraining on leakage or skew reproduces it.
"Maybe production data is just noisier." — untestable; name a mechanism you can check.
"CV was 0.94, so the model is good." — CV measures the split you built, not production.

ml-dl-q3.testing: whether you know the framework and its limits in the deep-learning era.
ml-dl-q3.trap: reciting the U-curve as a universal law in 2026, or naming only two terms.
ml-dl-q3.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Three terms "For squared loss, expected test error splits exactly into three terms: bias squared, variance, and irreducible noise. Bias is systematic error from wrong assumptions. Variance is how much the model changes if you retrain on a different sample. Noise is the floor no model can beat."
2 · The U-curve "The classical picture says capacity trades the two: more capacity lowers bias and raises variance, so test error is U-shaped and you pick the bottom. That still governs most tabular work."
3 · Where it misleads "It misleads in two places. Heavily over-parameterised models show double descent: past the point where the model fits the training set exactly, test error falls again. So I reason about effective capacity, not parameter count. And the clean decomposition only holds for squared loss; for 0–1 loss it's an analogy."
4 · What survives "What survives is the diagnostic value. The train–validation gap reads variance; high error on both reads bias."
5 · Fix the dominant term "Each has a different fix: variance wants more data, regularisation or bagging; bias wants more capacity or better features."
Close "So the framework's real job is telling me which one to attack."

stages.name: Decompose into three terms
stages.html:
"Expected squared error = bias² + variance + irreducible noise."

E[(y − f̂(x))²]  =  Bias[f̂(x)]²  +  Var[f̂(x)]  +  σ²
                    ↑ wrong on average   ↑ changes per sample   ↑ noise in y itself
Term The question it answers Looks like Example
Bias² averaged over many training sets, how far is the prediction from the truth? underfitting a straight line fitted to a curve
Variance how much does the prediction move if I retrain on another sample? overfitting a depth-30 tree on 500 rows
Noise σ² how random is the target itself? a floor two identical customers, different outcomes

Why this matters: most candidates stop at two terms. Naming noise tells the interviewer you know where the floor is.

stages.name: The classical U-curve
stages.html:
"As capacity rises, bias falls and variance rises, so test error is U-shaped."

  • Pick the capacity at the bottom, using validation error, not training error.
  • The right first answer for trees, linear models, k-NN and most tabular problems.

stages.name: Where it misleads
stages.claim: double descent, and the wrong loss
stages.html:
"Two places the classical picture breaks."

The classical claim Why it fails What to say instead
"More parameters always overfit" past the interpolation threshold, test error can fall again reason about effective capacity: architecture, regularisation, optimiser, data size
"Parameter count is capacity" SGD's implicit bias prefers simpler fits "a 1B-parameter model must overfit 10M rows" is not a valid argument
"The split works for any loss" it is exact only for squared error for 0–1 loss, bias and variance interact: it's an analogy

Why this matters: saying this is the difference between a textbook answer and one that has read past the textbook.

stages.name: What survives
stages.html:
"Operationally, it's still the right lens for debugging a model."

Observation Dominant term Read
Train error low, validation high variance gap = variance
Both high and close bias model can't represent the signal
Both low, close healthy check against the noise floor
Gap shrinks as data grows variance, data-hungry more data helps

A learning curve (error vs training-set size) separates "needs more data" from "needs more capacity".

stages.name: Fix the dominant term
stages.html:
"Different terms, different fixes, and using the wrong one makes things worse."

Dominant term Levers that reduce it What makes it worse
Variance more data · L1/L2 · dropout · early stopping · bagging · smaller model more capacity, less regularisation
Bias more capacity · better features · less regularisation · boosting dropout or a smaller model
Noise better labels or measurement nothing a model change can fix

Example: adding dropout to an underfitting model raises bias further. That's why diagnosis comes first.

followUps.question: Why does bagging reduce variance but not bias?
followUps.html:
Averaging cancels the error that differs between models, and bias is the part they share.

Var(average of B trees) = ρσ² + (1−ρ)σ²/B    ← second term shrinks as B grows
Bias(average)           = Bias(one tree)     ← unchanged by averaging

That's why bagging wants deep trees: low bias, high variance, and as uncorrelated as possible.

followUps.question: So should I just make every model huge?
followUps.html:
No. Capacity is a choice you validate, not a default.

  • Not guaranteed: double descent needs enough data, the right regularisation and the right optimiser.
  • The peak is real: near the interpolation threshold a model can be worse than a small one.
  • Tabular data: with modest rows, boosting still beats large networks.

followUps.question: How do you estimate the irreducible noise?
followUps.html:
From label disagreement, with human-level performance as a practical floor.

Signal How to read it
Duplicate or near-identical inputs, different labels direct evidence of noise
Inter-annotator agreement the ceiling for human-labelled data
Human-level or best-known score a proxy for the floor

If error is already near the floor, more modelling won't help; better labels or new features might.

followUps.question: Where does regularisation sit in this picture?
followUps.html:
It lowers effective capacity without changing the architecture: a little more bias for a lot less variance.

On the U-curve:stronger regularisationlower effective capacitymove leftvariance down, bias up

Weight decay, dropout, early stopping and data augmentation are all the same knob.

followUps.question: Does this matter for LLMs at all?
followUps.html:
The framing shifts: pretraining underfits, fine-tuning overfits.

Phase Regime What it means
Pretraining one epoch over a huge corpus: underfitting data scale is the regulariser; dropout is often zero
Fine-tuning on small data variance returns overfitting and memorisation are real
Evaluation contamination fakes a low "variance"

dontSay: "There's a trade-off: more complex models always overfit." — double descent contradicts it.
"Bias and variance." (two terms only) — you dropped the noise floor.
"Deep models have low bias, so they're always better." — effective capacity and data size decide.
"The decomposition works the same for accuracy." — exact only for squared loss.

ml-dl-q4.testing: whether one split design can defeat two independent leakage risks at once.
ml-dl-q4.trap: stratified K-fold because the class balance looked nicer.
ml-dl-q4.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Name the two leaks "The question names two separate risks, and a random split fails both."
2 · Split by time first "The first is entity leakage: if the same user is in train and test, the model memorises the user instead of learning the behaviour. The second is temporal leakage: with seasonality, a random split trains on the future and tests on the past."
3 · Keep users disjoint "So I'd split by time first: train on everything up to a cutoff, validate on the next window, test on the most recent one. Within that, I'd keep users disjoint, so no user in the test window was seen in training. Whether I enforce that strictly depends on production: if the model will score existing users, some overlap is realistic, but their test rows must still come after their training rows."
4 · Respect horizon and label delay "I'd also respect the prediction horizon and label delay: features only use data up to the prediction time, and I drop recent rows whose label window isn't fully observed yet."
5 · Walk forward and slice "Then I'd validate walk-forward across several cutoffs instead of one, report the metric per time slice, and check the test window covers a comparable season."
6 · Mirror production "The principle is that offline evaluation should mirror deployment exactly: train on the past, predict forward."

stages.name: Name the two leaks
stages.html:
"Two independent violations. Fix only one and the score is still fiction."

  • Entity leakage: a user appears in both sets. The model learns user identity (their habits, ID-correlated features) and scores well on "new" rows it has effectively seen.
  • Temporal leakage: random shuffling puts December in training and November in test. The model uses the future.
  • Seasonality adds a third subtlety: the test window must cover a comparable season, or you're measuring the calendar, not the model.

stages.name: Split by time first
stages.html:
"Time is the primary axis: train ≤ T, validate (T, T+Δ], test on the latest window."

|──────── train ────────|── val ──|── test ──|   time →
                        T        T+Δ
  • Mirrors deployment, where the model always predicts forward.
  • Leave a gap between train and validation equal to the prediction horizon, so labels from the train window can't overlap validation features.

stages.name: Keep users disjoint
stages.claim: decide it from the production case
stages.html:
"Then enforce user disjointness inside that time split, if production requires it."

Production scores… Split rule
mostly new users strict: no test-window user appears in training (GroupKFold-style on user id)
mostly existing users overlap allowed, but each user's test rows come strictly after their training rows

Example: a subscription-cancellation model scores the existing base monthly, so overlap is realistic; a sign-up fraud model sees only new users, so strict disjointness is the honest test.

Why this matters: "always group" and "never group" are both wrong. The split copies what production will see.

stages.name: Respect horizon and label delay
stages.html:
"Features stop at the prediction timestamp, and labels must be fully observed."

  • Point-in-time features: every feature is computed as-of the prediction time. Aggregates like "logins last 30 days" must not include days after it.
  • Label delay: a 30-day churn label isn't known for the last 30 days of data. Those rows look like non-churners, so drop them.
  • Watch features that change after the fact (account status, refunds): use their historical value, not today's.

stages.name: Walk forward and slice
stages.html:
"One cutoff is one sample. I validate across several."

Point What it means
Walk-forward CV expanding or rolling windows across several origins; report mean and spread.
Per-slice reporting metric per month in the test window. Steady decay tells you the retraining cadence you'll need.
Season check make sure at least one validation window covers the same season as the deployment period.

stages.name: Mirror production
stages.html:
"If my CV doesn't look like production, its number is decoration."

Write the split rule into the pipeline, not a notebook: time cutoffs, user rule, horizon gap and label-completeness filter. Keep a final time-ordered holdout that no tuning touches.

followUps.question: Why not stratified K-fold? Class balance is identical across folds.
followUps.html:
Balance isn't the risk. Time and user leakage are.

Stratified K-fold Grouped, time-ordered split
Class balance if stratified within it
Trains on the future yes no
Same user on both sides yes no

The score is optimistic in exactly the way production can't reproduce. Stratifying within the grouped, time-ordered split is fine when positives are rare.

followUps.question: You only have 14 months of data. How many walk-forward folds?
followUps.html:
Enough to cover a full season in validation at least once.

With 14 months:train on the first 9–12validate on 3–4 rolling one-month windowsreport the spread
  • Fewer, honest folds beat many leaky ones.
  • With few folds the variance of the estimate is high, so the spread matters as much as the mean.

followUps.question: A user's behaviour depends on account age. Does that break the user split?
followUps.html:
No, as long as account age is its value at prediction time.

  • Features: computed point-in-time.
  • Reporting: if production scores new and old users, report each cohort separately. A model that only works for tenured users hides behind a pooled number.

followUps.question: How do you handle a label that takes 90 days to observe?
followUps.html:
The newest usable training data is always 90 days old, so the model learns stale behaviour.

Option Cost
Shorter proxy label must be validated against the full label
Accept the lag, retrain on a schedule always behind
Monitor label-free signals meanwhile feature and prediction drift only

Always drop rows whose label window isn't complete.

followUps.question: How do you tune hyperparameters inside this scheme?
followUps.html:
Nested inside the time structure: tune on walk-forward windows, never on the final test window.

Order:walk-forward validation windowspick settingsfinal test windowreport

If data is scarce, the walk-forward folds are the inner loop and the most recent window is the outer estimate.

dontSay: "Stratified K-fold with shuffle." — breaks both time order and user disjointness.
"Just group by user." — fixes one leak and ignores time.
"Use all the data up to today." — the last label window is incomplete.
"One train/test cut is enough." — one origin tells you nothing about stability across seasons.

spine: Fix: nested CV or an untouched holdout
ml-dl-q5.testing: whether you separate selecting a model from estimating its performance.
ml-dl-q5.trap: treating the best CV score as the expected production score.
ml-dl-q5.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Name the bias "The number did two jobs. It was used to pick the hyperparameters, and then reported as the estimate of how well the model generalises. Once you select on a score, that score is optimistically biased."
2 · Why selection inflates "The reason is the winner's curse. Every configuration's CV score is its true performance plus some fold noise. When you pick the maximum across many configurations, you systematically pick the ones that got lucky on those particular folds. The more configurations you try, the bigger the inflation: small if you tried three settings, large if Optuna tried three hundred."
3 · How big it gets "The fix depends on how much data I have. With enough data, I keep a test set that nothing touches during selection and evaluate on it exactly once at the end. With scarce data, I use nested cross-validation: the inner loop tunes, the outer loop estimates the performance of the whole tuning procedure."
4 · Fix: nested CV or an untouched holdout "The same rule covers anything else chosen on those folds: feature selection, encoders, the decision threshold."
5 · Compare models honestly "And when comparing two models, I'd treat differences inside the CV noise as ties, using repeated CV with confidence intervals or a paired test, not a single leaderboard number."

stages.name: Name the bias
stages.claim: selection and estimation used the same data
stages.html:
"The CV score was used to select, so it can no longer estimate."

  • The folds were held out for training, but not for selection. Selection is a form of fitting.
  • Reported number = score of the configuration that did best on these exact folds.
  • In production, the model meets new data with new noise, and the lucky part disappears.

stages.name: Why selection inflates
stages.html:
"Each CV score is true performance plus noise. The max of many noisy scores is biased upward."

The same effect makes a stock-picking fund's best past year a bad forecast.

stages.name: How big it gets
stages.html:
"The bias grows with how hard you searched and shrinks with how much data each fold has."

Situation Inflation
3 hand-picked configs, large folds small
300-trial Bayesian search, small data large
Many features selected on CV + tuning larger again, because both steps overfit the folds

Why this matters: you can say how worried to be, instead of treating it as always fatal or always negligible.

stages.name: Fix: nested CV or an untouched holdout
stages.html:
"Two honest options."

Untouched test set Nested CV
How split a test set off first; tune with CV on the rest outer folds estimate; an inner CV tunes inside each outer training fold
What the score estimates the one final model the whole tune-then-train procedure
Cost one extra evaluation outer × inner × candidates fits
Pick when data is plentiful data is scarce

Option 1 — Untouched test set. Split off a test set first. Do all tuning with CV on the rest. Evaluate the final model once on the test set. Best when data is plentiful.

Option 2 — Nested CV. Outer loop splits data into k folds for estimation. Inside each outer training fold, an inner CV tunes hyperparameters. The outer score estimates the procedure (tune-then-train), not one configuration. Best when data is scarce. Cost: outer × inner × candidates fits.

  • Everything chosen on validation data goes inside the inner loop: feature selection, encoders, thresholds.
  • After nested CV, you still refit the tuning procedure on all data to get the model you ship.

stages.name: Compare models honestly
stages.html:
"Before claiming model A beats model B, I check the difference is bigger than the noise."

  • Repeated CV with different seeds: report mean ± spread.
  • Paired tests on the same folds or examples: McNemar's test, 5×2-CV paired t-test.
  • A 0.3-point gain inside a 1-point spread is a tie. Pick the simpler or cheaper model.

followUps.question: Nested CV is expensive. When is it worth it?
followUps.html:
When the data is too small to spare a clean holdout and the decision is costly.

cost = outer folds × inner folds × candidates    ← shrink the search space before nesting
Situation Use
Small data, costly decision (regulator, paper, go/no-go) nested CV
Large dataset one untouched test set: the same honesty, much cheaper

followUps.question: After nested CV, which hyperparameters do you ship?
followUps.html:
None of the per-fold winners. Nested CV estimates the procedure, not one model.

To ship:rerun the inner tuning on the full datasettrain with the winnerquote the outer score as the estimate for that procedure

If the outer folds chose wildly different settings, the tuning is unstable, which is itself a finding.

followUps.question: I also chose features using the same CV. Problem?
followUps.html:
Yes, the same problem, and often worse.

Leaky:select features on all rowscross-validate
Honest:splitselect inside the pipeline, refit per foldscore

Selecting on the full dataset means the features were chosen using the validation rows' labels. With nested CV, selection goes in the inner loop.

followUps.question: How much can you tune against a test set before it stops being a test set?
followUps.html:
Strictly, once. Every decision made after looking leaks information.

Use of the test set What it has become
Looked once a test set
Looked twice slightly optimistic, not catastrophic
Iterated against for months a validation set

Refresh it, or hold back a second, never-seen set for the final claim.

followUps.question: What's your threshold-tuning story here?
followUps.html:
The threshold is a hyperparameter too.

Order:validation datachoose the threshold from error costs or an alert budgettest setreport

Choosing it on the test set inflates precision and recall exactly the way tuning on CV inflated the score.

dontSay: "CV is unbiased, so the score is fine." — CV is unbiased for a fixed model, not a selected one.
"Just use more folds." — more folds don't remove selection bias.
"Nested CV always." — it's a budget decision; a clean holdout is often enough.
"Model B wins by 0.3%." — without a noise estimate that's not a result.

ml-dl-q6.testing: whether you frame from the business decision backwards, and have the judgement to say no.
ml-dl-q6.trap: accepting "predict churn" as the spec and jumping to model choice.
ml-dl-q6.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Pin the decision "'Reduce churn' is a goal, not a spec, so I'd work backwards from the decision. First, the decision: who gets which intervention, when, and at what cost? A discount, a call from customer success, a product nudge. If nobody can act on a prediction, there's no project."
2 · Define the label and horizon "Second, the label and horizon. Churn meaning a cancellation event, or no activity for 30 days? Predicted how far ahead? And is that label available historically without leakage, and how long until we observe it?"
3 · Choose the unit "Third, the unit: per user, per account or per subscription, scored daily, weekly or monthly."
4 · Price the errors "Fourth, the cost of errors. A false positive wastes a discount on someone who'd have stayed; a false negative loses the customer. That cost matrix, plus how many people the team can actually contact, picks the metric and the threshold. I'd also ask whether we should predict churn at all or the uplift from the intervention."
5 · Beat a baseline "Then I'd set a baseline, like a rule on recent inactivity, and a success threshold before modelling."
6 · Decide: ML or not "I'd say don't use ML when a stable rule captures most of the value, when there's no reliable label or feedback loop, or when the action is the same for everyone anyway."

stages.name: Pin the decision
stages.html:
"I start from what changes in the business if the prediction is right."

Ask:

  • What intervention exists? Discount, outreach call, onboarding fix, product change.
  • Who acts on it, and how many can they handle per week? (capacity constraint)
  • When must the prediction arrive to be useful? A week before renewal, not the day after.
  • What does one intervention cost?

Why this matters: the decision sets everything downstream: horizon, unit, metric and threshold.

stages.name: Define the label and horizon
stages.html:
"The label is a definition, and it's the most important modelling choice."

Point What it means
Event explicit cancellation, non-renewal, or inactivity for N days? Do pauses or downgrades count?
Horizon "will churn in the next 30 days" measured from the prediction date.
Availability can we reconstruct it historically, point-in-time, without leaking post-outcome data?
Label delay a 30-day label for last week's users isn't known yet.

Example: in B2B, "account churn" at renewal is quarterly and rare; in consumer apps, 14-day inactivity is frequent and noisy. Different problems.

stages.name: Choose the unit
stages.claim: what gets a score, how often
stages.html:
"The unit of prediction is a choice, not a given."

Option Fits when
Per user, weekly consumer app, cheap nudges
Per account, monthly B2B, account managers act
Per subscription at renewal-minus-30 renewal-driven businesses

Batch scoring on a schedule is usually enough for churn; say so, because it removes most of the serving infrastructure.

stages.name: Price the errors
stages.claim: the cost matrix picks the metric
stages.html:
"A false positive and a false negative have different prices, so accuracy is meaningless."

Point What it means
False positive discount given to someone who'd have stayed (cost = discount + margin loss).
False negative a churner missed (cost = lost lifetime value).
Capacity if the team can call 200 people a week, the metric is precision@200, not AUC.
Uplift, not churn the valuable users are the persuadable ones. Some churners leave whatever you do; some would stay anyway. If you can run experiments, model the treatment effect.

stages.name: Beat a baseline
stages.html:
"Before any model, I write down what we'd do without one, and what 'success' means."

  • Baselines: current process, a rule ("no login in 14 days and plan expires in 30"), a logistic regression on five features.
  • Success = measurable lift in retained revenue in an A/B test against the baseline, not an offline AUC.
  • If the rule gets most of the value, ship the rule and revisit later.

stages.name: Decide: ML or not
stages.html:
"'Don't use ML' needs conditions, not modesty."

Say no when Because
A simple stable rule captures most of the value ML adds cost and opacity for little gain
No reliable label, or it's hopelessly noisy nothing to learn from
No feedback loop to measure outcomes you can't tell if it works
The action is identical for everyone a prediction can't change the decision
Errors are costly and unbounded without human review put a human in the loop, or use rules

followUps.question: Why is predicting churn not the same as reducing it?
followUps.html:
Because the intervention only changes the outcome for some users.

User type Without the offer With the offer
Sure thing stays stays
Lost cause leaves leaves
Sleeping dog stays may leave
Persuadable leaves stays

A churn model targets high risk, which includes lost causes. An uplift model targets persuadables, and it needs randomised treatment data, so start with an experiment.

followUps.question: How do you avoid leakage in the churn label?
followUps.html:
Everything is computed as-of the prediction date, and nothing recorded after it is used.

  • Banned features: cancellation-flow visits, support tickets about cancelling, refund requests.
  • Split: by time.
  • Rows: drop recent ones whose label window hasn't closed.
  • Audit the top features: "would I know this on the prediction date?"

followUps.question: The business wants 95% accuracy. Your answer?
followUps.html:
Accuracy is the wrong target: with 5% churn, "nobody churns" scores 95%.

Reframe:business outcomemodel metric (precision at the team's capacity)target set from a baseline

The outcome reads like "retain N more customers a month at a cost below X": a target from a baseline, not a round number.

followUps.question: How do you prove the model reduced churn?
followUps.html:
With a randomised holdout. Offline metrics can't show it.

Experiment:score everyonetake high-risk usersintervene on one subset, leave a matched controlcompare churn
  • The difference is the causal effect of model plus intervention.
  • Keep a small permanent holdout to detect decay.

followUps.question: Batch or real-time scoring?
followUps.html:
Batch, unless the intervention fires in-session.

Batch (nightly job) Real-time
Fits daily or weekly churn decisions a save offer inside the cancellation flow
Cost simple, cheap, easy to monitor an online feature path and skew risk

Without an in-session trigger, real-time adds risk for no business benefit.

followUps.question: There's no history of interventions, only of churn. Can you still build it?
followUps.html:
A churn-risk model, yes. An uplift model, no: you've never observed what the intervention does.

Start:risk scoringrandomised pilot on high-risk usersmeasured effecttraining data for an uplift model later

The pilot treats a random half of the high-risk users and holds out the rest.

dontSay: "I'd train an XGBoost on user features." (first sentence) — model before framing.
"We'll optimise accuracy." — imbalanced label, and it ignores the cost of errors.
"ML is always better than rules." — the baseline decides.
"Predict who will churn and give them all a discount." — ignores capacity and persuadability.

links.target: 01-ML/15-System & Architecture/04-Online vs Batch vs Streaming Inference

ml-dl-q7.testing: whether you can translate a threshold-free metric into the decision the business actually makes.
ml-dl-q7.trap: defending the model with the metric instead of the decision.
ml-dl-q7.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Both are right "Both statements can be true, because ROC-AUC and the business are measuring different things."
2 · Check prevalence "ROC-AUC averages ranking quality over every possible threshold and is insensitive to class prevalence. If positives are rare, say half a percent, the false-positive rate's denominator is the huge negative class, so a model can flood the review queue with false alarms and still post 0.92."
3 · Look where the business operates "The business lives at one operating point: 'my team can review a hundred cases a day'. So I'd measure what they experience: precision at that budget, recall at that budget, and the precision–recall curve, which has the positives in the denominator and exposes what ROC hides."
4 · Check calibration "I'd also check calibration. If scores feed any downstream logic like 'act above 0.7', a good ranker with miscalibrated probabilities still breaks it. A reliability plot and the Brier score show that, and Platt or isotonic scaling fixes it."
5 · Set the threshold from cost "Then I'd set the threshold from the cost of errors or the capacity constraint, not at 0.5."
6 · Agree the metric up front "The real lesson is framing: the operating metric should be agreed with the business before training."
Close "A metric mismatch discovered after launch is a framing failure, not a modelling one."

stages.name: Both are right
stages.html:
"AUC answers 'does the model rank positives above negatives?' The business asks 'is the list I act on worth acting on?'"

AUC = P( score(random positive) > score(random negative) )   ← ranking, averaged over every threshold
business value = precision and recall at ONE threshold        ← the queue people actually work
  • AUC = probability a random positive scores above a random negative.
  • It's threshold-free: averaged over all thresholds, most of which the business never uses.
  • The business sees one threshold and one queue.

stages.name: Check prevalence
stages.html:
"With 0.5% positives, a small false-positive rate is still a flood."

ROC reports "80% TPR at 5% FPR", which sounds excellent. The analyst sees 13 false alarms for every real case.

stages.name: Look where the business operates
stages.html:
"Evaluate at the operating point, not across all of them."

precision@k = true positives in the top k / k                  ← k = daily review capacity
recall@k    = true positives in the top k / all positives      ← share of real cases caught
  • Precision@k, where k is daily review capacity.
  • Recall at that budget: what share of real cases we catch.
  • PR-AUC / average precision as the threshold-free summary, because precision uses positives in the denominator.
  • Slice by segment: the model may be useless for the segment the business cares about most.

stages.name: Check calibration
stages.html:
"If anyone acts on the score's value, the score has to mean what it says."

Brier score = (1/N) · Σ (pᵢ − yᵢ)²                             ← 0 is perfect; rewards honest probabilities
  • Reliability diagram: predicted probability vs observed frequency, binned.
  • Brier score: mean squared error of the probabilities.
  • Fix on a held-out set: Platt scaling (sigmoid, little data) or isotonic (flexible, more data).

Example: the business rule "escalate above 0.7" catches nothing if the model's scores cluster between 0.2 and 0.5.

stages.name: Set the threshold from cost
stages.html:
"The threshold is a business decision expressed in numbers."

  • Cost-based: pick the threshold that minimises FP cost × FP count + FN cost × FN count.
  • Budget-based: take the top k per day.
  • Revisit when costs, capacity or prevalence change; a threshold is not permanent.

stages.name: Agree the metric up front
stages.html:
"This was a framing failure. The metric should have been agreed before training."

Write down the decision, the capacity, the cost of each error and the target precision@k with the business. Report that number, with AUC as a secondary diagnostic.

followUps.question: When would you still prefer ROC-AUC?
followUps.html:
As a diagnostic of ranking quality, not as a business metric.

  • Different prevalence: comparing rankers across datasets, since ROC is prevalence-insensitive.
  • Balanced classes: roughly equal positives and negatives.
  • Early on: before an operating point is known.

followUps.question: PR-AUC is 0.12. Is the model bad?
followUps.html:
Not necessarily. A random classifier's PR-AUC equals the prevalence.

lift = PR-AUC / prevalence = 0.12 / 0.005 = 24×    ← 24 times better than random

The real question is whether precision at the business's budget is worth the team's time. Compare against the current process, not against 1.0.

followUps.question: How do you pick k if the team's capacity varies?
followUps.html:
Rank by score and let capacity set the cut each day, so the threshold floats.

Daily:rank by scoretoday's capacity sets kwork the top k
  • Report precision and recall at several k values so the business sees the trade-off.
  • If costs are known, give the expected value at each k and let them choose.

followUps.question: Can you improve precision at the top without retraining?
followUps.html:
Sometimes, by working only on the top of the list.

Lever What it does
Second-stage model or rules uses expensive features on the top candidates only
Re-rank with business context value at risk moves up
Dedupe related alerts the queue isn't padded

Retraining with a ranking objective focused on the top of the list is the longer fix.

followUps.question: Your AUC improved 0.92 → 0.94. Does the business care?
followUps.html:
Only if precision or recall at their operating point moved.

  • Why not: an AUC gain can come entirely from reordering cases far below the cutoff, which the business never looks at.
  • What I report: the change in precision@k and in expected cost.
  • When I claim a win: only if those moved.

dontSay: "0.92 is a great AUC, the business doesn't understand metrics." — the business is describing the operating point correctly.
"Let's use accuracy instead." — worse under imbalance.
"Set the threshold at 0.5." — arbitrary; costs and capacity set it.
"We need a better model." — maybe; first measure at the right operating point.

ml-dl-q8.testing: whether you know that the value of a probability matters as soon as money multiplies it.
ml-dl-q8.trap: "the AUC is 0.9, so the probabilities are good."
ml-dl-q8.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Ranking ≠ calibration "The problem is that a model can rank perfectly and still lie about the probability. Expected value multiplies the probability by money, so any distortion becomes a wrong bid."
2 · Why boosted scores lie "Boosted trees are often not calibrated. The scores come from an additive ensemble, and anything done to improve ranking makes it worse: class weights, resampling, early stopping on AUC. Resampling alone shifts the base rate, so every score is inflated."
3 · Diagnose with a reliability curve "AUC can't see this because it only measures ranking. I'd diagnose with a reliability diagram, predicted probability against observed frequency in bins, and the Brier score."
4 · Calibrate on held-out data "The fix is a post-hoc calibrator fitted on held-out data, never the training data: Platt scaling, a sigmoid, when data is limited, or isotonic regression when there's enough data, since it's more flexible but overfits small sets. If I resampled, I'd also correct the prior back to the true base rate."
5 · Correct for resampling "Then I'd re-check the reliability curve and only then compute expected value."
6 · Monitor calibration drift "Operationally, calibration drifts as the population changes, so I'd monitor predicted versus observed rates in production and recalibrate as part of retraining."
Close "The rule: whenever the probability itself enters a decision, calibration is a requirement."

stages.name: Ranking ≠ calibration
stages.html:
"Ranking asks 'which is more likely?' Calibration asks 'when I say 30%, does it happen 30% of the time?'"

expected value = p × payoff − cost            ← the decision uses the VALUE of p, not its rank
model says p = 0.30, truth is 0.15            ← AUC unchanged, every bid is twice what it should be
  • AUC is invariant to any monotone transform of the scores. Squash them all into 0.4–0.6 and AUC doesn't move.
  • Expected value = p × payoff − cost. A 30% that's really 15% doubles the bid.

Example: in ad bidding, EV = p(click) × value. Overconfident p means overbidding on every impression.

stages.name: Why boosted scores lie
stages.html:
"Several common choices push boosted scores away from true frequencies."

Cause Effect on probabilities
Resampling / SMOTE base rate inflated, every score shifted up
scale_pos_weight / class weights same shift, in the loss
Many boosting rounds scores pushed toward 0 and 1 (overconfident)
Early stopping on AUC optimised for ranking, not probability

Logistic loss alone can be reasonably calibrated; it's the extra ranking-driven choices that break it.

stages.name: Diagnose with a reliability curve
stages.html:
"Plot what the model says against what happened."

  • Bin predictions (deciles), plot mean predicted vs observed rate.
  • Brier score summarises it; expected calibration error (ECE) gives one number per model.
  • Check per segment: calibration can be good overall and bad for a key segment.

stages.name: Calibrate on held-out data
stages.html:
"Fit a mapping from raw score to probability on data the model didn't train on."

Platt scaling Isotonic regression
Fits a sigmoid on the raw scores (2 parameters) a monotone step function
Data needed little thousands of positives
Risk too rigid for an odd-shaped distortion overfits a small calibration set
Pick when distortion is a smooth S-shape plenty of calibration data

Platt scaling. Fit a sigmoid on the raw scores. Two parameters, stable with little data. Best when distortion is a smooth S-shape.

Isotonic regression. Fit a monotone step function. Flexible, handles any monotone distortion, needs thousands of positives, can overfit. Best with plenty of calibration data.

  • In sklearn: CalibratedClassifierCV with cross-validation, or a dedicated calibration split.
  • Never fit the calibrator on training data; the model's scores there are overconfident by construction.

stages.name: Correct for resampling
stages.html:
"If I oversampled positives, the model thinks they're more common than they are."

Either calibrate on a held-out set with the real class balance (the calibrator absorbs the shift), or apply the prior correction analytically: rescale the odds by (true rate / training rate). Then check the mean predicted probability matches the observed base rate.

stages.name: Monitor calibration drift
stages.html:
"Calibration is fitted to one population. When the population moves, it drifts."

  • In production, compare mean predicted probability with the observed rate, per day and per segment.
  • Recalibrate on recent data at each retrain; it's cheap.
  • Alert when observed/predicted diverges past a tolerance; it's often the first sign of drift.

followUps.question: Platt or isotonic — how do you choose?
followUps.html:
By data size and the shape of the distortion, then by Brier score on a separate split.

Platt Isotonic
Parameters two many (a step function)
Fixes sigmoid-shaped distortion only any monotone distortion
Data needed a few hundred positives a lot
Risk wrong shape overfits into jagged steps

followUps.question: Does calibration change the AUC?
followUps.html:
Calibration fixes the numbers, not the ordering. A bad ranker stays bad.

Method AUC
Platt unchanged: a strictly monotone transform
Isotonic can change slightly, because flat steps create ties; ranking doesn't improve

followUps.question: Which models are usually calibrated out of the box?
followUps.html:
Logistic regression, roughly. Most others need a calibration step.

Model Out of the box
Logistic regression (log loss) close, if well specified
Naive Bayes, SVM scores aren't probabilities at all
Random forest underconfident near 0 and 1
Deep network trained long overconfident; temperature scaling is the standard fix

followUps.question: How do you calibrate with very few positives?
followUps.html:
Use the method with the fewest parameters and make every positive count.

  • Method: Platt, not isotonic.
  • Data: calibrate with cross-validation so every positive contributes; pool segments that behave alike.
  • Honesty: confidence intervals on the reliability curve, since high-score bins may hold a handful of cases.
  • High stakes: widen the margin in the EV rule.

followUps.question: The EV system worked for months, then started overspending. Where do you look?
followUps.html:
Calibration drift.

Cause:base rate or population shiftsprobabilities that were right are now too highEV rule overspends
Fix:predicted vs observed rate by segment and over timerecalibrate on recent datakeep that comparison as a standing alert

The alert catches the next drift before the budget does.

dontSay: "AUC is high, so the probabilities are fine." — AUC ignores calibration completely.
"Calibrate on the training set." — scores there are overconfident by construction.
"Just use a threshold of 0.5." — doesn't fix probabilities feeding EV math.
"Boosted trees output true probabilities." — only if nothing distorted them, and usually something did.

links.label: Imbalanced Data — Class Weights, SMOTE ADASYN, Undersampling, Cost Sensitive Learning
links.target: 01-ML/11-Model Selection, Validation & Tuning/07-Imbalanced Data — Class Weights, SMOTE-ADASYN, Undersampling, Cost-Sensitive Learning

spine: Resample inside the training fold only
Measure with PR metrics at the budget
ml-dl-q9.testing: whether you know which imbalance mistakes silently invalidate the number.
ml-dl-q9.trap: SMOTE on the whole dataset before splitting, or evaluating on a rebalanced set.
ml-dl-q9.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Stratify every split "At 0.3% the binding constraint is how many positives each split contains, so every choice starts there."
2 · Weight before you resample "For splitting, I'd stratify on the target so every fold gets its share of positives, and use repeated stratified K-fold, because with a few hundred positives a single split is noisy. If there's time or user structure, that comes first and stratification sits inside it."
3 · Resample inside the training fold only "For training, my first move is class weights or scale_pos_weight, plus threshold tuning, not synthetic data. It's cheaper and doesn't distort the data. If I do resample, it happens inside the training fold only, after the split. SMOTE before splitting leaks synthetic neighbours of test points into training."
4 · Measure with PR metrics at the budget "The validation and test sets are never resampled. They must keep the real 0.3%, or the number describes a world that doesn't exist."
5 · Report the noise "For metrics, accuracy is meaningless: predicting 'negative' scores 99.7%. I'd use PR-AUC and, more importantly, precision and recall at the real review budget, like the top 500 alerts a day."
6 · Deliver a ranked list "I'd report confidence intervals, because a point of difference is often noise here."
Close "And I'd say the deliverable is really a ranked list under a capacity budget, not a classifier."

stages.name: Stratify every split
stages.html:
"With 0.3%, a random fold can end up with almost no positives."

Step Rows Positives (0.3%)
Whole dataset 100,000 300
One of 5 stratified folds 20,000 60
One of 5 random folds 20,000 anywhere from about 40 to 80
  • 100k rows → ~300 positives; 5 folds → ~60 per fold. Unstratified, some folds get 40, some 80.
  • Stratified K-fold, repeated with different seeds, to stabilise the estimate.
  • If data has time or entity structure, split by that first, then stratify within it.

stages.name: Weight before you resample
stages.html:
"Class weights change the loss, not the data."

scale_pos_weight = negatives / positives = 99,700 / 300 ≈ 332   ← each positive counts 332× in the loss
  • class_weight='balanced', scale_pos_weight = negatives / positives, or a focal-style loss.
  • No synthetic rows, no duplicated positives, no invented neighbours.
  • Combine with threshold tuning on validation; weighting shifts scores, so the default 0.5 is meaningless.
  • Weights distort probabilities; calibrate afterwards if scores feed decisions.

stages.name: Resample inside the training fold only
stages.html:
"Resampling is a training-time transform. It goes in the pipeline, per fold."

Mistake Why it's wrong
SMOTE before the split synthetic points are interpolations of test points, so the test set leaks into training
Resampling the validation/test set the metric describes a 50/50 world production never sees
Oversampling by duplication before CV the same positive appears in train and validation folds

Use imblearn.pipeline.Pipeline so the sampler runs only on each training fold. SMOTE also interpolates nonsense for categorical or high-dimensional features.

stages.name: Measure with PR metrics at the budget
stages.html:
"Measure what the operations team will experience."

Point What it means
Accuracy 99.7% by predicting all-negative. Useless.
ROC-AUC dominated by the huge negative class, so it flatters.
PR-AUC / average precision random = 0.003, so compare against that.
  • Precision@k, recall@k at the real alert budget (the number of cases reviewed per day).
  • Per-segment recall: which kinds of positives do we miss?

stages.name: Report the noise
stages.html:
"With ~300 positives, a two-point difference in recall is a handful of cases."

  • Bootstrap confidence intervals on precision@k and recall.
  • Repeated CV spread across seeds.
  • Paired comparison (same folds) when choosing between models.

stages.name: Deliver a ranked list
stages.html:
"With extreme imbalance, the output is a prioritised queue under a capacity budget."

The business question isn't "is this fraud?" but "which 500 cases should analysts look at today?" Design the model, metric and threshold around that list.

followUps.question: Why is SMOTE before the split leakage?
followUps.html:
Because a synthetic training point can be a near-copy of a test positive.

Leaky:SMOTE on all rowssplitneighbours of test positives sit in traininflated recall
Honest:splitSMOTE inside the training fold only

SMOTE interpolates between a positive and its nearest positive neighbours, so the model has effectively seen the test case.

followUps.question: When is undersampling the right call?
followUps.html:
When the negative class is huge and training cost is the bottleneck, say billions of rows.

Recipe:undersample negatives, keep every positivetraincorrect the prior, or recalibrate

The correction adjusts scores for the changed prior; recalibration uses real-prevalence data.

It throws information away, so check on a learning curve that the discarded negatives weren't helping.

followUps.question: Is ROC-AUC ever fine here?
followUps.html:
As a secondary diagnostic for comparing rankers when the operating point isn't fixed.

At 0.3%, two models can have near-identical ROC-AUC and very different precision in the top 500, which is what the business sees.

Role Metric
Decides PR metrics and precision@k
Secondary ROC-AUC

followUps.question: Only 50 positives in total. What changes?
followUps.html:
Supervised learning is barely viable, so simplify the model and invest in labels.

Area Change
Validation leave-one-out or repeated stratified CV
Model very simple, strongly regularised, plus domain rules
Alternatives anomaly detection, semi-supervised approaches
Labels active learning on the most uncertain cases gets positives fastest

Report intervals honestly; they'll be wide.

followUps.question: Your weighted model's probabilities are off. Problem?
followUps.html:
Only if the probabilities are used as probabilities.

Use Problem? Fix
Ranking only no none
Expected cost, risk thresholds yes: weighting inflates positive scores by design Platt or isotonic on a held-out set with real prevalence

dontSay: "I'd SMOTE the data to 50/50 and then split." — leakage.
"Balance the test set so the metric is fair." — the metric no longer reflects production.
"Accuracy is 99.7%." — the all-negative baseline gets that.
"ROC-AUC 0.95, done." — says little about the top of the queue.

links.target: 01-ML/11-Model Selection, Validation & Tuning/07-Imbalanced Data — Class Weights, SMOTE-ADASYN, Undersampling, Cost-Sensitive Learning
