ml-dl-q10.testing: whether you choose by conditions and evidence, not by reputation.
ml-dl-q10.trap: "XGBoost is better" and then spending a week tuning it with no baseline to beat.
ml-dl-q10.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "I don't pick by reputation. I'd train both with defaults, alongside a logistic regression as the floor, and let the gaps decide."
2 · Where Random Forest wins "The axis is variance versus bias. Random Forest averages deep, decorrelated trees, which cuts variance. It's robust, needs almost no tuning, handles noisy labels well, trains in parallel and gives an honest out-of-bag score for free. It rarely embarrasses you."
3 · Where boosting wins "Gradient boosting fits each tree to the ensemble's remaining errors, which cuts bias. It usually has a higher ceiling on tabular data and brings native missing-value handling, custom objectives like ranking or quantile loss, and regularisation. The price is a tuning budget: learning rate, depth, subsampling and early stopping on a validation set. LightGBM for large or wide data, CatBoost when categoricals dominate."
4 · The failure asymmetry "The failure modes are asymmetric. Random Forest's risk is mediocrity. Boosting's risk is overfitting noisy labels and exploiting leakage, because it chases residuals, and residuals of noise are noise."
5 · How I actually decide "So in practice: Random Forest is the baseline I must beat, boosting is usually the model I ship, and I only invest in tuning if the gap between them justifies it."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.html:
"They solve different problems."

  • Random Forest: bagging + random feature subsets → averages many high-variance trees → variance falls.
  • Gradient boosting: sequential trees fitted to residuals/gradients → bias falls.
  • Both are tree ensembles, so both handle nonlinearity, interactions and mixed scales without much preprocessing.

stages.name: Where Random Forest wins
stages.html:
"Random Forest is the strong default you can trust in an hour."

  • Near-zero tuning; defaults are usually close to optimal.
  • Robust to label noise and outliers, because averaging dampens them.
  • Embarrassingly parallel training.
  • OOB score: built-in validation without a separate split.
  • Stable across retrains, which matters for explainability and reason codes.

stages.name: Where boosting wins
stages.html:
"Boosting usually wins on accuracy when you can pay for tuning."

Need Why boosting
Highest accuracy on clean tabular data bias reduction; typical competition winner
Missing values native handling, learned default directions
Custom objectives ranking, quantile, Tweedie, Poisson losses
Large or wide data LightGBM (histograms, leaf-wise growth)
High-cardinality categoricals CatBoost (ordered target statistics)

Tuning core: learning rate + number of rounds with early stopping, max depth, row/column subsampling, L1/L2 on leaves.

stages.name: The failure asymmetry
stages.html:
"Their failure modes differ, and that matters in production."

  • Random Forest fails quietly: a few points below the best possible.
  • Boosting fails loudly: it will fit label noise, exploit a leaked feature harder, and can degrade faster under drift.
  • So a boosted model needs stricter validation (time splits, leakage audit) than a forest.

stages.name: How I actually decide
stages.html:
"Three models with defaults, one honest split, then read the gaps."

Result Read Next step
Logistic ≈ RF ≈ boosting signal is mostly linear or weak ship the simple model; work on features
RF ≫ logistic, boosting ≈ RF nonlinear, low ceiling left ship RF, skip tuning
Boosting > RF by a margin bias-limited, room at the top tune boosting, check stability
Boosting ≫ RF suspiciously possible leakage audit top features before celebrating

stages.name: What I'd pick here
stages.claim: usually boosting, with RF as the bar
stages.html:
"For most production tabular problems I ship boosting, after it beats the forest honestly."

Pick Random Forest when labels are noisy, tuning time is scarce, the team needs stable, low-maintenance models, or the accuracy gap is within noise.

followUps.question: Why not a neural network?
followUps.html:
On tabular data, tree ensembles still match or beat deep models with less tuning and cost. Research on deep tabular models keeps re-finding that.

I'd consider a network when Why
Text or images sit alongside the table trees can't read unstructured inputs
Very large data with high-cardinality IDs embeddings learn those IDs

followUps.question: XGBoost, LightGBM or CatBoost?
followUps.html:
Accuracy is usually similar after tuning; pick by data shape.

Library Strength Watch for
LightGBM fastest on large, wide data (histogram binning, leaf-wise growth) overfits small data unless leaves are capped
CatBoost many categoricals handled natively with ordered statistics; good defaults —
XGBoost the mature, well-supported middle —

followUps.question: Boosting beats the forest by 8 points. Suspicious?
followUps.html:
Worth auditing: boosting exploits leaked features harder than a forest does.

Audit:top featuresavailable at prediction time?re-score on a time-based holdoutreal bias reduction

A big gap can be leakage amplified, so it's a suspect until that check passes.

followUps.question: How does the number of trees behave in each?
followUps.html:
In a forest more trees only reduce variance; in boosting each tree adds capacity.

Random Forest Boosting
More trees plateaus, never gets worse eventually overfits
What it is a compute trade-off a capacity knob
Control pick enough early stopping on validation loss, small learning rate

followUps.question: Which is easier to operate in production?
followUps.html:
The forest is steadier across retrains; boosting is lighter to serve but needs discipline.

Random Forest Boosting
Retrains stable, fewer hyperparameters to drift sensitive to tuning and data shifts
Serving larger model files smaller and faster
Needs little early stopping on each retrain; watch feature-importance stability

Both export cleanly (ONNX, Treelite).

dontSay: "XGBoost always wins." — conditions decide, and the forest is the bar.
"Random Forest is outdated." — it's the most reliable baseline in tabular ML.
"More trees in XGBoost is always better." — without early stopping it overfits.
"I'd start by tuning XGBoost." — no baseline, no idea if tuning is worth it.

spine: Consequences for tree depth and tuning
ml-dl-q11.testing: whether you can explain the mechanism, not recite "parallel vs sequential".
ml-dl-q11.trap: "bagging is parallel, boosting is sequential." That's the implementation, not why.
ml-dl-q11.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Bagging averages errors "Bagging trains many models on bootstrap samples and averages them. Averaging cancels errors that are uncorrelated between models, and variance is exactly the part of the error that changes from sample to sample. So variance falls. Bias doesn't, because every model shares the same systematic assumptions, and the average of biased models is still biased."
2 · Decorrelation is the real lever "The variance reduction depends on how correlated the models are. Averaging n models shrinks variance roughly with n, but only the uncorrelated part. That's why Random Forest adds random feature subsets at each split: bootstrap alone leaves the trees too similar, so decorrelating them is the real lever."
3 · Boosting fits what's left "Boosting works the other way. Each new learner is fitted to what the current ensemble still gets wrong: the residuals, or more generally the negative gradient of the loss. So each round corrects systematic error, and bias falls. Formally, it's gradient descent in function space, where each tree is one step."
5 · Consequences for tree depth and tuning "That explains the design choices. Bagging wants deep, low-bias, high-variance trees, because it can average the variance away."
Close "Boosting wants shallow, weak learners, and since nothing cancels its variance, it needs a learning rate, subsampling and early stopping to avoid overfitting."

stages.name: Bagging averages errors
stages.claim: and variance is the averageable part
stages.html:
"Averaging removes what varies between models and keeps what they share."

  • Train each model on a bootstrap sample (sampling with replacement).
  • Each model's error = shared bias + its own sample-specific wobble (variance).
  • Averaging many wobbles that point in different directions cancels them. The shared bias survives intact.

Example: 100 deep trees each overfit different quirks of their bootstrap sample; the average keeps what they agree on, the real signal.

stages.name: Decorrelation is the real lever
stages.html:
"Averaging only helps as much as the models disagree."

For n models each with variance σ² and pairwise correlation ρ, the variance of their average is:

Var(avg) = ρσ² + (1 − ρ)σ² / n
  • As n grows, the second term vanishes, but ρσ² stays. Correlation sets the floor.
  • Bootstrap alone leaves trees similar (the same strong feature dominates every root split).
  • Random feature subsets per split (max_features) force trees to differ, lowering ρ. That's why max_features matters more than n_estimators.

stages.name: Boosting fits what's left
stages.html:
"Boosting is sequential because each learner depends on the ensemble's current mistakes."

  • Start with a simple prediction (the mean).
  • Compute residuals: what the ensemble still gets wrong.
  • Fit a small tree to those residuals; add a scaled version to the ensemble.
  • Repeat. Systematic error is chipped away round by round, so bias falls.

AdaBoost does the same thing by reweighting misclassified examples; gradient boosting generalises it to any differentiable loss.

stages.name: Gradient descent in function space
stages.html:
"Each tree is a step along the negative gradient of the loss, taken in the space of functions."

  • For squared loss, the negative gradient is the residual.
  • For log loss, Huber or ranking losses, fit the tree to the negative gradient (pseudo-residuals).
  • The learning rate is the step size; smaller steps + more trees generalise better.
  • XGBoost adds a second-order (Newton) step and regularises leaf weights.

stages.name: Consequences for tree depth and tuning
stages.html:
Bagging / Random Forest Boosting
Base learner deep trees (low bias, high variance) shallow trees / stumps (high bias, low variance)
Reduces variance bias
More estimators never hurts, plateaus eventually overfits
Overfitting control decorrelation (max_features) learning rate, early stopping, subsampling, depth
Label noise robust fits the noise if unchecked
Parallelism trivial within-tree only

followUps.question: Why does boosting eventually overfit if it only reduces bias?
followUps.html:
Because once the systematic error is gone, the residuals are mostly noise, and each new tree fits it.

Drift into overfitting:bias removedresiduals ≈ noisenext tree fits noisenothing averages it away
Defence Effect
Learning rate shrinks each step
Subsampling adds randomness: a little bagging inside boosting
Early stopping stops before noise-fitting starts

followUps.question: Would bagging shallow stumps work?
followUps.html:
Poorly. Averaging removes variance stumps don't have, and leaves their bias.

Base learner Bias Variance Bagging gives
Stump high low an average of near-identical weak models
Deep tree low high a real variance cut

followUps.question: What does subsampling do in gradient boosting?
followUps.html:
It's bagging's idea inside boosting: randomness that decorrelates consecutive trees.

Stochastic gradient boosting:sample rows and columns per treetrees less correlatedlower variance, faster training

Typical values are 0.5–0.9 of rows and columns, tuned on validation.

followUps.question: Where does stacking fit?
followUps.html:
Stacking trains a meta-model on the out-of-fold predictions of diverse base models.

  • Can reduce: both bias and variance, but only if the base models make different mistakes.
  • Needs: careful out-of-fold construction, or it leaks.
  • Pays: often a small gain for the operational cost.

followUps.question: In production, which ensemble degrades more under drift?
followUps.html:
Generally boosting.

Boosting Random Forest
Fits fine-grained structure, including relationships that may not persist averaged, more conservative
Leans on the strongest features, hardest spread across features

Either way: monitor feature distributions, and recalibrate early stopping on every retrain.

dontSay: "Bagging is parallel and boosting is sequential." (as the explanation) — that's how, not why.
"More trees in boosting always helps." — it overfits without early stopping.
"Bagging reduces bias too." — the average of biased models is biased.
"Random Forest is just bagging." — feature subsampling (decorrelation) is the point.

spine: How I use them in production
ml-dl-q12.testing: the last clause. Whether you know explanation ≠ causation ≠ justification.
ml-dl-q12.trap: presenting a SHAP plot as "the drivers of churn" to a stakeholder.
ml-dl-q12.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · SHAP: fair credit with guarantees "SHAP splits a prediction's difference from the baseline across features using Shapley values from game theory. It comes with guarantees: the attributions add up exactly to the prediction, and a feature that contributes more always gets more credit. For tree models, TreeSHAP computes it exactly and fast, which is why it dominates tabular work. Aggregating local values also gives a global view."
2 · LIME: a local surrogate "LIME perturbs the input around one example and fits a small interpretable model, usually sparse linear, to the black box's outputs there. It's model-agnostic and cheap, but it's unstable: the sampling and kernel width change the story, so two runs can disagree. So I default to SHAP where it's tractable and use LIME as a quick local check."
4 · The shared weakness: correlated features "Both share a weakness: with correlated features, perturbing one feature at a time creates unrealistic inputs, and credit gets split between correlated features arbitrarily."
5 · What neither can tell you "And what neither tells you is causality or fairness. They explain the model's function, not the world. A leaked feature or a proxy for a protected attribute shows up as 'important' with no flag that it's wrong to use."
Close "Explanation isn't justification, so a human still has to judge whether the model's reasons are acceptable reasons."

stages.name: SHAP: fair credit with guarantees
stages.html:
"SHAP answers: how much did each feature move this prediction away from the average?"

  • Based on Shapley values: a feature's credit = its average marginal contribution over all orderings of features.
    Point What it means
    Local accuracy attributions sum to prediction − baseline.
    Consistency if a model changes so a feature contributes more, its attribution never drops.
    TreeSHAP exact and polynomial-time for tree ensembles. KernelSHAP for arbitrary models is slow and approximate.
  • Global view: mean |SHAP| per feature, beeswarm and dependence plots.

stages.name: LIME: a local surrogate
stages.html:
"LIME answers: what simple model mimics the black box near this one point?"

  • Perturb the instance, score the perturbations with the model, weight them by closeness.
  • Fit a sparse linear model; its coefficients are the explanation.
  • Model-agnostic, works on text and images (superpixels, words).
  • Unstable: kernel width, number of samples and random seed change the result. No consistency guarantee.

stages.name: Where each wins
stages.html:
Need Choose
Tree ensemble, tabular, need reason codes SHAP (TreeSHAP)
Global feature ranking with local detail SHAP
Quick look at one prediction from any black box LIME
Text or image, fast intuition LIME (or gradient-based methods for deep nets)
Regulated reason codes that must be reproducible SHAP, never a stochastic method

stages.name: The shared weakness: correlated features
stages.html:
"Both perturb features as if they were independent, and real features aren't."

  • Perturbing income while holding tax_paid fixed creates impossible people. The model's output on them is meaningless.
  • Credit splits arbitrarily between correlated features; one may look unimportant only because its twin took the credit.
  • Mitigation: group correlated features, use conditional/interventional SHAP deliberately, and say which one you used.

stages.name: What neither can tell you
stages.claim: causality, and whether the reason is acceptable
stages.html:
"They explain the model, not reality."

Point What it means
Not causal "high SHAP for num_logins" means the model uses it, not that increasing logins reduces churn.
Not a fairness check a zip-code feature acting as a proxy for race looks like an ordinary important feature.
Not a leakage detector by itself a leaked feature appears very important, and only a human asks "should we know this at prediction time?"

That last clause is the answer the interviewer is waiting for.

stages.name: How I use them in production
stages.claim: debugging and reason codes, with review
stages.html:
Point What it means
Debugging an absurdly important feature is my first leakage suspect.
Reason codes top SHAP contributions per decision, for customer or regulator explanations.
Monitoring track global SHAP importance over time; a shift signals drift or a pipeline change.
Governance a human reviews whether the top reasons are legitimate to use.

followUps.question: SHAP vs permutation importance?
followUps.html:
Permutation importance is tied to the metric; SHAP is tied to individual predictions.

Permutation importance SHAP
Measures metric drop when a feature is shuffled each feature's share of one prediction
Scope global, model-agnostic local, aggregated up
Weak with correlated features correlated features

Permutation importance on validation data is a good sanity check. Impurity-based tree importance is biased toward high-cardinality features.

followUps.question: The business wants "the drivers of churn" from your SHAP plot. Response?
followUps.html:
The plot shows what the model relies on, which is correlational.

From plot to driver:SHAP as hypothesis generationpick the most actionable featureA/B test ita causal claim

Without an experiment, the minimum is causal-inference methods with stated assumptions.

followUps.question: Why are LIME explanations unstable, concretely?
followUps.html:
Because three arbitrary choices decide which sparse linear model fits best.

Choice Effect
Random perturbation samples a different sample, a different fit
Kernel width changes what "local" means
Surrogate complexity changes which features survive

More samples and fixed seeds reduce it, but nothing guarantees two reasonable settings agree.

followUps.question: How would you explain a deep network's prediction?
followUps.html:
With gradient-based attribution, and then I validate it.

Method Note
Integrated Gradients the usual choice for deep nets
DeepSHAP approximates Shapley values
Attention weights not reliable explanations on their own
Validate:remove the top-attributed featuresdoes the prediction actually change?

followUps.question: Can explanations be gamed?
followUps.html:
Yes.

Attack:perturbation explainers query off-manifold pointsa model behaves innocently there, discriminates on real dataLIME or KernelSHAP report the innocent behaviour

So explanations support governance but don't replace fairness testing on real outcomes by group.

dontSay: "SHAP shows the causes of the outcome." — it shows the model's reliance, not causation.
"LIME and SHAP give the same answer." — LIME is unstable and has no consistency guarantee.
"Feature importance proves the model is fair." — proxies look like ordinary features.
"Attention weights explain the model." — not reliable on their own.

links.target: 01-ML/12-Interpretability & Responsible ML/04-SHAP — Values, Math Intuition & Plots

links.label: Feature Importance — Permutation vs Impurity based
links.target: 01-ML/12-Interpretability & Responsible ML/02-Feature Importance — Permutation vs Impurity-based

links.label: Fairness — Demographic Parity, Equalized Odds, Equal Opportunity
links.target: 01-ML/12-Interpretability & Responsible ML/06-Fairness — Demographic Parity, Equalized Odds, Equal Opportunity

ml-dl-q13.testing: whether you design against train–serve skew structurally, not by being careful.
ml-dl-q13.trap: a "small" reimplementation of the feature in the serving service.
ml-dl-q13.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Name the enemy: skew "The enemy is train–serve skew: training features computed in warehouse SQL, serving features in application code. Two implementations always drift, and the model degrades silently."
2 · One definition, two materialisations "So the design goal is one feature definition, materialised twice. A feature store gives you that: an offline store for training and an online store, a low-latency key-value store, serving the same definitions at request time, kept in sync by one pipeline."
3 · Point-in-time correctness "The offline side must be point-in-time correct: each training example gets feature values as they were at that example's timestamp, not as they are today. Otherwise you train on the future."
4 · Ship preprocessing with the model "Stateless preprocessing, like scaling, encoding and imputation, ships inside the model artefact as a pipeline object, so the service can't reimplement it."
5 · Version together, roll back together "The model and its feature versions are deployed and rolled back together, behind a prediction service with a validated input schema."
6 · Detect it anyway "And I'd still detect skew: log the features actually served, replay them offline, and compare distributions. I'd also challenge the serving need."
Close "For something like churn, nightly batch scoring into a table removes the online path, and most of the skew risk, entirely."

stages.name: Name the enemy: skew
stages.claim: two code paths, one feature name
stages.html:
"Skew happens whenever the same feature is computed by two different pieces of code."

Where it hides Example
Defaults SQL treats null as 0; service drops the row
Time UTC in the warehouse, local time in the service
Windows "last 30 days" inclusive vs exclusive of today
Availability feature exists in the warehouse but not at request time, so it's defaulted
Library versions tokenizer or encoder changed on one side

It doesn't raise errors. It shows up as a model that's "worse in production".

stages.name: One definition, two materialisations
stages.html:
"Write each feature once; let the platform compute it for both paths."

            feature definition (one place)
                 │                 │
          batch pipeline     streaming / on-demand
             │        │              │
     offline store   online store ◀──┘
  (point-in-time,    (low latency,
    for training)      for serving)
             │              │
         training     prediction service

Feast and Tecton implement this; the pattern matters more than the product.

stages.name: Point-in-time correctness
stages.claim: features as they were at the event
stages.html:
"Training joins must use feature values as of each label's timestamp."

Training row Event time Naive join attaches As-of join attaches
purchase in March 14 Mar lifetime_spend as of today (future leakage) lifetime_spend as of 14 Mar
same, feature lands 2 h late online 14 Mar 10:00 value written at 10:30 latest value written before 08:00
  • A naive join attaches today's value of lifetime_spend to an event from last March. That's future leakage.
  • Offline stores do an as-of join: for each event, take the latest feature value with timestamp ≤ event time.
  • Also account for feature latency: if a feature lands in the online store with a 2-hour delay, the offline join should apply the same delay.

stages.name: Ship preprocessing with the model
stages.html:
"Anything stateless travels inside the artefact."

  • sklearn Pipeline / ColumnTransformer, or preprocessing layers exported with the model.
  • The service passes raw inputs; the artefact applies the exact fitted transforms.
  • Same for tokenizers in NLP: version-pinned and bundled.

stages.name: Version together, roll back together
stages.html:
"A model trained on feature set v3 must never be served v4."

  • Model registry entry records the feature definitions and versions it was trained on.
  • Prediction service validates the input schema (types, ranges, required fields).
  • Deploy and roll back model + feature versions as one unit.

stages.name: Detect it anyway
stages.html:
"Design reduces skew; monitoring catches what design missed."

  • Log served feature vectors with the model version.
  • Nightly: compare served distributions and null rates with the training profile (PSI/KS).
  • Periodically replay logged requests through the offline pipeline and diff feature values row by row.

followUps.question: You don't have a feature store and can't buy one.
followUps.html:
Then get one definition without one, in either of two ways.

Option How Cost
Shared library or dbt layer imported by both the training job and the service discipline to keep one copy
Log and wait the service computes and logs features; train on the logs waiting for data to accumulate

Log and wait makes training and serving identical by construction.

followUps.question: Batch or online scoring for churn?
followUps.html:
Batch.

Batch (nightly job) Online
Fits daily or weekly churn decisions an in-session save offer in the cancellation flow
Skew almost none: one pipeline trains and scores a second feature path
Cost cheaper, easier to monitor higher

followUps.question: How do you handle a feature that needs to be fresh within seconds?
followUps.html:
A streaming aggregation into the online store, with the same logic backfilled offline.

Fresh path:eventsFlink, Kafka Streams or the store's streaming pathonline store
Training path:same event logsame logic in batchoffline store

The hard part is proving the two agree: test both on the same event log.

followUps.question: How do you know skew is the cause of a production drop?
followUps.html:
Replay: recompute the features offline for the same entities and timestamps, and compare.

Served vs recomputed Served vs training distribution Verdict
differ — skew
match differ drift
match match the offline evaluation was optimistic

followUps.question: What does a feature store cost you?
followUps.html:
Operational complexity. I adopt one when skew or duplicated feature work is a demonstrated cost.

  • You pay: another system to run, materialisation jobs, online-store latency and cost, a learning curve.
  • Overkill for: a single batch model.
  • Pays for itself with: many models sharing real-time features.

dontSay: "We'll just reimplement the feature carefully in the service." — two implementations always diverge.
"Join the latest feature values to the training labels." — future leakage.
"A feature store solves skew automatically." — only if every feature goes through it and joins are point-in-time.
"We need real-time serving." (without checking) — often batch is enough.

ml-dl-q14.testing: whether you treat drift as an operational decision loop, not "retrain nightly".
ml-dl-q14.trap: a nightly retrain cron as the answer to drift.
ml-dl-q14.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Is it real? "I'd treat it as a decision loop with four questions."
2 · Rule out the impostors "First, is the drop real? Are labels complete, or is the most recent period still waiting on delayed labels? Is the metric computed the same way, on the same population?"
3 · Classify the drift "Second, is it drift at all, or an impostor? A pipeline break, a schema change upstream, a new client version or a product change all produce the same symptom, and retraining would just bake them in. I'd check feature null rates and value ranges and line changes up against deploys."
4 · Localise it "Third, which drift? Covariate shift, where the input mix moved; label shift, where the base rate moved; or concept drift, where the relationship between inputs and outcome changed. Input and prediction drift are visible without labels through PSI or KS per feature; concept drift needs labels."
5 · Decide the response "Fourth, where? Slice by segment, because a 6-point average drop is often a 20-point drop in one segment."
6 · Retrain through a gate "Then the response: retraining on recent data fixes covariate and label shift; concept drift may need new features or a rethink. Every retrain goes through the same offline gate and canary as a new model."
7 · Run it as a loop "And I'd run this as a loop with time-to-detect and time-to-recover as SLOs."

stages.name: Is it real?
stages.html:
"Before diagnosing the model, I check the measurement."

Point What it means
Label delay if outcomes take weeks to arrive, the latest period looks worse (or better) until labels land.
Metric definition same metric, same threshold, same filters as before?
Population did a new market, client or acquisition channel change who's being scored?
Noise is 6 points outside normal week-to-week variation? Look at the confidence interval.

stages.name: Rule out the impostors
stages.html:
"Retraining on a broken pipeline trains the model on the bug."

Impostor Signature
Upstream schema/unit change step change in one feature, aligned with a deploy
Broken join / missing source null rate jumps; defaults flood in
New client/app version a segment's features change shape overnight
Product or pricing change behaviour changed on purpose; the model needs to be told
Train–serve skew served features differ from recomputed offline features

Abrupt + local = break. Gradual + broad = drift.

stages.name: Classify the drift
stages.html:
"Three different things can move, with different detection and different fixes."

Type What moved Detect Retraining fixes it?
Covariate shift P(X): input mix PSI/KS per feature, no labels needed usually yes
Label shift P(y): base rate predicted vs observed positive rate yes, plus recalibration
Concept drift P(y|X): the relationship rolling metrics once labels arrive maybe not; may need new features

Example: after a pricing change, users with the same activity churn at a different rate. That's concept drift; retraining on old data won't capture it until enough post-change labels exist.

stages.name: Localise it
stages.html:
"Aggregate metrics hide localised rot."

  • Slice by segment: region, device, customer tier, acquisition channel, tenure.
  • Find which features drifted most (PSI ranking) and which segments lost most.
  • Often a single segment explains most of the drop, and the fix is targeted.

stages.name: Decide the response
stages.claim: match the fix to the cause
stages.html:
Diagnosis Response
Pipeline break fix the pipeline; don't retrain
Covariate or label shift retrain on recent data; recalibrate
Concept drift new features, new label definition, or model redesign; short-term, retrain on post-change data
One segment segment-specific model or features; or route that segment to a fallback
Within noise watch; no action

stages.name: Retrain through a gate
stages.html:
"A retrained model is a new model and goes through the same checks."

  • Offline gate: beats the incumbent on a recent time-ordered holdout, per segment.
  • Shadow or canary on live traffic before full rollout.
  • Trigger options: scheduled (simple), drift/metric-triggered (responsive, needs good monitors), continual (rarely worth the validation risk).

stages.name: Run it as a loop
stages.html:
"Drift response is an operational loop, not an event."

  • Monitor labels-free signals (feature PSI, prediction distribution) daily; delayed-label metrics as they land.
  • Define time-to-detect and time-to-recover as SLOs.
  • Keep a runbook: check impostors → classify → localise → respond → gate.

followUps.question: Why not just retrain every night?
followUps.html:
Because it hides the diagnosis and can ship a regression.

Nightly retraining Why it fails
Pipeline break retrains on broken data
Concept drift needs new features, not new rows
No gate a regression ships quietly
No diagnosis you never learn why performance moves

A schedule is fine as a baseline cadence; each retrain still needs evaluation and a canary.

followUps.question: PSI says a feature drifted but performance is fine. Act?
followUps.html:
Not necessarily.

  • No action needed: drift in an unimportant feature, or drift the model handles well.
  • Weight alerts by feature importance.
  • Alert on prediction drift and performance, not raw PSI alone.

Otherwise the alerts become noise and get ignored.

followUps.question: Labels arrive 60 days late. How do you detect problems sooner?
followUps.html:
With signals that don't need the label.

Proxy Example
Label-free drift feature drift, prediction distribution shift
Early calibration against any early signal
Short-horizon proxy label 7-day engagement for 60-day churn
Faster business metrics ones that react before the label does

followUps.question: How much recent data should the retrain use?
followUps.html:
Trade freshness against sample size, and let a recent holdout decide.

Test:train on the last 3, 6 and 12 monthsscore each on a recent holdoutkeep the best, or weight recent data more

After concept drift, pre-change data can actively hurt, so a shorter window wins once there are enough post-change labels.

followUps.question: Who owns this loop?
followUps.html:
The team that owns the model, with on-call like any service.

Owner Owns
Model team detection and response
Upstream data owners data contracts: schema, freshness, ranges, so breaks are caught at the source

Without clear ownership, drift alerts are routed nowhere and time-to-recover is measured in months.

dontSay: "Set up a nightly retrain." — not a framework; it can ship regressions and hides causes.
"It's concept drift." (without evidence) — check impostors and label delay first.
"Retraining will fix it." — not for pipeline breaks, and not reliably for concept drift.
"Monitor accuracy." — labels may be late; you need label-free signals too.

spine: Suspect the label in the feature
Why high cardinality makes it worse
ml-dl-q15.testing: whether a suspiciously good result triggers an audit, not a celebration.
ml-dl-q15.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Suspect the label in the feature "Target encoding replaces each category with a statistic of the target itself, usually its mean. So if a row's own label contributed to its encoding, that feature partly is the answer, and a big AUC jump is often self-leakage rather than signal."
2 · Why high cardinality makes it worse "High cardinality makes it worse. With 5,000 levels, many appear only a handful of times, and a level seen once is encoded as exactly that row's label."
3 · Test it honestly "To test it, I'd check how the encoding was computed: if it was fit on the full training set, or before the CV split, the validation score is contaminated. I'd recompute it honestly and re-score, ideally on a time-ordered holdout, because random CV is exactly where this failure hides."
4 · Encode safely "The safe construction is out-of-fold encoding: each row is encoded using statistics from folds it isn't in, computed strictly inside each training fold. Rare levels get smoothing toward the global mean, weighted by how often the level appears, and unseen levels at serving time fall back to the prior."
5 · Handle rare and unseen levels "Then I'd compare against leak-free alternatives: frequency encoding, feature hashing, or CatBoost's ordered target statistics."
6 · Compare the leak-free alternatives "If the jump survives an honest time-split evaluation, I'll believe it."

stages.name: Suspect the label in the feature
stages.html:
"A feature built from the target is guilty until proven innocent."

  • Target encoding: city → mean(churned) for that city.
  • If computed using all rows, row i's encoding includes row i's own label.
  • The model learns "encoding high → label 1" partly because the encoding was made from the label.

stages.name: Why high cardinality makes it worse
stages.html:
"With 5,000 levels, most have few rows, and few rows means the encoding is the label."

Level count Encoding without smoothing
1 row exactly that row's label (0 or 1)
3 rows mean of 3 labels, heavily includes this row
10,000 rows stable; self-contribution negligible

The long tail of rare levels produces near-perfect separation on training data and nothing at serving time.

stages.name: Test it honestly
stages.html:
"I don't argue about it. I rebuild it properly and see if the jump survives."

  • Was the encoder fit before the split, or on the full training set outside CV? Then validation is contaminated.
  • Put the encoder inside the pipeline, fitted per fold, and re-score.
  • Re-score on a time-ordered holdout; random CV hides encoding leakage because the same levels and labels sit on both sides.
  • Compare to the same model with frequency encoding. A large gap that collapses under honest evaluation was leakage.

stages.name: Encode safely
stages.html:
"Each row's encoding must come from rows that aren't it, and from training data only."

Out-of-fold encoding. Split training data into k parts; encode each part using statistics from the other k−1. Default choice.

Leave-one-out. Encode each row with the level mean excluding itself. Cheaper but can still leak through the row's own absence; add noise.

  • Nest it: inside each CV training fold, run the out-of-fold encoding again. The validation fold is encoded with the full training fold's statistics.
  • sklearn's TargetEncoder (1.3+) does internal cross-fitting for fit_transform.

stages.name: Handle rare and unseen levels
stages.html:
"Rare levels shrink toward the global mean; unseen levels get the prior."

encoded = (n · level_mean + m · global_mean) / (n + m)
  • n = rows for the level, m = smoothing strength (tuned on validation).
  • Unseen at serving: use the global mean, or a parent-level mean if a hierarchy exists (city → region).
  • Optional Gaussian noise on training encodings adds regularisation.

stages.name: Compare the leak-free alternatives
stages.html:
Option Trade-off
Frequency / count encoding no leakage; captures popularity only
Feature hashing bounded width; collisions are a controlled cost
CatBoost ordered target statistics target encoding done safely by design
Entity embeddings good in neural models; need data per level
Group rare levels into "other" simple; loses tail information

followUps.question: Why doesn't random CV catch this?
followUps.html:
Because both sides of a random split carry the same levels with similar label patterns.

Encoder fitted What random CV sees
Before CV every fold's validation rows helped create the encoding
Per fold memorised level effects still look like generalisation

A time split shows whether level effects persist into the future.

followUps.question: Why not one-hot the 5,000 levels?
followUps.html:
For trees, one-hot on high cardinality is usually the worst option.

  • Size: 5,000 sparse columns inflate memory and training time.
  • Fit: most columns are nearly empty, so linear models overfit rare levels and trees struggle to split on them.
  • Serving: it breaks when new levels appear.

followUps.question: How does CatBoost avoid this leakage?
followUps.html:
Ordered target statistics: a row never sees its own label.

Encoding:shuffle rows into a random orderencode each row from the rows before it onlyrepeat over several permutations

The extra permutations reduce the variance this introduces. It's out-of-fold encoding taken to the limit.

followUps.question: The honest AUC is still higher than without the feature. Ship?
followUps.html:
Then the category has real signal, so yes, with conditions.

  • Smoothing tuned on validation.
  • A fallback for unseen levels.
  • Monitoring of the share of unseen levels in production.

If new levels arrive constantly (new merchants, new devices), the feature's value decays, so watch it.

followUps.question: How would you catch this class of bug in review?
followUps.html:
With a rule, a standard check and a tripwire.

Guard What it says
Review rule any feature derived from the target is computed inside the per-fold pipeline
Standard check train with and without the suspect feature on a time-split holdout
Tripwire a single feature that moves AUC by several points is a leakage suspect until audited

dontSay: "Great, target encoding really helped." — without an honest re-score, you don't know.
"I fit the encoder on the whole training set, then ran CV." — that's the leak.
"Rare levels are fine, the model will handle it." — rare levels encode their own labels.
"Unseen categories won't happen." — they always do in production.

spine: Offline data is biased by the old policy
ml-dl-q16.testing: whether you understand that logged data isn't a neutral test set for a ranking system.
ml-dl-q16.trap: trusting an offline ranking metric as the launch decision.
ml-dl-q16.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Offline data is biased by the old policy "Offline-up, online-down is expected in recommenders, and there are three classic mechanisms."
2 · Position bias "First, feedback-loop bias. The offline data was logged under the old model: users only clicked on what the old model showed. Items it never showed have no labels. So offline evaluation rewards agreeing with the old model more than being right, and a genuinely different ranker can look worse, or a subtly worse one better."
3 · Diversity collapse "Second, position bias. Clicks in logs are inflated for items that were shown near the top, regardless of relevance. NDCG on those clicks treats them as pure relevance. When the new model reshuffles positions, it loses that borrowed advantage."
4 · Rule out the boring causes "Third, diversity collapse. NDCG scores each list independently. A model that maximises it can converge on similar popular items. Users get staler, more repetitive feeds, and click less over a session, which per-query metrics can't see."
5 · Let the A/B decide "I'd also rule out the boring causes: train–serve skew in features, a latency regression that cut impressions, or a population mismatch between offline and online."
6 · Fix the evaluation loop "The rule is that offline metrics gate a launch and the online A/B decides it."
Close "Long term, I'd log propensities, the probability each item was shown, so offline evaluation can be corrected counterfactually."

stages.name: Offline data is biased by the old policy
stages.claim: you can only grade what was shown
stages.html:
"Logged data records the old model's choices, not the world."

Item Did the old model show it? Clicks in the log Offline label
popular item yes some relevant
near-duplicate of a popular item yes some relevant
fresh long-tail item the new model likes no none possible counted as irrelevant
  • Users click only among items the old model displayed.
  • Items the new model wants to show but the old model never did have no labels, so they count as irrelevant offline.
  • Offline evaluation therefore favours rankers that imitate the old one. This is the off-policy evaluation problem.

Example: a new model that surfaces fresh long-tail content scores poorly offline because the logs contain no clicks on it.

stages.name: Position bias
stages.claim: clicks measure rank, not just relevance
stages.html:
"Rank 1 gets clicks because it's rank 1."

  • Click-through falls sharply with position regardless of quality.
  • Logged clicks at high positions overstate relevance; NDCG treats them as ground truth.
  • The new model moves items; those items lose the positional boost they had in the logs.
  • Fix direction: estimate position propensities and reweight clicks (inverse propensity scoring), or use randomised position experiments to measure the bias.

stages.name: Diversity collapse
stages.html:
"NDCG rewards each list; users experience the feed."

  • Optimising per-query relevance can concentrate on popular, near-duplicate items.
  • Users see repetition, get bored, and click less across the session.
  • Novelty, coverage and diversity metrics, plus session-level engagement, catch it; NDCG doesn't.

stages.name: Rule out the boring causes
stages.html:
Check Why
Train–serve skew online features differ from offline replay
Latency regression slower ranking → fewer impressions → lower CTR
Population mismatch offline NDCG on all users; CTR dominated by heavy users
Candidate generation online candidate set differs from what offline ranked
Metric definition CTR counted differently after the deploy

stages.name: Let the A/B decide
stages.html:
"Offline metrics are a filter, never a verdict."

  • A/B test on the business metric (CTR, engagement, retention), long enough to see novelty effects fade.
  • Interleaving (mix results from both rankers in one list) detects preference with far less traffic, useful for comparing many candidates.
  • Guardrail metrics: latency, diversity, revenue.

stages.name: Fix the evaluation loop
stages.html:
"Log what you need for counterfactual evaluation."

  • Log propensities: the probability each item was shown at each position.
  • Use IPS / doubly robust estimators to evaluate new policies offline.
  • Reserve a small exploration slice (randomised items) so logs contain data outside the current policy.
  • Track diversity and coverage alongside NDCG.

followUps.question: How does inverse propensity scoring work here?
followUps.html:
Each logged click is weighted by how unlikely it was to be shown.

weight = 1 / P(item shown at that position | logging policy)
  • Effect: rarely shown items get large weights, correcting for their few chances to be clicked.
  • Catch: unbiased in expectation but high-variance, so clip the weights or use a doubly robust estimator.

followUps.question: CTR dropped but time-on-site rose. Did the model fail?
followUps.html:
Not necessarily. CTR may be the wrong north-star metric.

Possible story:fewer, better clicksusers find what they want faster, or engage more deeply

I'd check the downstream metrics (conversions, retention, dwell time) and agree with product which metric the ranker should serve.

followUps.question: Why not just train on more logged data to fix it?
followUps.html:
More data from the same policy carries the same bias.

Loop:old ranker decides what is shownonly shown items get clicksmodel learns to imitate the old ranker
Data from outside the policy
Exploration traffic a slice of users sees other items
Randomisation positions shuffled
Counterfactual reweighting logged data re-weighted

followUps.question: How long should the A/B test run?
followUps.html:
Long enough for statistical power and to see past novelty: usually one to two full weekly cycles at least.

  • Power: on the primary metric.
  • Novelty or primacy: check the effect over time; a gain that decays after a week was novelty.
  • Peeking: pre-register the metric and the duration.

followUps.question: How do you add diversity without hurting relevance too much?
followUps.html:
Re-rank the top candidates with a diversity-aware step.

Pipeline:rank by relevancetake the top candidatesdiversity-aware re-rankfinal list

The re-rank step is maximal marginal relevance or a determinantal point process.

It trades a little per-item relevance for coverage. Tune the trade-off with online tests: the right balance depends on how users react, not on offline NDCG.

dontSay: "NDCG went up, so the model is better." — offline data is biased toward the old policy.
"Users are being irrational." — position and presentation effects are predictable.
"Retrain on more click logs." — same bias, more of it.
"Offline metrics should decide launches." — they gate; A/B decides.

ml-dl-q17.testing: whether you say "chain rule" and "reuse" in the same breath.
ml-dl-q17.trap: "the error propagates backwards through the network" with no mechanism.
ml-dl-q17.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Chain rule over a graph "Backpropagation is the chain rule applied to a computation graph, run in reverse, with the intermediate results reused."
2 · Forward pass caches "A network is a chain of simple operations, each of which knows its own local derivative. In the forward pass, I compute the output and the loss, and cache every intermediate activation."
3 · Backward pass reuses "In the backward pass, I start from the loss and walk the graph in reverse. Each operation receives the gradient of the loss with respect to its output, multiplies it by its local derivative, and passes the result to its inputs. When I reach a weight, that product is the weight's gradient."
4 · Why it's cheap "It's dynamic programming: each upstream gradient is computed once and reused by everything below it. That's why one backward sweep gives the gradient for every parameter at roughly the cost of two forward passes, no matter how many parameters there are."
5 · What it isn't "Two clarifications. Backprop only computes gradients; the optimiser, like SGD or Adam, decides how to update."
Close "And because the forward activations must be kept for the backward pass, activations, not weights, dominate training memory, which is what gradient checkpointing trades back for recompute."

stages.name: Chain rule over a graph
stages.html:
"A network is a composition of functions; its derivative is a product of local derivatives."

x ──W1──▶ h = σ(W1·x) ──W2──▶ ŷ ──▶ L(ŷ, y)

∂L/∂W1 = ∂L/∂ŷ · ∂ŷ/∂h · ∂h/∂W1

Every operation (matmul, add, ReLU, softmax) implements two things: forward, and "given dL/d(output), return dL/d(inputs)".

stages.name: Forward pass caches
stages.claim: keep what the backward pass will need
stages.html:
"The forward pass computes the loss and stores every intermediate value."

  • Local derivatives depend on forward values: ReLU needs to know which inputs were positive; matmul needs the input activations.
  • So activations are cached per layer, per example in the batch.

stages.name: Backward pass reuses
stages.html:
"Walk the graph in reverse; each node multiplies and passes down."

  • Start with ∂L/∂L = 1.
  • Each node: receive upstream gradient → multiply by its local Jacobian → send to its inputs.
  • Where a value feeds several nodes, gradients from each path are summed.
  • At a parameter, the arriving gradient is ∂L/∂θ.

stages.name: Why it's cheap
stages.html:
"One backward sweep yields every parameter's gradient."

Mode Cost for gradient of one scalar loss w.r.t. n parameters
Finite differences n+1 forward passes
Forward-mode autodiff ~n passes (one per input direction)
Reverse-mode (backprop) ~2–3× one forward pass, independent of n

This is memoisation: each intermediate gradient is computed once and shared.

stages.name: What it isn't
stages.html:
"Backprop computes gradients. The optimiser uses them."

  • SGD, Momentum, Adam and AdamW are separate, swappable components.
  • Backprop also doesn't guarantee good gradients: vanishing and exploding gradients are properties of the network, which backprop faithfully computes.

stages.name: The memory consequence
stages.html:
"Training memory is mostly cached activations, which is why batch size and sequence length drive it."

  • Activation memory grows with batch × sequence length × depth × width.
  • Gradient (activation) checkpointing: store only some activations, recompute the rest during the backward pass. Trades compute for memory.
  • Inference needs no cache for gradients, which is why inference fits where training doesn't.

followUps.question: Why do activations dominate training memory?
followUps.html:
Because the backward pass needs the forward values, so every layer's activations are kept until it reaches them.

Stored Scales with
Weights once model size
Activations per layer, for the whole batch batch size × sequence length × depth

Checkpointing recomputes activations instead of storing them.

followUps.question: Why reverse mode and not forward mode?
followUps.html:
One scalar loss, millions of parameters.

Mode Cost For a neural network
Reverse one sweep per output 1 sweep
Forward one sweep per input direction millions of sweeps

Forward mode wins only with few inputs and many outputs.

followUps.question: What happens to the gradient at a ReLU?
followUps.html:
It passes through or it is blocked.

dReLU/dx = 1  if x > 0     ← gradient passes unchanged
         = 0  if x < 0     ← gradient blocked
         = 0  at x = 0     ← undefined; frameworks pick 0 by convention

A unit whose input is always negative gets zero gradient forever: a dead ReLU.

followUps.question: Is backprop how the brain learns?
followUps.html:
Probably not directly, and that's irrelevant to engineering.

  • Biology lacks: symmetric backward weights and a separate backward phase, which backprop needs.
  • For us: backprop is an exact, efficient algorithm for computing gradients of a differentiable program.

followUps.question: How does autograd in PyTorch implement this?
followUps.html:
It records a graph on the way forward and walks it in reverse.

Autograd:forward pass records a dynamic graph with saved tensorsloss.backward() walks it in reverse topological ordereach op's backward function runsgradients accumulate into .grad
  • Accumulate is why you zero gradients between steps.
  • Saved tensors are why in-place ops on them raise errors.

dontSay: "The error flows back through the network." (alone) — no mechanism.
"Backprop is how the network learns." — it computes gradients; the optimiser learns.
"It's expensive because it computes each gradient separately." — the point is reuse.
"Weights take most of the training memory." — activations do.

links.label: Optimizer Family
links.target: 02-DL/05-Training Mechanics that make transformers work/08-Optimizer Family

ml-dl-q18.testing: whether you can derive the mechanism from the chain rule, not just name it.
ml-dl-q18.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Name it "That's vanishing gradients, and it falls straight out of backprop."
2 · Mechanism "The gradient reaching layer 1 is a product of one factor per layer above it: the layer's weights times the activation's derivative. The sigmoid's derivative is at most 0.25, and much smaller when the unit saturates. Multiply twelve of those and the gradient at the bottom is orders of magnitude smaller than at the top. The same product explodes if the weight scales sit above one; vanishing and exploding are two ends of one mechanism."
3 · Confirm "I'd confirm it by logging per-layer gradient norms: a clean exponential decay toward the input is the signature."
4 · Fix "Then the fixes, in order. One: ReLU-family activations, whose derivative is 1 in the positive region. Two: variance-preserving initialisation, He for ReLU. Three: normalisation layers to keep activations in a healthy range. And for real depth, residual connections, which give the gradient an identity path around each layer."
5 · Verify "After the fix, the per-layer gradient norms should sit within an order of magnitude of each other."
Close "Raising the learning rate doesn't fix it; it just destabilises the top layers."

stages.name: Name it: vanishing gradients
stages.html:
"Symptom pattern: last layers' weights change, first layers' weights stay near their initial values."

What you see Why
Loss decreases slowly and plateaus early only the top few layers are actually learning
Early layers act like fixed random features their gradient is too small to move the weights
Happens with sigmoid or tanh in deep plain stacks those activations shrink the signal at every layer

stages.name: The multiplicative mechanism
stages.html:
"The gradient at layer 1 multiplies one Jacobian per layer above it."

∂L/∂h₁ = ∂L/∂h₁₂ · Π (k = 2…12) [ W_k · σ'(z_k) ]     ← one factor per layer above
σ'(z)  ≤ 0.25                                          ← the sigmoid's best case, at z = 0
0.25¹¹ ≈ 2.4 × 10⁻⁷                                    ← eleven layers, before the weights

What the product does to the gradient on its way down (sigmoid's best case, weights ignored):

Layers passed Factor Gradient left
1 0.25 25%
3 0.25³ 1.6%
6 0.25⁶ 0.024%
11 0.25¹¹ 0.000024%
  • Saturated units (large |z|) have σ' ≈ 0, which makes it worse.
  • If the per-layer factor is above 1, the same product explodes.

stages.name: Confirm with per-layer gradient norms
stages.html:
"Log the gradient norm of each layer's weights for a few steps."

Pattern Diagnosis
Exponential decay toward input vanishing gradients
Exponential growth, NaNs, loss spikes exploding gradients
Uniform but tiny everywhere learning rate or loss scaling issue
One layer near zero dead units or a bug in that layer

Also check activation statistics: sigmoid outputs pinned near 0 or 1 mean saturation.

stages.name: Fix: activations, init, normalisation, residuals
stages.html:
"Four fixes, cheapest first. Each one protects the gradient's scale in a different way."

# Fix What it does to the product Note
1 ReLU-family activation derivative is 1 for positive inputs, so no per-layer shrink Leaky ReLU or GELU avoid dead units
2 Variance-preserving init He (variance 2/fan_in) for ReLU, Xavier for tanh: scale is stable at the start needed with any activation
3 Normalisation BatchNorm or LayerNorm keeps pre-activations centred, so units don't saturate also speeds training
4 Residual connections h = x + f(x) adds an identity path the gradient takes around each block what made very deep networks trainable

Gradient clipping helps the exploding case, not vanishing.

stages.name: Verify
stages.html:
"After the fix, per-layer gradient norms should be within an order of magnitude of each other, and the first layers' weights should move."

Re-check Healthy reading
Per-layer gradient norms roughly flat across depth
Training curve loss keeps falling, no early plateau
Early-layer weights change meaningfully across epochs

followUps.question: Which fix made truly deep networks possible?
followUps.html:
Residual connections.

h = x + f(x)
∂h/∂x = I + ∂f/∂x      ← the identity term carries the gradient even when ∂f/∂x is small

That took networks from tens of layers to hundreds, and it's the backbone of every transformer.

followUps.question: Why not just increase the learning rate for early layers?
followUps.html:
Because a fixed rate can't track a ratio that is 10⁶ or more and keeps changing.

Idea Why it falls short
Fixed per-layer rate the ratio between layers moves during training
Large global rate destabilises the top layers
Adam normalises per-parameter scale, but doesn't fix signal loss in the forward pass

Fix the architecture.

followUps.question: Does ReLU have its own failure mode?
followUps.html:
Yes: dead ReLUs.

Mechanism:input always negativeoutput 0gradient 0the unit never recovers
  • Causes: a high learning rate, poor initialisation.
  • Reduce it: Leaky ReLU, GELU, careful init.
  • Monitor: the fraction of units that never activate.

followUps.question: How does this relate to RNNs forgetting long sequences?
followUps.html:
Same mechanism, worse.

12-layer MLP RNN over 500 steps
Product of 12 different Jacobians the same recurrent Jacobian, 500 times
Result vanishes vanishes or explodes faster
Fix residual connection LSTM's additive cell path

Both fixes add a path the gradient can travel without being multiplied away.

followUps.question: Where does BatchNorm cause problems?
followUps.html:
Wherever batch statistics are unreliable.

Case Problem
Small batches noisy statistics
Variable-length sequences statistics mix real and padded positions
Inference wrong running statistics, or eval mode not set

That's why transformers use LayerNorm: it normalises per example and doesn't depend on the batch.

dontSay: "The learning rate is too low." — the ratio between layers is the problem, not the global scale.
"Add more layers so it learns better." — deepens the product that's vanishing.
"Use gradient clipping." — that's for exploding gradients.
"Sigmoid is fine if you train longer." — the early layers' signal is gone, not slow.

ml-dl-q19.testing: whether you can give the mechanism, not "it just works better".
ml-dl-q19.trap: "cross-entropy is for classification, MSE is for regression" with no reason.
ml-dl-q19.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The principled reason: maximum likelihood "Two reasons: one statistical, one about gradients. The statistical reason: a classifier outputs a probability distribution, and cross-entropy is the negative log-likelihood of the true label under that distribution. Minimising it is maximum-likelihood estimation for a Bernoulli or categorical model, the principled loss for probability outputs."
2 · The gradient mechanism "The gradient reason is the one interviewers want. Take a sigmoid output p. With MSE, the gradient with respect to the logit is (p − y) times σ'(z). That σ' term goes to zero when the sigmoid saturates, which happens exactly when the model is confidently wrong: say it predicts 0.001 for a true positive. The error is huge, but the gradient is tiny, so learning stalls. With cross-entropy, the σ' cancels, and the gradient with respect to the logit is simply p − y. Big error, big step. The same holds for softmax with categorical cross-entropy."
4 · Landscape and penalties "Cross-entropy also punishes confident wrong answers heavily, because log p goes to minus infinity, which is the behaviour you want."
5 · The practical corollary "The practical corollary: use the fused, numerically stable loss that takes logits, like BCEWithLogitsLoss or CrossEntropyLoss, never a hand-written log of a softmax."

stages.name: The principled reason: maximum likelihood
stages.html:
"Cross-entropy is what you get when you ask for the most likely parameters."

  • Binary: L = −[y log p + (1−y) log(1−p)], the negative log-likelihood of a Bernoulli.
  • Multiclass: L = −log p_true, the NLL of a categorical.
  • Equivalent to minimising KL divergence from the label distribution to the model's.
  • MSE is the NLL of a Gaussian, the right assumption for continuous targets, not labels.

stages.name: The gradient mechanism
stages.html:
"Differentiate both through the sigmoid and look at what's left."

p = σ(z)

MSE:  L = ½(p − y)²          ∂L/∂z = (p − y) · σ'(z)
CE:   L = −y log p − ...     ∂L/∂z = (p − y)

The σ'(z) = p(1−p) factor is what MSE keeps and cross-entropy cancels.

stages.name: Where MSE stalls
stages.html:
Case p y MSE ∂L/∂z CE ∂L/∂z
Confidently wrong 0.001 1 ≈ −0.999 × 0.001 ≈ −0.001 −0.999
Unsure 0.5 1 −0.5 × 0.25 = −0.125 −0.5
Confidently right 0.999 1 ≈ 0 ≈ −0.001

The worst mistakes get the weakest correction under MSE. That's the killer argument.

stages.name: Landscape and penalties
stages.html:
• For logistic regression, CE is convex in the weights; MSE through a sigmoid is not, with flat plateaus.
  • CE's penalty grows without bound as p → 0 for the true class, so confident errors dominate the loss.
  • MSE caps the per-example loss at 1, treating a confident error almost like an unsure one.

stages.name: The practical corollary
stages.html:
"Pass logits to the fused loss; never compute log(softmax(x)) by hand."

  • BCEWithLogitsLoss, CrossEntropyLoss (PyTorch) use the log-sum-exp trick internally.
  • Hand-composed log(softmax) underflows to log(0) = −inf for large logits.
  • Label smoothing is a small, useful modification when models become overconfident.

followUps.question: Is MSE ever acceptable for classification?
followUps.html:
It can work, but cross-entropy is the default for good reasons. Use MSE only with evidence.

MSE on a classifier Cross-entropy
Likelihood reading lost yes
Gradient at the logits not the clean form p − y
Calibration tends to be poor better

It can be competitive with a linear output and well-scaled targets, and some work has shown that.

followUps.question: What does label smoothing do to cross-entropy?
followUps.html:
It softens the target, so the model stops pushing logits to infinity.

target = (1 − ε) on the true class, ε spread over the others
  • Gain: less overconfidence; often better calibration and generalisation.
  • Cost: the probabilities no longer target the true frequencies exactly.

followUps.question: Why is log(softmax) numerically dangerous?
followUps.html:
Because the two steps done separately overflow or underflow before the log.

Logit softmax then log
very large exp(1000) overflows NaN
very negative underflows to 0 −inf, gradient NaN
Fix:subtract the max logitcompute log-softmax directly (log-sum-exp)fused losses do this for you

followUps.question: Cross-entropy with severe class imbalance?
followUps.html:
Plain cross-entropy is dominated by the majority class.

Option What it does
Class-weighted CE raises the cost of minority errors
Focal loss down-weights easy, well-classified examples so training focuses on hard ones

Both distort probabilities, so recalibrate if scores are used as probabilities.

followUps.question: How does this connect to LLM training?
followUps.html:
LLMs are trained with exactly this loss: next-token cross-entropy over the vocabulary.

loss       = −log p(true next token)       ← averaged over positions
perplexity = exp(average cross-entropy)
∂loss/∂z   = p − y                         ← the same clean gradient at the logits

That gradient property is why the objective trains stably at scale.

followUps.question: Why not train directly on accuracy, since that's what we report?
followUps.html:
Accuracy has no usable gradient.

Accuracy Cross-entropy
As a function of the weights a step function smooth and differentiable
Gradient zero almost everywhere, undefined at the flips informative everywhere
Rewards only being right confidence in the right answer

Report accuracy, optimise cross-entropy.

dontSay: "Cross-entropy just works better." — no mechanism.
"MSE is for regression, CE for classification, that's the rule." — a rule, not a reason.
"I compute softmax then take the log." — numerically unstable.
"The two losses give the same gradients." — MSE carries σ', CE doesn't.

spine: The layer collapses to one neuron
ml-dl-q20.testing: whether you separate breaking symmetry, setting scale, and determinism.
ml-dl-q20.trap: confusing reproducibility with a constant initial value.
ml-dl-q20.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Symmetry never breaks "The network won't learn anything useful, because of symmetry. If every weight in a layer starts at zero, every neuron in that layer computes the same output and receives exactly the same gradient. They update identically, so they stay identical forever. A layer of 512 units behaves like a single unit repeated 512 times. With ReLU it's even worse: zero inputs give zero outputs and zero gradients, so nothing moves. Any constant has the symmetry problem, not just zero."
3 · What init is really for "Random initialisation breaks the symmetry. But the real job of initialisation is scale: keeping the variance of activations and gradients stable from layer to layer, so signals neither vanish nor explode before training even starts. That's what the named schemes do. Xavier or Glorot scales by fan-in and fan-out and suits tanh or sigmoid. He initialisation uses variance 2 over fan-in for ReLU, where the factor of two compensates for ReLU zeroing half its inputs."
5 · Get reproducibility the right way "As for reproducibility, that comes from seeding: fix the seeds for Python, NumPy and the framework, and enable deterministic kernels where needed."
Close "A seeded random init is perfectly reproducible and actually trains."

stages.name: Symmetry never breaks
stages.html:
"Same weights → same outputs → same gradients → same updates, forever."

h₁ = h₂ = σ(w·x + b)              ← same weights, so every unit in the layer outputs the same value
∂L/∂w₁ = ∂L/∂w₂                   ← same output, so the same gradient
w₁ − η·∂L/∂w₁ = w₂ − η·∂L/∂w₂     ← still identical after the update: the layer is one neuron
  • All hidden units in a layer compute w·x + b with the same w: identical outputs.
  • Backprop gives each the same gradient.
  • After the update they're still identical. No step can ever separate them.
  • With zeros specifically, many gradients are exactly zero too (e.g. through ReLU, or the product of zero weights).

stages.name: The layer collapses to one neuron
stages.html:
"Effective capacity = one unit per layer, whatever the width."

Setting Result
Zero init, ReLU outputs 0, gradients 0: nothing trains
Zero init, sigmoid all units output 0.5; they move, but together
Constant c ≠ 0 symmetric, same collapse
Only biases zero, weights random fine; common practice

stages.name: What init is really for
stages.html:
"Randomness breaks symmetry; the scale is what the schemes are about."

goal:    Var(layer output) ≈ Var(layer input)     ← signal neither explodes nor dies with depth
Xavier:  Var(w) = 2 / (fan_in + fan_out)          ← tanh, sigmoid
He:      Var(w) = 2 / fan_in                      ← ReLU, which zeroes half its inputs
  • Too large → activations and gradients explode through layers.
  • Too small → they shrink toward zero: vanishing signal before training starts.
  • Target: Var(output of a layer) ≈ Var(input), and similarly for gradients going backwards.

stages.name: Pick the scheme by activation
stages.html:
Scheme Variance Use with
Xavier / Glorot 2 / (fan_in + fan_out) tanh, sigmoid (symmetric around 0)
He / Kaiming 2 / fan_in ReLU family (half the inputs zeroed)
Scaled residual init output projections scaled down by depth transformers: start close to identity

Framework defaults are usually sensible; check them when using unusual activations.

stages.name: Get reproducibility the right way
stages.html:
"Determinism is a property of the run, not of the initial values."

  • Seed Python random, NumPy, and the framework (torch.manual_seed), including data-loader workers.
  • Enable deterministic algorithms (torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)) where exact repeatability matters; some GPU ops are otherwise non-deterministic.
  • Log seeds, library versions and hardware with each run.

followUps.question: Is initialising biases to zero also a problem?
followUps.html:
No. The random weights break symmetry, so zero biases are the standard default.

Variant Why
Small positive bias on ReLU layers avoids dead units at the start
Output bias = log of the class prior speeds up early training

followUps.question: Why the factor of 2 in He initialisation?
followUps.html:
ReLU zeroes about half its inputs, which halves the signal's variance. The 2 puts it back.

Var(W) = 2 / fan_in      ← He: output variance of each layer matches its input variance

Without it, the signal shrinks by half per layer.

followUps.question: With good initialisation, do we still need BatchNorm?
followUps.html:
Yes for deep networks: they do different jobs.

Tool When it acts
Initialisation sets good statistics at step zero
Normalisation keeps them good as the weights change
Residual connections carry the signal through depth

Some architectures train without normalisation using careful init and scaling, but that's the exception.

followUps.question: Two seeded runs still give slightly different results. Why?
followUps.html:
Because a seed doesn't control everything that's random or order-dependent.

Source Fix
Non-deterministic GPU kernels (atomic adds in some convolutions and scatter ops) enable deterministic algorithms
Multi-threaded data loading fix worker seeds
Library or driver versions pin them
Different hardware expect small floating-point differences even then

followUps.question: How does initialisation work when fine-tuning a pretrained model?
followUps.html:
The pretrained weights are the initialisation; only new layers start fresh.

  • New head: initialised small, so it doesn't disrupt the pretrained features.
  • LoRA adapter: one matrix random, the other zero.
Zero side:one matrix starts at zerothe product is zerothe adapter begins as a no-op
Random side:the other matrix is randomgradients differ per unitsymmetry is still broken

dontSay: "Zero init is fine, the optimiser will fix it." — identical neurons stay identical.
"Reproducibility needs constant initial weights." — seeds give reproducibility.
"Any random init works." — scale matters; badly scaled init vanishes or explodes.
"Only zero is a problem." — any constant has the same symmetry.

ml-dl-q21.testing: whether you know inverted dropout precisely enough to predict the bug's symptom.
ml-dl-q21.trap: chasing a data bug when the symptom is run-to-run variance on the same input.
ml-dl-q21.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · What train mode does "In train mode, dropout zeroes each unit with probability p on every forward pass and scales the survivors by 1 over 1 minus p. That's inverted dropout. The scaling keeps the expected activation the same as without dropout, and randomly removing units stops them co-adapting; effectively you train a shifting ensemble of sub-networks."
2 · What eval mode must be "Because the scaling already happened at training time, eval mode should be the identity: no zeroing, no scaling, fully deterministic, using the whole network."
3 · What leaving it on does "If dropout is left on at evaluation, every forward pass samples a different random sub-network. The same input gives different predictions on each run, and average quality drops, because each prediction comes from a thinned network rather than the full one."
4 · The symptom and its twin "That's exactly the classic symptom: two 'identical' evaluation runs give different numbers with no data, code or seed change. BatchNorm is the twin bug: in train mode it normalises with the current batch's statistics instead of the running averages, so predictions depend on what else is in the batch."
5 · Fix and guard "The fix is model.eval() before evaluation, which flips both, plus torch.no_grad() or inference mode."
Close "And I'd guard it: an evaluation helper that sets eval mode itself, and a test asserting two passes on the same input match."

stages.name: What train mode does
stages.html:
"Each forward pass drops units at random and scales up the rest."

train:  h' = h · mask / (1 − p)      mask ~ Bernoulli(1 − p)
        E[h'] = h                    (expected value preserved)
  • Prevents co-adaptation: units can't rely on specific partners.
  • Interpretable as training an ensemble of 2^n sub-networks with shared weights.

stages.name: What eval mode must be
stages.html:
"Because scaling happened in training, evaluation is just the full network."

train:  h̃ = m ⊙ h / (1 − p),   m ~ Bernoulli(1 − p)   ← drop with probability p, rescale the rest
        E[h̃] = h                                      ← the rescale keeps the expected value
eval:   h̃ = h                                         ← no mask, no scaling, deterministic
  • No mask, no scaling, deterministic.
  • (Original, non-inverted dropout scaled at test time instead; modern frameworks use inverted dropout so inference needs no change.)

stages.name: What leaving it on does
stages.html:
"Each prediction comes from a different thinned network."

Effect Why
Different output each run on the same input new random mask per forward pass
Lower average accuracy each thinned network is weaker than the full one
Noisier metrics across evaluation runs variance from masks, not from data
Surprising in production users see non-deterministic answers

stages.name: The symptom and its twin
stages.html:
"Non-reproducible eval numbers with nothing changed is the fingerprint."

Layer In train mode In eval mode If left in train mode at inference
Dropout random mask, rescaled identity noisy, non-reproducible predictions
BatchNorm uses this batch's mean and variance uses running averages output depends on who else is in the batch; batch size 1 can break
  • BatchNorm in train mode uses the batch's mean and variance, not the running averages. Predictions depend on batch composition and batch size; batch size 1 can break outright.
  • Both are flipped by model.eval(); both are forgotten by the same mistake.

stages.name: Fix and guard
stages.html:
"Fix the call, then make it impossible to forget."

  • model.eval() + torch.no_grad() (or torch.inference_mode()) for every evaluation and serving path.
  • Evaluation helper functions set the mode themselves and restore it after.
  • Test: two forward passes on the same input must be identical in eval mode.
  • Serving: export the model in eval mode (TorchScript/ONNX export after .eval()).

followUps.question: Is dropout at inference ever intentional?
followUps.html:
Yes: Monte Carlo dropout.

Method:dropout onmany forward passesaverage the predictionstheir spread is the uncertainty estimate
Monte Carlo dropout The bug
Passes many, averaged one
Intent deliberate and documented accidental

followUps.question: Why is dropout often zero in large LLM pretraining?
followUps.html:
Because single-epoch pretraining underfits: the data scale is the regulariser.

Phase Sees an example Dropout
Pretraining on a huge corpus once: little memorisation to prevent often zero; it would slow learning
Fine-tuning on small data many times: overfitting is real back on

followUps.question: Does torch.no_grad() turn off dropout?
followUps.html:
No. They control different things, and you need both.

Call Controls Gives you
torch.no_grad() gradient tracking speed and memory
model.eval() the training flag that Dropout and BatchNorm read correct behaviour

followUps.question: Where does dropout sit in a transformer?
followUps.html:
In three places, all switched off by the same model.eval().

  • Attention weights.
  • Sub-layer outputs: after attention and after the feed-forward block, before the residual add.
  • Embeddings.

followUps.question: How would you catch this in CI?
followUps.html:
With a determinism test on the evaluation and serving paths.

Test:load the model through the service's own coderun the same input twiceassert identical outputs

Also assert model.training is False at the serving entry point. Cheap tests, and they catch both the dropout and the BatchNorm versions.

dontSay: "Dropout at eval just adds a bit of noise." — it evaluates a weaker random sub-network.
"Scale the outputs by (1 − p) at test time." — not with inverted dropout; you'd double-scale.
"no_grad fixes it." — it doesn't touch dropout.
"Must be a data-loading bug." — the same input varying is the dropout fingerprint.
