spine: Gap vs no gap: two diseases
Open with the one-batch overfit test
Model B: optimisation or bug path
ml-dl-q22.testing: whether "loss is high" triggers a structured triage, not random tuning.
ml-dl-q22.trap: treating both as one diagnosis, or tuning hyperparameters before checking the pipeline works.
ml-dl-q22.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Gap vs no gap: two diseases "They're two different diseases."
2 · Open with the one-batch overfit test "Model A, train 0.1 and validation 2.3, has a huge gap: it has memorised the training set. Model B, stuck at 2.3 on both, has no gap: it isn't learning at all, which is underfitting or a broken pipeline."
3 · Model A: variance path "For both, my first move is the same five-minute experiment: try to overfit a single small batch to near-zero loss. If the model can't, there's a bug: in the loss, the labels, the architecture wiring or the data pipeline, and no tuning will help."
4 · Model B: optimisation or bug path "For model A, the gap path: first rule out a bad validation set, like leakage, a distribution mismatch or mislabelled data. Then more or better data and augmentation, then regularisation: weight decay, dropout, early stopping on validation loss, and a smaller model last."
5 · Read the loss against baselines "For model B, the no-gap path: sweep the learning rate first, since it's the most common cause in both directions. Check the labels are aligned with the inputs and actually learnable, check input normalisation and the loss wiring, and only then add capacity or training time."
6 · Verify each fix "I'd also read the number itself."
Close "2.3 is suspiciously close to ln(10), the loss of uniform guessing over ten classes, which would mean model B has learned nothing."

stages.name: Gap vs no gap: two diseases
stages.html:
Model Train Val Reading
A 0.1 2.3 memorisation: high variance
B 2.3 2.3 not learning: bias, optimisation or a bug

"The gap is the first split. Everything after depends on it."

stages.name: Open with the one-batch overfit test
stages.html:
"Take 8–32 examples, turn off regularisation, train until loss → ~0."

Result Meaning
Loss goes to ~0 the model and pipeline can learn; problem is data or optimisation scale
Loss plateaus above 0 bug: labels misaligned, wrong loss, frozen layers, broken data pipeline

Five minutes, and it separates "broken" from "undertuned" before you waste a day on hyperparameters.

stages.name: Model A: variance path
stages.html:
Step 0 — Check the validation set. Leakage between train and val (duplicates), distribution mismatch, noisy val labels.

Step 1 — Data. More examples, better labels, augmentation.

Step 2 — Regularise. Weight decay, dropout, early stopping on validation loss.

Step 3 — Capacity. Smaller model or fewer features, last.

Watch the validation loss curve: if it bottomed out early and rose, early stopping alone recovers a lot.

stages.name: Model B: optimisation or bug path
stages.html:
"If the one-batch test passes, it's usually the learning rate."

  • LR sweep (or LR range test): too low → flat; too high → noisy plateau or divergence.
    Point What it means
    Labels shuffled independently of inputs? Wrong class mapping?
    Inputs normalised? Any NaNs or constant features?
    Loss wiring softmax applied twice? Logits passed where probabilities expected? Wrong reduction?
    Architecture frozen layers, dead ReLUs, vanishing gradients (check per-layer gradient norms).
  • Then capacity and training time.

stages.name: Read the loss against baselines
stages.html:
"Compare the loss with what trivial predictors score."

Baseline Cross-entropy
Uniform over K classes ln K (ln 10 ≈ 2.30, ln 50,000 ≈ 10.8)
Predicting class frequencies entropy of the label distribution

A loss sitting exactly at ln K means the model outputs uniform probabilities: a bug or zero learning.

stages.name: Verify each fix
stages.html:
• Change one thing, re-run, compare curves.
  • A: validation loss should fall while train rises slightly.
  • B: training loss should start dropping below the trivial baseline within the first epochs.

followUps.question: Why is the one-batch overfit test so valuable?
followUps.html:
It turns a vague "not learning" into a yes/no question in minutes.

One batch Meaning
Memorised the wiring works; the problem is generalisation or tuning
Not memorised gradients don't reach the right place, or the targets are wrong

Any correctly wired model with enough capacity can memorise a handful of examples.

followUps.question: Model A's validation set came from a different source. Does the plan change?
followUps.html:
Yes. The gap may be distribution shift, and regularisation won't close a shift.

Check:compare input distributions between the setsvalidate on a split from the training sourceit's shift

The fix is then representative training data or domain adaptation.

followUps.question: The learning rate sweep didn't help model B. Next?
followUps.html:
Go back to data and wiring.

Check Looking for
Input-label pairs, by eye wrong or shuffled targets
Loss function's expected input logits vs probabilities
Optimiser's parameter list does it actually hold the model's parameters?
Gradient norm per layer vanishing or zero gradients

followUps.question: Should I just add dropout to model B too?
followUps.html:
No. Regularisation is for a gap, and model B has none.

Symptom Disease Treatment
Low train loss, high val loss overfitting regularise
High loss on both underfitting or broken optimisation less regularisation, fix optimisation, add capacity

Dropout raises bias and would make B worse.

followUps.question: What's the LLM-era version of model A?
followUps.html:
Duplication and contamination, not classic overfitting.

Setting The gap disease Fix
Single-epoch pretraining data duplication or benchmark contamination: the model has seen test-like text deduplication and contamination checks, not dropout
Fine-tuning on small data classic overfitting returns regularise, stop early

dontSay: "Both have high loss, so tune the hyperparameters." — two diseases, two paths.
"Add regularisation to both." — makes model B worse.
"Train model B for longer." — first prove it can learn at all.
"2.3 is just a high loss." — it's the uniform-guessing baseline for 10 classes.

links.label: LR Schedules & the Loss Landscape
links.target: 02-DL/05-Training Mechanics that make transformers work/09-LR Schedules & the Loss Landscape

ml-dl-q23.testing: the multiplicative argument, and why it's worse than depth in an MLP.
ml-dl-q23.trap: "RNNs have short memory" with no mechanism.
ml-dl-q23.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Unroll in time: BPTT "The forgetting is a training problem: the gradient from the end of the document can't reach the beginning."
2 · One matrix, multiplied T times "To train an RNN, you unroll it over the sequence, which turns it into a very deep network with one layer per time step, and backpropagate through time. The gradient from step T back to step 1 is a product of T Jacobians, one per step, and they all involve the same recurrent weight matrix."
3 · Vanish vs explode "Multiplying by the same matrix hundreds of times is worse than a deep MLP, where layers at least differ. If the matrix's largest singular value, combined with the activation derivative, is below one, the product shrinks exponentially and early tokens get essentially zero gradient: the model can't learn long-range dependencies no matter its capacity. Above one, it explodes, which shows up as loss spikes."
4 · The patches: clipping, truncation "Exploding is easy to patch with gradient clipping. Truncated backprop caps the horizon, which admits the problem rather than fixing it. Vanishing is the hard one."
5 · Gated cells: an additive path "LSTMs and GRUs address it with a gated cell state updated additively, so the gradient can flow through time without being repeatedly multiplied. That's a longer leash, not an unlimited one."
6 · The second failure: sequential compute "And there's a second, independent failure: each step depends on the previous one, so training can't be parallelised across the sequence."
Close "Attention fixed both, which is why transformers won."

stages.name: Unroll in time: BPTT
stages.claim: an RNN is a deep network in time
stages.html:
"Training unrolls the recurrence into T copies with shared weights."

h_t = tanh(W_h · h_{t−1} + W_x · x_t)

x1 → [h1] → [h2] → … → [hT] → loss
        W_h    W_h        W_h      (same matrix every step)

Backpropagation through time (BPTT) is ordinary backprop on this unrolled graph.

stages.name: One matrix, multiplied T times
stages.html:
"The gradient to step 1 is a product of T Jacobians sharing W_h."

∂h_T/∂h_1 = Π (t=2..T) diag(tanh'(z_t)) · W_h
  • Same W_h every step, so the product behaves like W_h^T.
  • Largest singular value (with tanh' ≤ 1) below 1 → exponential decay; above 1 → exponential growth.
  • Worse than an MLP, whose layers have different weights and fewer multiplications.

stages.name: Vanish vs explode
stages.html:
Vanishing Exploding
Symptom early tokens don't influence learning; long dependencies never learned loss spikes, NaNs
Detectable quietly; model just underperforms on long contexts loudly
Patch architecture change needed gradient clipping

"Exploding is loud and easy. Vanishing is silent and hard."

stages.name: The patches: clipping, truncation
stages.html:
• Gradient clipping rescales the gradient when its norm exceeds a threshold. Fixes exploding, does nothing for vanishing.
  • Truncated BPTT backpropagates only k steps. Saves memory and compute, and explicitly gives up on dependencies longer than k.

stages.name: Gated cells: an additive path
stages.html:
"LSTMs replace repeated multiplication with a gated addition."

c_t = f_t ⊙ c_{t−1} + i_t ⊙ g_t
  • The cell state c is updated additively; when the forget gate f ≈ 1, the gradient passes through nearly unchanged (the "constant error carousel").
  • Gates are learned, so the network decides what to keep.
  • Result: dependencies of hundreds of steps become learnable. Still finite, still degrading with distance.

stages.name: The second failure: sequential compute
stages.html:
"Even a perfect RNN can't be trained in parallel across time."

  • h_t needs h_{t−1}, so the T steps run in sequence on a GPU built for parallel work.
  • Attention connects every position to every other in one step: path length 1 for gradients, and fully parallel training.
  • The cost moves to O(T²) attention compute and memory, which modern variants attack.

followUps.question: Why is the RNN case worse than a deep MLP?
followUps.html:
Because an RNN multiplies the same matrix at every step.

Deep MLP RNN
Jacobians a different one per layer the same one every step
Length of the product tens of layers hundreds or thousands of steps
Effect no systematic compounding the dominant singular value raised to a huge power

followUps.question: Does gradient clipping fix vanishing gradients?
followUps.html:
No. Clipping only caps gradients that are too large.

Problem Gradient Clipping
Exploding huge caps it
Vanishing tiny never touches it

The information from the early tokens is already gone from the gradient.

followUps.question: GRU vs LSTM?
followUps.html:
A GRU is the lighter one; performance is often similar.

GRU LSTM
State cell and hidden merged separate cell state
Gates two three, including an output gate
Parameters fewer, trains faster more
Edge speed sometimes very long dependencies

In practice: try both, or use attention.

followUps.question: Do transformers have no long-range problem at all?
followUps.html:
They have a different one.

RNN Transformer
Gradient to a far position through every step one step
Limit training dynamics finite context window, quadratic attention cost
Still weak early tokens the middle of long contexts is used less reliably

The limit moves to compute, context length and learned attention patterns.

followUps.question: Where would you still use an RNN today?
followUps.html:
Where input arrives one step at a time and memory and latency must stay constant.

  • Streaming or on-device: keyword spotting, some sensor pipelines.
  • Modern version: state-space models (the Mamba family) revive recurrence with parallelisable training for long sequences.

dontSay: "RNNs just have a short memory." — no mechanism.
"Clipping solves it." — only the exploding half.
"LSTMs have infinite memory." — a longer leash, not unlimited.
"Transformers won because they're bigger." — parallelism and path length won.

spine: Frame it as a judgement call
ml-dl-q24.testing: judgement, not knowledge. Can you argue against the fashionable tool, with conditions?
ml-dl-q24.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame it as a judgement call "Deep learning earns its cost when the data is unstructured, like images, audio or text, and plentiful. Outside that, I'd argue against it in four situations."
2 · Tabular data "First, tabular data with up to a few hundred thousand rows. Gradient-boosted trees still match or beat deep models there, train in minutes on a CPU, need less tuning and are easier to explain. Research on deep tabular models keeps re-finding this."
3 · Small data with strong structure "Second, small data where the structure is known. If I can write down the relationship, a physical law, a business rule, seasonality, then a simple model with that structure built in beats a network that has to learn it from few examples."
4 · Interpretability you must defend "Third, when I need interpretability I can defend to a regulator or a customer, like credit decisions. A scorecard or a monotone-constrained boosted model gives reasons I can stand behind; post-hoc explanations of a network are harder to defend."
5 · Cost, latency and the edge "Fourth, when the inference bill is the constraint: tight latency, high volume or an edge device. A smaller model or a well-engineered classical one may give most of the value at a fraction of the cost."
6 · Say what you'd ship instead "And the strongest version of this answer names the alternative: I'd benchmark a boosted model and a simple baseline first, and only move to deep learning if the gain justifies the cost."

stages.name: Frame it as a judgement call
stages.html:
"Deep learning has real costs: data, compute, tuning, opacity and operations. It has to earn them."

  • DL shines with unstructured, high-dimensional data and lots of it: vision, speech, language.
  • Everywhere else, benchmark it against cheaper options before committing.

stages.name: Tabular data
stages.html:
"For typical tabular problems, gradient boosting is the default to beat."

On typical tabular data Gradient-boosted trees Deep network
Mixed types, missing values, odd scales handled natively need encoding, imputation, scaling
Training fast on CPU, strong with defaults GPU, careful tuning
At moderate data size the default to beat rarely worth the tuning cost
Wins when most tabular problems rich text or image columns, very high-cardinality IDs
  • Handles mixed types, missing values and irregular feature scales natively.
  • Trains fast on CPU, strong with defaults, strong with modest tuning.
  • Deep tabular models occasionally match it at large scale; they rarely justify their tuning cost at moderate scale.
  • Exception: tables with rich text or image columns, or very high-cardinality IDs where learned embeddings help.

stages.name: Small data with strong structure
stages.claim: encode the prior, don't learn it
stages.html:
"If I know the shape of the relationship, I build it in."

Structure you know Better choice
Physical or accounting law parametric or physics-informed model
Seasonality and trend classical time-series models or boosting with lags
Monotone business rules monotone-constrained GBM, scorecards
Few hundred labelled examples regularised linear models, or a pretrained model fine-tuned

The last row is the nuance: with pretrained foundation models, small unstructured datasets can use DL via transfer learning.

stages.name: Interpretability you must defend
stages.html:
"When I must explain each decision, the model's structure has to be explainable."

  • Credit, insurance, hiring, healthcare: adverse-action reasons, audits, fairness reviews.
  • Scorecards, GAMs, monotone-constrained GBMs give stable, defensible reasons.
  • Post-hoc explanations (SHAP on a network) are approximations and harder to defend in an audit.

stages.name: Cost, latency and the edge
stages.html:
"At high volume, the model's cost is paid on every request."

  • Tight latency budgets (single-digit milliseconds), millions of calls a day, or on-device constraints.
  • Options: classical models, distillation into smaller networks, rules plus a model for hard cases.
  • Measure cost per decision against the value of the accuracy gained.

stages.name: Say what you'd ship instead
stages.html:
"Name the decision process, not just the objection."

  1. Baseline: rules or logistic regression.
  2. Strong classical model: gradient boosting.
  3. Deep learning only if it beats (2) by a margin that justifies data, compute, latency and explainability costs.

Best of all, name a real project where you argued against DL and what you shipped instead.

followUps.question: With LLMs available, isn't DL always the answer now?
followUps.html:
No. For a structured prediction on tabular data an LLM is slower, costlier and usually less accurate than a boosted model.

A pattern that works:textextracted featuresclassical model on topprediction

LLMs are excellent for language tasks and for bootstrapping labels.

followUps.question: Small image dataset of 500 examples. DL or not?
followUps.html:
DL, but through transfer learning.

Approach On 500 images
Train from scratch overfits
Pretrained backbone, frozen or lightly fine-tuned, small head works

Augmentation for the invariances you know still helps. "Small data" isn't automatically "no DL" when a relevant pretrained model exists.

followUps.question: How do you convince a team that wants a neural network?
followUps.html:
With evidence, not opinion.

Benchmark:boosted baseline and the networkcomparethe cheapest model that meets the target wins
Compare on
Accuracy
Training cost
Inference latency and cost per decision
Explainability

If the network wins by enough, great; the benchmark decides.

followUps.question: When does DL win on tabular data?
followUps.html:
In four situations.

Situation Why DL helps
Very large datasets capacity is used
Mixed modalities text or images alongside columns
Many high-cardinality IDs embeddings
Multi-task setups shared representations

Recommendation systems are the classic case: embedding-based deep models dominate there.

followUps.question: What's the operational cost people forget?
followUps.html:
Total cost of ownership.

Deep model Boosted model
Hardware GPUs for training, often for serving a CPU
Training longer, less stable, harder to reproduce retrains in minutes
Operations more complex monitoring, specialised skills fewer failure modes

dontSay: "It depends on the use case." (and stop) — name the conditions.
"Deep learning is always more accurate." — not on typical tabular data.
"Neural networks can't be explained, so never use them in finance." — too absolute; say what's defensible.
"We'd use deep learning to be future-proof." — cost without evidence.

links.target: 02-DL/09-diagnostics & engineering Judgement/05-When DL is the Wrong Choice

links.label: Build vs Buy vs Fine tune

spine: The constraint that made it hard
What I built around the model
ml-dl-q25.testing: whether you see ML as a system (decision, data, latency, evaluation, failure), not a model.
ml-dl-q25.trap: telling it as a modelling story ("I tried three models and tuned…"). They asked about everything else.
ml-dl-q25.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The decision it served "At Velocit AI I built VhAIre, an agentic AI interviewer that runs a live spoken interview. The models were the easy part: we called GPT-4-class models and Groq through APIs, and picking between them took days. Everything around them took months."
2 · The constraint that made it hard "The constraint was turn-taking. A conversation stops feeling human if the response takes more than about a second, and a single turn chains voice detection, streaming speech-to-text, a reasoning step, the LLM call and text-to-speech."
3 · Options I weighed "I weighed a single monolithic LLM call per turn against a LangGraph state machine, and chose <fill: which, and the deciding factor>. For the models, I routed <fill: which turn types went to Groq for latency and which to GPT-4.1 for quality>."
4 · What I built around the model "Most of the work was around the model: streaming partial transcripts so the model could start early, handling barge-in when the candidate interrupts, checkpointing the interview state, and a fallback when a provider returned errors. We also had to decide how to evaluate interview quality at all: <fill: human rubric, automated checks, or both>."
5 · What broke "What broke in production was <fill: the scar>, and we changed <fill: what changed after>."
6 · The number "The result was <fill: p50/p95 turn latency and one business outcome>."
Close "The lesson I took: the model is a component; latency, state and evaluation are the product."

stages.name: The decision it served
stages.html:
"Open with what the system decides, not the stack."

Point What it means
Product VhAIre, an agentic interview product at Velocit AI.
Decision served conducting and assessing a candidate interview in real time; the output drives <fill: who uses the assessment, and for what decision>.
Why it matters a bad turn doesn't just lower a metric; the candidate experiences a broken conversation.

stages.name: The constraint that made it hard
stages.html:
"Name the constraint before the solution. It's what makes the story senior."

  • Sub-second turn-taking is the product; above ~1 s the conversation stops feeling human.
  • The turn is a pipeline: mic → VAD → streaming STT → partial transcript → graph node → LLM → TTS → playback.
  • Every stage spends part of one latency budget.

stages.name: Options I weighed
stages.html:
"Name what you rejected, unprompted."

Decision Options Chose / why
Orchestration monolithic LLM call per turn vs LangGraph state machine <fill>
Speech-to-text Deepgram Flux vs Whisper streaming vs provider-native <fill>
LLM GPT-4/4.1 for quality vs Groq for latency <fill: routing rule>

stages.name: What I built around the model
stages.html:
"This is the answer to the question: the non-modelling parts."

  • Streaming partial transcripts so reasoning can start before the candidate finishes.
    Point What it means
    Barge-in what happens when the candidate interrupts mid-answer. <fill: how it's handled>
    State what's checkpointed in the graph, and why. <fill>
    Failure handling provider 500s or slow responses: degrade or wait? <fill>
    Evaluation how interview quality is measured. <fill: rubric / human review / automated checks>
    Safety stopping the agent from being talked into revealing the rubric. <fill>

stages.name: What broke
stages.html:
"A story without a scar reads as engineer, not architect."

  • <fill: what failed in production>
  • <fill: how you found it: metric, user report, trace>
  • <fill: what changed in the design or process afterwards>

stages.name: The number
stages.html:
"End on a measured result and one lesson."

  • <fill: p50 / p95 turn latency before and after>
  • <fill: one business or user outcome: completion rate, candidate rating, interviews per week>
  • Lesson: the model is a component; latency, state and evaluation are the product.

followUps.question: The candidate interrupts mid-answer. What happens?
followUps.html:
<fill> Shape of a good answer:

Barge-in:VAD detects speech during playbackTTS cancelled immediatelypartial agent turn recorded as interrupted in stategraph routes to a "listen" node

Say what you did about half-spoken content and how the next turn uses it.

followUps.question: The LLM is slow on one turn. Degrade or wait?
followUps.html:
<fill> Shape:

Degrade:per-turn latency budgetfaster model, or a scripted acknowledgementfull answer completes behind it

The acknowledgement is a line such as "Let me think about that…". State which you chose and why, and how often the fallback fired.

followUps.question: How did you evaluate interview quality?
followUps.html:
<fill> Shape:

Layer What it checks
Human rubric a sample of interviews, for calibration
Automated checks covered the required competencies? followed up on weak answers? leaked the rubric?
Tracking over time and per model version

Name what you'd add now.

followUps.question: Why not just use one model for everything?
followUps.html:
Because quality and latency pull in different directions per turn type.

Setup What breaks
One high-quality model the latency budget on simple turns
One fast model assessment quality
Routing by turn type nothing: latency is spent only where quality matters

Give your actual routing rule.

followUps.question: What would you do differently?
followUps.html:
<fill> Shape: one concrete design change with its trade-off.

  • For example: building evaluation harnesses earlier, or instrumenting per-stage latency from day one.
  • Avoid: "nothing", and "everything".

followUps.question: "You called an API. That's not really building a model."
followUps.html:
Own it; it's the point of the question.

  • The model: a commodity component.
  • The engineering: routing between models by turn type, streaming, state, failure handling, evaluation.
  • What was modelling: <fill: e.g. how turn types were classified for routing, prompt or rubric design, how quality was scored>.

dontSay: "I tried several models and XGBoost/GPT-4 performed best." — that's the modelling story they didn't ask for.
"It worked well." — give the number.
Any metric you can't defend in follow-ups — the <fill> rule: real numbers only.
Opening with the tech stack — open with the constraint.
ml-dl-q25.warning: This answer is built on S1 · VhAIre from PROJECT-STORIES. Situation, constraint and options come from the vault; every <fill> is a fact only you have. Don't invent a latency number or an outcome in the room. If you have a classical ML project that fits better, keep this spine and swap the content.

spine: What it does to training and data
ml-dl-q26.testing: whether you connect textbook taxonomy to latency, memory and cost in production.
ml-dl-q26.trap: "non-parametric means no parameters." It means the number of parameters isn't fixed in advance.
ml-dl-q26.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Define by what grows "The cleanest way to say it is: what grows when the data grows?"
2 · Instance-based vs model-based "A parametric model has a fixed number of parameters no matter how much data you have: linear and logistic regression, naive Bayes, a neural net of fixed size. It makes strong assumptions, needs less data, and inference is constant-time and cheap."
3 · What it does to serving "A non-parametric model's complexity grows with the data: kNN, decision trees grown to purity, kernel SVMs, Gaussian processes. Fewer assumptions and more flexibility, but more variance, more data needed, and memory and inference cost that grow with n. Non-parametric doesn't mean no parameters; it means the count isn't fixed in advance."
4 · What it does to training and data "The second axis is when the work happens. Model-based learning compresses the data into parameters at training time. Instance-based learning, like kNN, stores the data and does all the work at query time."
5 · Pick by the operational constraint "Operationally that decides artifact size, p99 latency, whether you can serve on CPU or on a device, and whether retraining can be incremental. kNN is the extreme: zero training cost, expensive queries."
Close "That's why production kNN becomes an approximate-nearest-neighbour index like FAISS or HNSW, which is really a retrieval system."

stages.name: Define by what grows
stages.html:
"Ask what gets bigger as n grows."

Parametric Non-parametric
Parameter count fixed grows with data
Examples linear/logistic regression, naive Bayes, fixed-size NNs kNN, deep trees, kernel SVM, Gaussian processes
Assumptions strong (functional form) weak
Bias / variance higher bias higher variance
Data needed less more

stages.name: Instance-based vs model-based
stages.html:
"Eager learners compress at training time; lazy learners compute at query time."

  • Model-based (eager): training summarises data into parameters; the data can be thrown away.
  • Instance-based (lazy): keep the data; every prediction compares against stored examples (kNN, kernel methods).
  • A tree is non-parametric but model-based: it grows with data yet compiles into a structure you query cheaply.

stages.name: What it does to serving
stages.html:
"This is where the distinction earns its interview slot."

Point What it means
Artifact size a logistic model is kilobytes; a kNN model is the dataset.
Latency parametric inference is O(features); exact kNN is O(n · d) per query.
Hardware fixed-size models fit on CPU or edge; instance-based needs memory for the whole corpus.
Production kNN becomes an approximate nearest neighbour index (FAISS, HNSW, ScaNN), trading exactness for sub-linear queries.

stages.name: What it does to training and data
stages.html:
• Instance-based "retrains" by inserting rows: trivially incremental.
  • Parametric models need refitting, or partial_fit for SGD-trained ones.
  • Non-parametric models keep improving with more data; parametric ones plateau once their assumptions bind.

stages.name: Pick by the operational constraint
stages.html:
Constraint Lean toward
Tight latency, CPU or device parametric
Little data, strong prior parametric
Lots of data, complex boundary non-parametric (trees/ensembles)
Similarity search over a corpus instance-based via ANN index
Frequent additions, no retraining instance-based

followUps.question: Is a neural network parametric?
followUps.html:
Yes, formally: a fixed architecture has a fixed parameter count, whatever n is.

  • Blurred in practice: people scale model size with data.
  • Operational meaning: for any trained network, inference cost doesn't grow with the training set.

followUps.question: Is a random forest parametric?
followUps.html:
No, but it is model-based.

Axis Random forest
Parametric? no: trees grow deeper, with more splits, as data grows
Instance-based? no: inference traverses fixed trees, not stored examples

That's why "non-parametric" and "slow inference" aren't the same thing.

followUps.question: How does HNSW make kNN viable at scale?
followUps.html:
It replaces a full scan with a walk through a layered proximity graph.

Query:enter at the coarse top layergreedily walk towards the querydrop a layerrepeat to the finest layer
  • Trade: some recall for logarithmic-ish query time, tuned with ef and M.
  • Cost: memory; the graph lives in RAM alongside the vectors.

followUps.question: Where do Gaussian processes fit, and why are they rare in production?
followUps.html:
Non-parametric with calibrated uncertainty, and too expensive to scale.

training:   O(n³)      ← n × n kernel matrix
prediction: O(n) each
  • Limit: beyond tens of thousands of points you need sparse approximations.
  • Where they shine: small data, such as Bayesian optimisation of hyperparameters.

followUps.question: Which would you pick for an on-device keyboard suggestion model?
followUps.html:
Parametric: a small neural or n-gram model, quantised.

Parametric Instance-based
Memory fixed the whole history on the phone
Latency constant grows with usage
User corpus on disk none all of it

dontSay: "Non-parametric models have no parameters." — the count just isn't fixed.
"kNN is cheap because it has no training." — you pay at every query.
"Parametric means linear." — neural nets are parametric and non-linear.

spine: Decouple feature freshness from weight freshness
ml-dl-q27.testing: whether you split two constraints the question fuses, and default to the operable option.
ml-dl-q27.trap: "the data is streaming, so we need online learning."
ml-dl-q27.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Separate size from recency "There are two separate constraints hiding in that sentence, and they have different answers."
2 · Size: out-of-core "The first is size: the data doesn't fit in memory. That's an out-of-core problem: stream it in chunks with mini-batch training, partial_fit, or a distributed trainer. It says nothing about how often the model changes."
3 · Recency: retrain cadence "The second is recency: new data keeps arriving and the world may drift. That's a retraining-cadence question. Streaming data doesn't automatically mean online learning. My default is scheduled batch retraining, daily or weekly, because it's reproducible, you can validate the new model before shipping it, A/B it and roll it back."
4 · What online learning breaks "True online learning, updating weights on every event, breaks in specific ways: no clean train/test split, a bad burst of data can drag the model off a cliff, poisoning risk, no reproducibility, and a learning rate that has to be right forever. You lose validate-before-ship."
5 · Decouple feature freshness from weight freshness "The architect move is to decouple freshness of features from freshness of weights."
Close "A model retrained daily but fed real-time features, like 'transactions in the last five minutes', usually beats an online-updated model with stale features, and it's far easier to operate."

stages.name: Separate size from recency
stages.html:
Constraint Question it raises Answer family
Size can I train on data bigger than RAM? out-of-core / mini-batch / distributed
Recency how fast must the model reflect new data? retrain cadence, online learning

stages.name: Size: out-of-core
stages.claim: stream the data, not the model
stages.html:
• Chunked readers (Parquet row groups, Arrow datasets), partial_fit for SGD-based linear models and naive Bayes, mini-batch deep learning, distributed trainers (Spark, Ray, XGBoost distributed).
  • Caveats: shuffling is hard, so chunks may be correlated; scaling needs running statistics; many algorithms (vanilla Random Forest, kernel SVM) don't fit incrementally.
  • Often simpler: train on a well-drawn sample, then check with a learning curve whether more data would help.

stages.name: Recency: retrain cadence
stages.html:
"Scheduled retraining keeps every safety property of offline ML."

Scheduled batch retraining True online learning
Update daily or weekly, on a recent window on every event
Validation before release yes: newest slice, compare to incumbent, canary no clean hold-out
Reproducible yes hard
Pick when almost always the world shifts faster than you can retrain
  • Train on a recent window, validate on the newest slice, compare to the incumbent, canary, promote.
  • Cadence comes from measured decay: how fast does the metric drop over time?
  • Trigger-based retraining (on drift) when decay is irregular.

stages.name: What online learning breaks
stages.html:
• No held-out evaluation before a change reaches users.
    Point What it means
    Catastrophic drift one bad burst (a bot, an outage) pulls weights far off.
    Poisoning adversaries can steer the model with crafted traffic.
    Reproducibility you can't recreate yesterday's model exactly.
    Hyperparameters forever the learning rate must suit every future regime.

Legitimate uses: bandits, ad click models with heavy guardrails, and systems where hours of staleness genuinely cost money.

stages.name: Decouple feature freshness from weight freshness
stages.html:
"Most of the value of 'online' comes from fresh inputs, not fresh weights."

  • Real-time features (counts in the last N minutes, session state) through a streaming feature pipeline.
  • Weights retrained on a schedule with full validation.
  • You get responsiveness without giving up reproducibility or rollback.

followUps.question: The business insists on minute-level adaptation. Now what?
followUps.html:
First check whether real-time features deliver it. Only then move the weights.

Guardrail on online updates
Bounded learning rate no single event swings the model
Validated, filtered events only bad data stays out
Shadow evaluation against a frozen baseline continuous
Auto-revert on a metric drop

Keep periodic full retrains to reset accumulated drift.

followUps.question: Which sklearn models support incremental fitting?
followUps.html:
Those with partial_fit.

Supports it Doesn't
SGDClassifier / SGDRegressor sklearn random forests
MultinomialNB / GaussianNB sklearn gradient boosting
MiniBatchKMeans, PassiveAggressive, Perceptron, MLPClassifier

XGBoost and LightGBM can continue training from an existing booster, but that's not online learning.

followUps.question: Why is shuffling a problem out-of-core?
followUps.html:
Because data arrives sorted, so consecutive chunks aren't i.i.d.

Failure:sorted by time or usereach chunk shares structuregradients biased per chunkthe model oscillates
  • Fix: a shuffle buffer, pre-shuffled shards, or a random order of files and row groups.

followUps.question: Doesn't daily retraining risk shipping a regression every day?
followUps.html:
Only without a gate. Automation without evaluation is the risk, not frequency.

Every retrain:offline checks against the incumbentcanarypromote

The offline checks run on the newest data, per segment. If either step fails, the incumbent stays.

followUps.question: How do you pick the training window length?
followUps.html:
Let a recent holdout choose.

Test:train on the last 1, 3, 6 and 12 monthsscore on a recent holdoutkeep the best, or weight recent data more
Window Gives
Longer more data
Shorter tracks change

After a known regime change (pricing, policy), drop or down-weight pre-change data.

dontSay: "Streaming data means online learning." — size and recency are separate.
"Online learning is more advanced, so it's better." — it trades away validation and rollback.
"Just get a bigger machine." — sometimes right, but name out-of-core and sampling first.

ml-dl-q28.testing: whether you run EDA toward decisions under a time box, not a plot gallery.
ml-dl-q28.trap: listing plots ("histograms, box plots, a heatmap…").
ml-dl-q28.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame EDA as decisions "I'd frame the day around the decisions EDA has to produce: what the target's base rate is, which columns are unusable, what the split strategy is, what each feature needs, and whether anything leaks."
2 · Sample and audit the schema "I'd start by sampling, stratified on the target, so it fits in memory and iterates fast. Then a schema and type audit: numbers that are really IDs, dates stored as strings, sentinel values like minus 999 or 1900-01-01."
3 · Missingness, target and cardinality "Next, missingness per column and jointly, because missingness is often informative. The target distribution and base rate. Cardinality of categoricals. Duplicates and near-duplicates. Then per-feature relationships with the target, correlation clusters, and temporal coverage: does each column exist across the whole time range, or appear after some date?"
4 · Hunt leakage and traps "The thing I actively hunt is leakage: features that are too good, near-perfectly correlated with the target, are guilty until proven innocent."
5 · Automate the first pass "I'd use an automated profiler like ydata-profiling for the first pass to save hours, but I don't treat its report as the analysis."
6 · Deliver by end of day "By end of day I deliver a written data-quality note with issues and decisions, a split strategy, a feature shortlist, and a trained baseline, because a baseline model is the fastest way to learn which columns matter."

stages.name: Frame EDA as decisions
stages.html:
By end of day I can answer Because it decides
What is the target and its base rate? the metric and the baseline
Which columns are unusable? what is dropped before modelling
What is the split strategy? whether validation can be trusted
What does each kept feature need? the preprocessing pipeline

By end of day I must be able to answer:

  • What is the target and its base rate?
  • Which columns are unusable (leaky, constant, broken)?
  • What's the split strategy (time? groups?)?
  • What does each kept feature need (encoding, transform, imputation)?

stages.name: Sample and audit the schema
stages.html:
Check What I look for Action
Sample a stratified 1–2M rows that fits in memory iterate fast; confirm on full data later
Types IDs and zip codes as ints, dates as strings, "Y"/"N" booleans recast
Sentinels −999, 0, 1900-01-01, "unknown" convert to missing
Constant columns one value, or nearly drop candidates
  • Stratified sample (e.g. 1–2M rows) to iterate in memory; confirm conclusions on the full data later.
  • Types: numeric IDs, zip codes as ints, dates as strings, booleans as "Y"/"N"/"".
  • Sentinels: −999, 0, 1900-01-01, "unknown" masquerading as values.
  • Constant or near-constant columns → drop candidates.

stages.name: Missingness, target and cardinality
stages.html:
Check Why
Missingness per column and co-missingness informative missingness, broken sources
Target distribution, base rate metric choice, imbalance handling
Categorical cardinality encoding strategy, leakage risk (IDs)
Duplicates / near-duplicates split leakage, inflated metrics
Temporal coverage per column schema changes, features that appear late

stages.name: Hunt leakage and traps
stages.claim: the part that saves the project
stages.html:
Trap How it shows up
Too-good feature near-perfect correlation or AUC by itself
Post-outcome field a timestamp or status written after the label event
Unit change scale shifts mid-series
Late-appearing category levels that only exist after a date
  • Too-good features: anything with near-perfect target correlation or AUC on its own.
  • Post-outcome fields: timestamps or statuses written after the label event.
  • Units and scales changing mid-series.
  • Categorical levels that only exist after a date.

stages.name: Automate the first pass
stages.html:
• ydata-profiling, sweetviz on the sample: distributions, correlations, missingness in an hour.
  • Then targeted manual work on the suspicious columns the report flagged.

stages.name: Deliver by end of day
stages.html:
1. Data-quality note: issues found and the decision for each.
  2. Split strategy with the reason.
  3. Feature shortlist with needed transforms.
  4. Baseline model (logistic or a quick GBM) with feature importance: which columns actually carry signal.

followUps.question: Why train a model during EDA?
followUps.html:
Because it's the fastest honest signal of which columns matter and whether any leak.

What the day-one model shows Why it matters
A feature that dominates importance either your best feature or leakage; find out before building on it
A first score the bar every later model must beat

followUps.question: How big should the sample be?
followUps.html:
Big enough to keep rare classes and rare categorical levels represented.

Sampling:stratify on the targetcap per-level counts if neededa few million rows for distributionsconfirm on the full data with a SQL aggregate

followUps.question: A feature has AUC 0.99 on its own. What now?
followUps.html:
Assume leakage, then find out when and how the column is written relative to the label.

Finding Action
Recorded after the outcome, or derived from it drop it
Genuinely available at prediction time the problem may be trivial; tell the business that too

followUps.question: How do you check missingness is informative?
followUps.html:
Compare the target rate with the value missing against the value present.

Test:target rate when missing vs presentbaseline with and without missing-indicator featuresmissingness isn't random

In that case imputation alone would throw the signal away.

followUps.question: What would you do on day two?
followUps.html:
Turn day one's findings into things that last.

Day two Output
Validate the split a quick CV sanity check
Build the feature pipeline properly everything inside a Pipeline
Agree the metric with the business
Data-quality checks on the columns that showed problems, so they're monitored, not rediscovered

dontSay: "I'd make a pairplot of all 300 columns." — unreadable and slow.
"The profiling report covers it." — it's a first pass, not the analysis.
"EDA doesn't need a model." — a baseline is the fastest EDA tool.

links.target: 01-ML/02-Data Handling & EDA/02-Data Profiling — Structure, Univariate, Bivariate & Multivariate

spine: The rule: what the model computes with values
ml-dl-q29.testing: whether you reason from the algorithm's arithmetic instead of habit.
ml-dl-q29.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The rule: what the model computes with values "The rule is: scaling matters when the algorithm compares or combines feature magnitudes, and it's a no-op when the algorithm only uses their order."
2 · Where it matters "It matters in three families. Distance-based models: kNN, K-means, RBF SVMs, where a feature measured in thousands swamps one measured in fractions. Gradient-descent-trained models: linear and logistic regression with SGD, neural nets, where unscaled features make the loss surface badly conditioned and training slow or unstable. And regularised linear models, because the penalty is scale-sensitive: an unscaled feature gets shrunk more or less than it should."
3 · Where it's a no-op "It's a no-op for tree-based models: random forests, gradient boosting. Splits depend on ordering, not magnitude, so scaling them is ritual."
4 · Which scaler "For which scaler: standardisation by default; min-max when you need a bounded range; robust scaling when outliers would distort the mean and standard deviation; and log or Box-Cox/Yeo-Johnson when the problem is skew, which changes the shape, not just the scale."
5 · Fit it inside the fold "And the operational rule: fit the scaler on the training data only, inside the pipeline and inside each CV fold."
Close "PCA is the sneaky case: it maximises variance, so unscaled features with big units dominate the components."

stages.name: The rule: what the model computes with values
stages.html: "Distances, gradients and penalties see magnitude. Splits see order."

stages.name: Where it matters
stages.html:
Family Why scale matters
Distance-based: kNN, K-means, SVM-RBF large-unit features dominate the distance
Gradient-trained: linear/logistic via SGD, NNs ill-conditioned loss, slow or unstable convergence
Regularised linear: Ridge, Lasso, Elastic Net penalty shrinks features unequally by unit
PCA variance is unit-dependent; big units hijack components

stages.name: Where it's a no-op
stages.html:
• Decision trees, Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost: splits are thresholds on sorted values, invariant to monotone transforms.
  • Naive Bayes per-feature likelihoods: largely unaffected (Gaussian NB fits each feature's own mean and variance).

stages.name: Which scaler
stages.html:
Scaler Use when
StandardScaler (z-score) default
MinMaxScaler need a bounded range (e.g. some NN inputs, images)
RobustScaler (median, IQR) outliers would distort mean/std
Log / Box-Cox / Yeo-Johnson heavy skew; changes shape, not just scale

stages.name: Fit it inside the fold
stages.html:
• Fit on training data only; transform validation and test with those statistics.
  • Put it in a Pipeline so CV refits it per fold automatically.
  • Ship the fitted scaler inside the model artifact so serving applies the identical transform.

followUps.question: Does scaling help gradient boosting at all?
followUps.html:
Not for the splits: on standard tree boosters it's wasted work.

Where scale can matter How much
Histogram binning edge cases slightly
Linear boosters yes
Standard tree boosters not at all

What can help trees is transforming the target, not the features.

followUps.question: Why does Lasso need scaled features?
followUps.html:
Because the penalty is on coefficient size, and coefficient size depends on units.

penalty = λ · Σ |βⱼ|      ← a feature in small units needs a large β for the same effect
Unscaled:small unitslarge coefficientpenalised moredropped first, regardless of importance

Standardising puts every coefficient on the same footing.

followUps.question: Scale before or after the train/test split?
followUps.html:
After, and fit on train only.

Leaky:fit scaler on all rowssplit
Honest:splitfit scaler on traintransform train and test
  • The leak: test-set mean and variance influence training. Mild, but real.
  • The other cost: serving can no longer reproduce the transform from training data alone.

followUps.question: Do neural nets need input scaling if they have BatchNorm?
followUps.html:
Yes, scale inputs anyway.

Normalises
BatchNorm activations inside the network
Input scaling what the first layer sees

Badly scaled inputs still hurt the first layer's conditioning and the initialisation assumptions. Scaling is cheap and removes a failure mode.

followUps.question: How do you handle a feature with extreme skew, like income?
followUps.html:
Compress the tail first, then standardise if the model needs it.

Scale-sensitive model:log or Yeo-Johnsonstandardise

Trees: leave it alone

Whether to cap the extremes is a data decision, not a scaling one.

followUps.question: How do you guarantee serving scales inputs exactly like training did?
followUps.html:
Ship the fitted scaler inside the model artifact, and never reimplement it in the service.

Guarantee:scaler inside the Pipelinefitted means and variances logged with the model versionserved feature distributions monitored against them

A drifting mean means the scaling no longer centres production data: both a skew signal and a drift signal.

dontSay: "Always scale." — trees don't care.
"Scaling fixes skew." — standardising keeps the shape; you need a transform.
"I scaled the whole dataset first, then split." — leakage.

links.label: Scaling — Standardization, MinMax, MaxAbs, Robust; When It Matters vs Trees
links.target: 01-ML/03-Feature-engineering/01-Scaling — Standardization, MinMax, MaxAbs, Robust; When It Matters vs Trees

ml-dl-q30.testing: whether you see pipelines as correctness and deployment guarantees, not style.
ml-dl-q30.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Guarantee 1: leakage-free CV "Two guarantees, and neither is about tidiness. The first is leakage-free cross-validation. A Pipeline refits every transform, imputers, scalers and encoders, inside each CV fold, so they never see the validation rows. Doing preprocessing once up front and then cross-validating is the classic silent leak; the Pipeline makes the correct thing the default."
2 · Guarantee 2: one artifact for serving "The second is train-serve consistency. The fitted pipeline is one serialised artifact containing preprocessing and model together, so serving applies byte-identical transforms. It's the small-scale version of what a feature store does for a platform."
3 · ColumnTransformer: declarative wiring "ColumnTransformer adds declarative wiring: numeric, categorical and text columns each get their own path in one object, bound by column name, so there's no hand-maintained index bookkeeping to drift."
4 · Tune the whole function "A bonus: hyperparameter search covers preprocessing choices too, like the imputation strategy or encoder type, so you tune the whole function, not just the estimator."
5 · The pipeline as a contract "Architecturally, the pipeline is a contract: raw schema in, prediction out."
Close "That makes it testable, versionable and swappable behind an API."

stages.name: Guarantee 1: leakage-free CV
stages.html:
pipe = Pipeline([("prep", preprocess), ("model", LogisticRegression())])
cross_val_score(pipe, X, y, cv=5)   # imputer/scaler/encoder refit on each training fold

Without it: scaler.fit(X) on all rows → every fold's validation data shaped the scaler.

stages.name: Guarantee 2: one artifact for serving
stages.html:
• joblib.dump(pipe) stores fitted preprocessing and model together.
  • The service calls pipe.predict(raw_df): no hand-coded transforms to drift.
  • Version the pipeline; roll back model and preprocessing atomically.

stages.name: ColumnTransformer: declarative wiring
stages.html:
preprocess = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer()), ("scale", StandardScaler())]), num_cols),
    ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), cat_cols),
])
  • handle_unknown="ignore" makes unseen categories safe at serving.
  • New columns can't silently shift positions.

stages.name: Tune the whole function
stages.html:
• param_grid = {"prep__num__impute__strategy": ["mean", "median"], "model__C": [0.1, 1, 10]}
  • Encoder choice, feature selection k, polynomial degree: all searchable in one CV loop.

stages.name: The pipeline as a contract
stages.html:
• Unit-testable: fixed input frame → expected output.
  • Schema validation at the edge (pandera, pydantic) before the pipeline.
  • Swappable behind an API: the service doesn't care what's inside.

followUps.question: What leaks if you impute before CV?
followUps.html:
The imputed values are computed with validation rows included.

Transform fitted before CV What leaks into training
Mean or median imputation validation rows' values
KNN imputation validation rows as neighbours
Target encoding validation labels: the extreme case

followUps.question: How do you add a custom transform?
followUps.html:
A class with fit and transform, or FunctionTransformer if it's stateless.

Transform Use
Learns something from data a class inheriting BaseEstimator and TransformerMixin
Stateless function FunctionTransformer

Keep every learned value in fit, so it's refit per fold.

followUps.question: What doesn't belong in the pipeline?
followUps.html:
Three things.

Doesn't belong Where it goes
Anything needing data unavailable at prediction time nowhere
Row filtering that changes the target before the split, deliberately
Heavy feature computation shared across models a feature store or an upstream job

followUps.question: Pickled pipelines break across sklearn versions. How do you manage that?
followUps.html:
Pin, record and test.

Lifecycle:pin library versions in the model's environmentrecord them with the artifactload-and-predict test in CI for each new version

For long-lived or cross-language serving, export to ONNX or another portable format.

followUps.question: Where do resamplers like SMOTE go?
followUps.html:
In an imblearn.pipeline.Pipeline.

Pipeline Sampler runs at
imblearn.pipeline.Pipeline fit only
sklearn Pipeline predict time as well

Resampling must happen on training folds only.

dontSay: "Pipelines are just for clean code." — they're correctness and deployment guarantees.
"I preprocess the full dataset, then run CV." — leakage.
"The service reimplements the preprocessing." — train-serve skew waiting to happen.

spine: You can't prove it from data
ml-dl-q31.testing: whether imputation choices follow from assumptions, not habit.
ml-dl-q31.trap: "fill with the mean and move on."
ml-dl-q31.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Ask what missingness depends on "The mechanism decides which methods are unbiased, so it decides what you're allowed to do."
2 · MCAR: deletion is safe "MCAR, missing completely at random, means missingness is independent of everything, observed or not. Then dropping incomplete rows is unbiased, just wasteful. It's the only case where deletion is safe, and it's the rarest in practice."
3 · MAR: model-based imputation "MAR, missing at random given the observed data, means other columns explain the missingness, for example older customers skip a field more often. Then model-based imputation like KNN or MICE is justified, because the observed columns carry the signal needed to recover the value."
4 · MNAR: missingness is signal "MNAR, missing not at random, means missingness depends on the unobserved value itself, like income left blank because it's high. Then no imputation is unbiased. The honest move is a missing-indicator feature, plus a sentinel or 'missing' category, so the model can learn from the missingness itself."
5 · You can't prove it from data "You can't prove the mechanism from data alone. You reason from how the data was generated, form logic, sensor behaviour, and check whether missingness correlates with other columns."
6 · Ship it in the pipeline "And whatever you choose, the imputer is fitted on training data only, lives in the pipeline, and the serving path handles a column being entirely absent, not just NaN."

stages.name: Ask what missingness depends on
stages.html:
Mechanism Missingness depends on Example
MCAR nothing random sensor dropout
MAR observed columns older users skip "social handle"
MNAR the missing value itself high earners skip "income"

stages.name: MCAR: deletion is safe
stages.html:
MCAR:  P(missing | observed, unobserved) = P(missing)             ← unrelated to anything
MAR:   P(missing | observed, unobserved) = P(missing | observed)  ← explained by columns you have
MNAR:  depends on the unobserved value itself                     ← the value hides because of what it is
  • Complete-case analysis is unbiased; you lose rows and power.
  • Simple imputation (mean/median) is fine too, though it shrinks variance.

stages.name: MAR: model-based imputation
stages.html:
Imputer for MAR How it fills the gap Note
KNN imputer borrows values from similar rows needs scaled features
MICE / IterativeImputer models each column from the others, iterates slower, most faithful
Mean or median one constant biased here: ignores the relationship MAR relies on
  • KNN imputer: borrow values from similar rows.
  • MICE / IterativeImputer: model each column from the others, iterate.
  • Mean imputation here is biased: it ignores the relationship the MAR assumption relies on.

stages.name: MNAR: missingness is signal
stages.html:
"The fact that it's missing tells you something about the value."

  • Add a missing indicator column.
  • Fill with a sentinel or "missing" category (or let GBMs route NaN natively).
  • Consider modelling the missingness process explicitly if inference matters.

stages.name: You can't prove it from data
stages.html:
• Test MCAR against MAR: does missingness correlate with observed columns? (Little's test, or a classifier predicting missingness.)
  • MNAR is untestable from observed data alone: argue from how the value is produced.

stages.name: Ship it in the pipeline
stages.html:
• Imputer fitted per training fold; stored in the artifact.
  • Serving handles NaN and absent columns.
  • Monitor production missingness rates against training.

followUps.question: Why not always add missing indicators?
followUps.html:
It's often a good default, especially for trees, and it's cheap.

Cost When it bites
Extra columns wide data
A skew channel missingness patterns differ between training and serving

So monitor missingness rates in production.

followUps.question: Does XGBoost's native missing handling solve this?
followUps.html:
It handles informative missingness well, but not a change in the missingness rate.

Native handling
How learns a default direction per split for missing values
MNAR uses missingness as signal, which is what you want
True value not recovered
Train/serve rate difference no protection

followUps.question: Can MICE make things worse?
followUps.html:
Yes, under MNAR.

Failure:impute plausible values from observed columnsconfidently wrong, in a systematic direction
  • Also: slow on large data, and it leaks if fitted outside the fold.
  • Check: validate imputation choices by downstream model performance.

followUps.question: How much missingness is too much to keep a column?
followUps.html:
There's no fixed cutoff. A column 90% missing can still be valuable if its presence is informative.

Judge by Question
Validation performance does the column plus its indicator improve it?
Stability is its missingness rate stable in production?

followUps.question: In medical data, why does the mechanism matter beyond accuracy?
followUps.html:
Because conclusions and fairness depend on it, not only metrics.

Example:doctors order a lab test only for sicker patientsmissing means "not suspected"imputing a "normal" value misrepresents patientsbiased decisions for groups tested less often

The mechanism affects validity.

dontSay: "I always mean-impute." — biased except under MCAR.
"I dropped rows with nulls." — safe only under MCAR.
"I tested and it's MNAR." — MNAR can't be confirmed from observed data alone.

spine: It's a skew question, not imputation
ml-dl-q32.testing: whether you diagnose why the rates differ before filling the hole.
ml-dl-q32.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · It's a skew question, not imputation "This isn't an imputation question yet. A gap from 2% to 30% means training and serving see different data, so I'd diagnose the discrepancy first."
2 · Suspect availability timing "My first suspect is availability timing. The training set was probably built from a warehouse where the value eventually arrives, say a device fingerprint that lands a few minutes after the transaction. At prediction time it isn't there yet. So the training feature effectively used the future, and the model learned to rely on something production rarely has."
3 · Rule out a pipeline break "The second suspect is a pipeline break: an upstream service or schema change started dropping the field."
4 · Fix point-in-time correctness "If it's timing, imputation is a band-aid over leakage. The real fix is to rebuild the feature as it was available at prediction time, point-in-time correctness, and retrain."
5 · Protect the model now "If it's a break, I page the owning team, and meanwhile check the model degrades gracefully: gradient-boosted trees route missing values along a learned path, and a fitted imputer at least doesn't crash."
6 · Monitor null rates "Either way I'd add monitors on per-feature null rates and distributions at serving time, compared against the training profile, because this failure is invisible in model metrics until fraud losses show up."

stages.name: It's a skew question, not imputation
stages.html: "Two different worlds are producing this feature." Before touching the model, find out why.

stages.name: Suspect availability timing
stages.html:
Step Time What training (backfilled) sees What serving sees
transaction scored 10:00:00 — feature not yet written → null
device fingerprint lands 10:00:07 — too late for this request
warehouse backfill, later overnight value present —
  • Training data backfilled from a warehouse: the value is present because it arrived later.
  • Serving computes at request time: the value often hasn't arrived.
  • Check: compare the feature's write timestamp with the transaction timestamp in training rows.

stages.name: Rule out a pipeline break
stages.html:
Pattern in the null rate Diagnosis
a step change on one date pipeline break: line it up with deploys and schema changes
concentrated in one client, region or app version a client-side bug
a constant gap since launch availability skew: the feature arrives after scoring
  • Did the null rate jump on a date? Line it up with deploys and schema changes.
  • Is it one client, region or app version?
  • A step change is a break; a constant gap since launch is availability skew.

stages.name: Fix point-in-time correctness
stages.html:
Before After
Training features whatever the warehouse holds today only what existed at each event's timestamp (as-of join)
Missing rate in training far lower than production matches production
Extra signal none a missing indicator: "fingerprint not yet available" can itself predict fraud
  • Recompute training features using only data available at each event's timestamp (the as-of join a feature store enforces).
  • Retrain; the model now learns from the missingness rate it will actually see.
  • Add a missing indicator: in fraud, "fingerprint not yet available" can itself be a signal.

stages.name: Protect the model now
stages.html:
• Estimate current damage: score recent traffic with and without the feature; check precision at the review budget.
  • Temporary options: fall back to a model trained without the feature, tighten rules for affected traffic, or raise review capacity.

stages.name: Monitor null rates
stages.html:
• Per-feature null rate and distribution vs training profile, alerting on divergence.
  • Data contracts with upstream owners: freshness, completeness, schema.

followUps.question: Why not just impute with the training mean?
followUps.html:
Because a constant fill on 30% of traffic gives confident, wrong scores.

If the cause is Mean imputation
A feature the model relies on heavily wrong scores for a third of traffic
Leakage hides the real bug: the offline performance was never achievable in production

followUps.question: How would a feature store have prevented this?
followUps.html:
Point-in-time joins, and one definition for both stores.

Without:value arrives minutes after the transactionjoined into the training row anyway2% missing offline, 30% live
With:point-in-time jointhe late value is absent from that rowavailability behaves the same offline and online

followUps.question: Could missingness be the fraud signal?
followUps.html:
Yes. Fraudsters may block device fingerprinting or use emulators.

  • Then: missingness is predictive, and an indicator feature helps.
  • Condition: its rate in training must match production.
  • Rule: model it deliberately; don't discover it by accident.

followUps.question: How fast would you have noticed without monitoring?
followUps.html:
Possibly weeks, when the chargebacks arrive.

Signal Visible
Null rates, score distributions immediately
Outcomes (fraud labels) weeks later

That's why input monitoring matters most for delayed-label problems.

followUps.question: What's in the post-incident review?
followUps.html:
Four findings and four structural fixes.

Findings Structural fixes
Root cause: timing or break point-in-time training data
Time to detect null-rate alerts
Business impact: missed fraud, false positives a data contract with the upstream team
a pre-launch check of serving feature distributions against training

dontSay: "Impute and retrain." (first) — hides the cause.
"Production data is just messier." — a 15× difference has a mechanism.
"The model metrics look fine." — fraud labels arrive late.
