links.target: 01-ML/04-Missing Data & Outliers/02-Imputation — CCA, Mean-Median, Mode, Random Sample, End-of-Distribution

spine: Legitimate extremes: keep, cap or transform
ml-dl-q33.testing: whether you decide by origin and model, not by a z-score threshold.
ml-dl-q33.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Classify by origin first "I classify the outlier by origin first, because the treatment follows from the origin, not from how many standard deviations away it is."
2 · Errors: correct or remove "Error outliers, a sensor glitch, a unit mix-up, an age of 250, get corrected if I can, removed if I can't."
3 · Legitimate extremes: keep, cap or transform "Legitimate extremes, a real customer who spends a hundred times the median, stay in the data. If they'd distort a scale-sensitive model like linear regression or kNN, I cap them with winsorisation or log-transform the feature. Tree models mostly don't care, so often the answer there is do nothing."
4 · The signal itself: never touch "And sometimes the outlier is the whole point: in fraud or anomaly detection, the extremes are the positives. Removing them destroys the task."
5 · Detection only flags "Detection methods only flag. Z-scores assume normality, IQR is more robust, and Isolation Forest or LOF catch multivariate oddities. The decision still needs the origin."
6 · Make it a pipeline policy "Whatever I do lives in the pipeline, with thresholds fitted on training data only, and I log what was removed and why."
Close "Silently deleting inconvenient rows before the split is unreproducible and leaky, and it's how audit findings start."

stages.name: Classify by origin first
stages.html:
Origin Example Treatment
Error age 250, price in cents vs dollars correct or remove
Legitimate extreme whale customer, viral post keep; cap/transform for sensitive models
The phenomenon itself fraud, machine failure keep; it's the target

stages.name: Errors: correct or remove
stages.html:
• Impossible values violate domain rules: fix units, re-derive, or drop.
  • Report upstream; an error class that recurs is a data contract issue.

stages.name: Legitimate extremes: keep, cap or transform
stages.html:
Model Action
Linear, kNN, K-means, NNs winsorise at percentiles, or log / Yeo-Johnson
Trees, GBMs usually nothing
Regression target with heavy tail robust loss (Huber) or transformed target

stages.name: The signal itself: never touch
stages.html:
• Fraud, intrusion, equipment failure: outliers are what you're predicting.
  • Cleaning them away produces a model that's excellent at normal data and useless for the task.

stages.name: Detection only flags
stages.html:
Method Assumes / suits
Z-score roughly normal data
IQR / percentiles robust, univariate
Isolation Forest multivariate, fast, few assumptions
LOF local density differences
One-Class SVM small, clean normal data

stages.name: Make it a pipeline policy
stages.html:
• Thresholds fitted on training folds; applied identically at serving.
  • Log counts and reasons for removed or capped rows.
  • An outlier policy is a data-contract decision, reviewable like code.

followUps.question: Cap or remove a legitimate extreme in a regression target?
followUps.html:
Usually neither. Keep the row and change the loss or the target.

Option Effect
Robust loss (Huber) extremes pull less
Transformed target (log) the tail is compressed
Remove real high values predictions biased downward exactly where the business may care most

followUps.question: Why is removing outliers before the split leaky?
followUps.html:
Two leaks at once.

  • Thresholds: the mean, std or percentiles are computed with test data.
  • Test distribution: it is now cleaner than production.

The evaluation then overstates performance on real traffic, which will contain those extremes.

followUps.question: How do you handle outliers at serving time?
followUps.html:
With the same fitted transform, plus an alert.

Serving:inputclip to training-derived bounds, or the same logmodel
Far outside the training range:alertlower trust or a fallback

The model is extrapolating there.

followUps.question: Isolation Forest flags 5% of rows. Remove them?
followUps.html:
Not blindly. 5% is a setting, not a finding.

Before removing anything:the contamination parameter set the share flaggedinspect a sample by originkeep them

Removing 5% of real behaviour hurts the model.

followUps.question: Who should own the outlier policy?
followUps.html:
The model owner together with the domain team.

Who Can tell
Engineers that a value is unusual
Domain experts whether it's impossible or merely rare

Document the policy with the data contract, so changes are reviewed and not made in a notebook.

dontSay: "Anything beyond 3σ goes." — assumes normality and ignores origin.
"I clean outliers in the whole dataset first." — leaky and unreproducible.
"Outliers are noise." — sometimes they're the task.

links.label: Judgment — Remove vs Cap vs Keep
links.target: 01-ML/04-Missing Data & Outliers/06-Judgment — Remove vs Cap vs Keep

links.label: Outlier Detection — Z score, IQR, Percentile, Winsorization
links.target: 01-ML/04-Missing Data & Outliers/04-Outlier Detection — Z-score, IQR, Percentile, Winsorization

links.label: Model Based Outliers — Isolation Forest, LOF, One Class SVM
links.target: 01-ML/04-Missing Data & Outliers/05-Model-Based Outliers — Isolation Forest, LOF, One-Class SVM

ml-dl-q34.testing: whether you can name concrete mechanisms, not "more features is bad".
ml-dl-q34.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Distances concentrate "Three concrete things break. First, distances concentrate. As dimensions grow, the nearest and farthest neighbours of a point end up almost the same distance away, so distance stops discriminating. Anything built on distance degrades first: kNN, K-means, kernel methods, and quietly, vector similarity search."
2 · Data becomes sparse "Second, data becomes sparse. The volume you need to cover grows exponentially with dimensions, so any fixed dataset becomes a thin scatter. Local methods and density estimators starve: there's no neighbourhood with enough points in it."
3 · Spurious correlations multiply "Third, spurious correlations multiply. With many features and finite rows, some features correlate with the target by pure chance, so overfitting risk rises and feature selection becomes large-scale multiple testing."
4 · Who breaks first, who resists "Who resists? Regularised linear models, because the penalty handles more features than rows. Trees and boosting, because axis-aligned splits ignore irrelevant dimensions reasonably well. And models with built-in selection like Lasso."
5 · The response ladder "My response ladder: prune with domain knowledge first, then filter, wrapper or embedded feature selection, and only then projection like PCA."
Close "Selection keeps interpretability; projection keeps variance but mixes features."

stages.name: Distances concentrate
stages.claim: near and far look the same
stages.html: Hit first: kNN, K-means, RBF-kernel SVMs, similarity search.

stages.name: Data becomes sparse
stages.html:
• To keep 10 bins per axis covered: 10 points in 1-D, 10¹⁰ in 10-D.
  • Density estimation, kNN and local regression find almost nothing in any neighbourhood.

stages.name: Spurious correlations multiply
stages.html:
• With 10,000 random features and 1,000 rows, some will correlate with any target.
  • Univariate filter selection becomes multiple testing: expect false discoveries unless corrected.

stages.name: Who breaks first, who resists
stages.html:
Suffers Resists
kNN, K-means, kernel methods (distance) L2/L1-regularised linear models
density estimators, local regression trees, GBMs (axis-aligned splits)
unregularised models with p ≈ n Lasso / Elastic Net (built-in selection)

stages.name: The response ladder
stages.html:
Step 1 — Domain pruning. Drop IDs, duplicates, near-constant and leaky columns.

Step 2 — Feature selection. Filter (mutual information, chi-square), wrapper (RFE), embedded (Lasso, tree importance). Keeps original, interpretable features.

Step 3 — Projection. PCA, or UMAP for visualisation. Keeps variance, loses interpretability.

Step 4 — Better representation. Learned embeddings for high-cardinality or text data.

followUps.question: Why do embedding search systems still work in 768 dimensions?
followUps.html:
Because real embeddings aren't uniform random points.

Data Distances
Isotropic, uniform concentrate: everything is equally far
Embeddings near a low-dimensional manifold keep meaning

That's also why cosine similarity on normalised vectors and ANN indexes work well in practice.

followUps.question: How does regularisation help when p > n?
followUps.html:
It picks one solution out of infinitely many perfect fits.

Penalty Picks
Ridge the smallest-norm solution
Lasso the sparsest solution

A little more bias for a lot less variance.

followUps.question: Feature selection or PCA for a regulated credit model?
followUps.html:
Selection.

Feature selection PCA
Output named, original features mixtures of features
Adverse-action reasons can be given to a customer can't be explained
Use the explanation surface internal exploration

followUps.question: Does gradient boosting have no dimensionality problem?
followUps.html:
More robust, not immune.

  • Problem: many irrelevant features dilute the split search and raise the chance of fitting noise, especially on small data.
  • Helps: column subsampling, early stopping, and removing junk features first.

followUps.question: How do you avoid false discoveries in filter selection?
followUps.html:
Three guards.

Guard What it stops
Selection inside CV folds validation data picking the features
Multiple-testing correction or stability selection features chosen by chance; keep those picked consistently across resamples
Permuted-target baseline mistaking noise for signal

dontSay: "More features always hurt." — trees and regularised models cope well.
"Just apply PCA." — it's the last rung, and it kills interpretability.
"Distance-based methods are fine with scaling." — scaling doesn't fix concentration.

links.label: PCA — Intuition, Math, Explained Variance & Limitations
links.target: 01-ML/05-Dimensionality Reduction/03-PCA — Intuition, Math, Explained Variance & Limitations

ml-dl-q35.testing: whether you know PCA's objective and its blind spots, not just "reduces dimensions".
ml-dl-q35.trap: using PCA before a classifier and assuming it keeps the useful signal.
ml-dl-q35.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The objective "PCA finds orthogonal directions of maximum variance in the data; equivalently, it's the linear projection with the smallest reconstruction error."
2 · The linear algebra "Mechanically, those directions are the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, or more stably the right singular vectors from an SVD of the centred data. Each eigenvalue is the variance explained by its component."
3 · Three assumptions "It quietly assumes three things. Linearity: components are linear combinations of features. That variance equals relevance: the high-variance directions are the ones that matter. And comparable scales: a feature measured in large units hijacks the first component unless you standardise."
4 · Where it silently fails "Where it silently fails: it's unsupervised, so the direction that separates your classes can live in a low-variance component you just threw away. It can't unfold non-linear structure like a swiss roll; that needs kernel PCA or UMAP. And components are mixtures of every feature, which is a real cost when you have to explain a model."
5 · Choosing k "To choose k, use explained-variance thresholds or the scree plot, but if the downstream task is supervised, pick k by the downstream metric."
6 · The supervised alternative "When labels exist and separation is the goal, LDA maximises class separation instead of variance."

stages.name: The objective
stages.html:
• First component: the direction along which projected data varies most.
  • Each next component: maximum remaining variance, orthogonal to the previous ones.
  • Same thing: the k-dimensional subspace that best reconstructs the data (least squares).

stages.name: The linear algebra
stages.html:
X centred (n × d)
C = XᵀX / (n − 1)            covariance
C v = λ v                    components v, variance λ
X = U Σ Vᵀ                   SVD: columns of V are components, λ = σ² / (n − 1)

SVD is preferred: numerically stabler and doesn't form XᵀX.

stages.name: Three assumptions
stages.html:
Assumption Violation Fix
Linear structure curved manifolds kernel PCA, UMAP
Variance = relevance signal in low-variance directions supervised methods, validate downstream
Comparable scales one big-unit feature dominates standardise first

stages.name: Where it silently fails
stages.html:
Point What it means
Discarded signal two classes separated along a low-variance axis collapse on top of each other.
Outliers variance is squared-distance based; a few extremes rotate the components.
Interpretability each component mixes all features, which is hard to defend to a regulator.
Leakage fitting PCA on all data before CV.

stages.name: Choosing k
stages.html:
• Compression or visualisation: cumulative explained variance (e.g. 90–95%) or the scree elbow.
  • Feeding a supervised model: treat k as a hyperparameter, tuned by CV on the downstream metric.

stages.name: The supervised alternative
stages.html:
• LDA maximises between-class separation relative to within-class spread; at most (classes − 1) components.
  • Use it when labels exist and separation is the point.

followUps.question: Why centre the data before PCA?
followUps.html:
Without centring, the first component points at the mean, not along the spread.

First component captures
Centred the direction of greatest variance
Not centred location

sklearn's PCA centres automatically; a raw SVD doesn't.

followUps.question: Does PCA help tree models?
followUps.html:
Usually not, and it can hurt.

Model family PCA
Trees rotation destroys the axis-aligned structure they split on, and interpretability
Linear or distance-based, correlated inputs can help

followUps.question: How do you use PCA without leakage?
followUps.html:
Put it in the pipeline.

Order:scalePCAmodel, all fitted on each training fold only

The fitted projection then ships with the model.

followUps.question: PCA vs t-SNE vs UMAP?
followUps.html:
PCA is the only one whose distances you can trust.

PCA t-SNE UMAP
Kind linear, deterministic non-linear non-linear, faster
Preserves global variance local neighbourhoods local, plus a bit more global
New points
Use features and plots visualisation only plots; map distances still not trustworthy

followUps.question: PCA on 10 million rows and 5,000 features?
followUps.html:
Avoid the full covariance matrix.

Plan:choose k on a samplerandomized SVD or IncrementalPCAtransform in batches

On GPU, cuML's PCA handles this comfortably.

dontSay: "PCA keeps the most important features." — it keeps the most variance, as mixtures.
"I don't need to scale for PCA." — big-unit features dominate.
"Explained variance tells me the right k for my classifier." — validate on the downstream metric.

links.label: PCA — Intuition, Math, Explained Variance & Limitations
links.target: 01-ML/05-Dimensionality Reduction/03-PCA — Intuition, Math, Explained Variance & Limitations

spine: Use it as a picture, not a ruler
ml-dl-q36.testing: whether you know which properties of an embedding are meaningful.
ml-dl-q36.trap: agreeing that the plot's cluster sizes and gaps are findings.
ml-dl-q36.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · What t-SNE preserves "I'd tell them the plot is a good picture but a bad ruler. t-SNE preserves local neighbourhoods: points that are close in the original space stay close. It deliberately doesn't preserve anything else. Distances between clusters are meaningless. Cluster sizes and densities are artifacts, because the algorithm tends to equalise them. And the layout changes with the perplexity setting and the random seed; at the wrong perplexity you can see clusters in pure noise."
2 · What it distorts "So the segment sizes and distances in the report aren't findings about customers."
3 · Use it as a picture, not a ruler "The legitimate use is visualisation and hypothesis generation. The fix is to cluster in the original space, or a PCA-reduced version of it, then use t-SNE only to look at the result."
4 · Cluster in the real space "UMAP is faster, keeps a bit more global structure and can place new points, but the same rule applies: don't measure the map."
5 · Validate the segments "Then validate the segments properly: silhouette in the clustering space, stability across seeds and resamples, and above all, whether the segments differ on business variables the clustering never saw."
6 · Say it kindly "And I'd say it kindly: it's like measuring country sizes on a Mercator map."
Close "The map is useful; the measurement isn't."

stages.name: What t-SNE preserves
stages.html:
high-D:  p(j|i) ∝ exp( −‖xᵢ − xⱼ‖² / 2σᵢ² )      ← how likely j is a neighbour of i
2-D:     q(i,j) ∝ ( 1 + ‖yᵢ − yⱼ‖² )⁻¹            ← heavy-tailed, so far points can spread out
minimise KL( P ‖ Q )                              ← only neighbour relations are matched
  • It matches the probability that points are neighbours in the original space and in 2-D.
  • Neighbours stay neighbours; that's the whole promise.

stages.name: What it distorts
stages.html:
Plot feature Meaningful?
Which points sit together mostly
Gap between clusters
Cluster size / area (densities equalised)
Cluster count depends on perplexity, can appear from noise
Layout, orientation changes with seed

stages.name: Use it as a picture, not a ruler
stages.html:
Use the plot for Don't use it for
spotting structure and outliers cluster sizes
finding label noise distances between clusters
a sanity look at embeddings defining the segments, or any reported number
  • Good for: spotting structure, outliers, label noise, a sanity look at embeddings.
  • Not for: sizes, distances, cluster definitions, or anything reported as a number.

stages.name: Cluster in the real space
stages.html:
• Scale features; optionally reduce with PCA.
  • Run K-means / GMM / HDBSCAN there.
  • Colour the t-SNE or UMAP plot by those cluster labels to show them.

stages.name: Validate the segments
stages.html:
Point What it means
Internal silhouette, Davies-Bouldin in the clustering space.
Stability same clusters across seeds, bootstrap samples (ARI between runs).
External significant differences on revenue, churn, product usage not used to build them.

stages.name: Say it kindly
stages.html: "The picture is right about neighbours and wrong about sizes, like a world map. Let's define segments in the data, then use the plot to show them."

followUps.question: What does perplexity control?
followUps.html:
Roughly the effective number of neighbours each point considers.

Perplexity Effect
Low very local structure; can fragment data into spurious clusters
High merges clusters

Always compare several values before reading structure into a plot.

followUps.question: Is UMAP safe to cluster on?
followUps.html:
Safer than t-SNE, and still not trustworthy on its own.

  • Common recipe: UMAP, then HDBSCAN.
  • Still distorted: distances and densities depend on its parameters.
  • If you do it: validate stability and external differences just as strictly, and don't report map distances.

followUps.question: Can new customers be placed on a t-SNE map?
followUps.html:
Not properly.

Method New points
Standard t-SNE no transform; a rerun moves everything
UMAP, parametric t-SNE can transform new data

followUps.question: The stakeholders already loved the plot. How do you correct course?
followUps.html:
Keep the visual, change the evidence.

Path:re-derive the segments properlyshow which key segments still hold (maybe most)present sizes and differences from the real clustering

Frame it as making the result defensible, not as wrong work.

followUps.question: What would make you trust a segmentation?
followUps.html:
Four tests.

Test Passes when
Stability it survives resampling
External difference segments differ on variables they weren't built from
Persistence they hold over time
Actionability each fits in one actionable sentence

dontSay: "Segment B is twice as big as segment C." (from the plot) — sizes are artifacts.
"These two groups are far apart, so very different." — inter-cluster gaps mean nothing.
"t-SNE is wrong, don't use it." — it's a fine visualisation tool.

spine: Ask what the model is for
Constant variance and normality break intervals
ml-dl-q37.testing: whether you separate what breaks coefficients, predictions, standard errors and interpretation.
ml-dl-q37.trap: reciting LINE as a checklist where every violation is fatal.
ml-dl-q37.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Ask what the model is for "Which assumptions matter depends on whether the model is for prediction or for explanation, because each one breaks something different."
2 · Linearity breaks predictions "Linearity breaks predictions. If the true relationship is curved, the model is simply wrong. You fix it with transforms, polynomial or spline terms, or a different model; a residuals-versus-fitted plot with structure is the tell."
3 · Independence breaks validation "Independence of errors breaks inference and validation. With time series or grouped data, errors are correlated, so standard errors and random cross-validation are wildly optimistic. It's the one people violate without noticing."
4 · Constant variance and normality break intervals "Constant variance and normality of errors break intervals, not point predictions. The coefficients stay unbiased; the confidence and prediction intervals lie. Fix with robust standard errors, weighted least squares, or modelling the variance."
5 · Multicollinearity breaks interpretation "Multicollinearity breaks interpretation. Correlated predictors give unstable, sign-flipping coefficients with huge VIFs while predictions stay fine. That's fatal if the deliverable is 'which factor matters', harmless if it's the forecast."
6 · Diagnose with residuals "So for prediction I care most about linearity and independence; for explanation I need all of them."

stages.name: Ask what the model is for
stages.html:
Assumption Breaks Matters for prediction? For explanation?
Linearity predictions (bias)
Independent errors standard errors, CV (validation)
Homoscedasticity intervals, SEs only for intervals
Normal errors small-sample inference rarely (small n)
No multicollinearity coefficient stability

stages.name: Linearity breaks predictions
stages.html:
y = β₀ + β₁x₁ + … + βₚxₚ + ε,    ε ~ N(0, σ²), independent    ← the model every assumption refers to
Symptom Fix
a curved pattern in residuals vs fitted log or Box-Cox, polynomial or spline terms, interactions, or a non-linear model
  • Symptom: curved pattern in residuals vs fitted.
  • Fix: log/Box-Cox, polynomial or spline terms, interactions, or a non-linear model.

stages.name: Independence breaks validation
stages.html:
Where it happens Symptom Fix
time series, repeated rows per customer, clustered data autocorrelated residuals (Durbin-Watson, ACF); CV far above production time- or group-aware splits, lagged terms, mixed models, clustered standard errors
  • Time series, repeated measures per customer, clustered data.
  • Symptoms: autocorrelated residuals (Durbin-Watson, ACF plot), CV scores far above production.
  • Fix: time/group-aware splits, lagged terms, mixed models, clustered standard errors.

stages.name: Constant variance and normality break intervals
stages.html:
• Heteroscedasticity: fan-shaped residuals; SEs and intervals wrong, coefficients unbiased.
  • Fix: robust (HC) standard errors, weighted least squares, log target.
  • Normality matters mainly for small-sample inference; by the CLT, less so at scale.

stages.name: Multicollinearity breaks interpretation
stages.html:
• VIF > 5–10: coefficients unstable, can flip sign between samples.
  • Fix for explanation: drop or combine correlated features, Ridge, or domain-driven selection.
  • For prediction: often leave it.

stages.name: Diagnose with residuals
stages.html: Residuals vs fitted, Q-Q plot, scale-location, residuals vs time/order. Plus VIFs. Ten minutes that tell you which conclusions you're allowed to draw.

followUps.question: Must the features be normally distributed?
followUps.html:
No. The assumption is about the errors, not the inputs.

Must be normal?
Features X no; skewed features are fine
Errors yes, for the standard intervals and tests

Transforming a skewed feature can help linearity, but normality of X isn't required.

followUps.question: Coefficients flip sign when you add a feature. Why?
followUps.html:
Multicollinearity, or the new feature is a confounder.

What changed:the coefficient now means "effect holding the new feature constant"that can differ in sign from the marginal relationship (Simpson's-paradox territory)

Check VIFs and think causally before interpreting.

followUps.question: How does heteroscedasticity hurt a pricing model's prediction intervals?
followUps.html:
One interval width is wrong at both ends.

Item A single width is Consequence
Cheap too wide wasted caution
Expensive too narrow risk underestimated exactly where the money is largest

Fix: model log price, or use quantile regression for the interval bounds.

followUps.question: Is R² a good check of assumptions?
followUps.html:
No. R² measures variance explained, not validity.

  • Counter-example: high R² with badly autocorrelated or heteroscedastic residuals.
  • Look at instead: residual plots and out-of-sample error.

followUps.question: An executive asks "what drives sales?" from your regression. What caveats do you give?
followUps.html:
Three caveats, then a better design.

Caveat Meaning
Association, not cause a coefficient is an effect holding the other variables fixed
Confounders and collinearity can mislead
Intervals assume the error model holds

For a decision, pair the regression with an experiment or a causal design.

dontSay: "Features must be normally distributed." — it's the errors.
"Multicollinearity ruins predictions." — it ruins interpretation.
"Every assumption must hold or the model is useless." — depends on the use.

links.label: Linear Regression — OLS Closed Form & Matrix Formulation
links.target: 01-ML/06-Regression Models/01-Linear Regression — OLS Closed Form & Matrix Formulation

ml-dl-q38.testing: the geometric reason L1 gives zeros, and choosing by the structure of the truth.
ml-dl-q38.trap: "Lasso is better because it selects features."
ml-dl-q38.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Both trade bias for variance "Both add a penalty on coefficient size, trading a little bias for a lot less variance. They differ in the shape of the penalty."
2 · Ridge: smooth shrinkage "Ridge uses L2, the sum of squared coefficients. It shrinks everything smoothly toward zero but never exactly to zero. Geometrically the constraint region is a circle, with no corners for the loss contours to touch on an axis. It wins when there are many small, correlated effects: it spreads weight across correlated features and stabilises them."
3 · Lasso: exact zeros from corners "Lasso uses L1, the sum of absolute values. Its constraint region is a diamond whose corners sit on the axes, so the optimum often lands exactly on a corner, with some coefficients at zero. That's built-in feature selection, and it wins when the truth is sparse: a few real drivers among many candidates."
4 · Lasso's weakness "Lasso's weakness: among correlated features it picks one arbitrarily and drops the rest, so the selection is unstable, and with more features than rows it selects at most n."
5 · Elastic Net "Elastic Net blends both: selection plus grouped stability for correlated features."
6 · Practicalities "Two practicalities: all of them need standardised features, because the penalty is scale-sensitive, and lambda is chosen by cross-validation."
Close "For depth: Ridge is a Gaussian prior on coefficients, Lasso a Laplace prior."

stages.name: Both trade bias for variance
stages.html:
Ridge:        min ‖y − Xβ‖² + λ Σ βⱼ²
Lasso:        min ‖y − Xβ‖² + λ Σ |βⱼ|
Elastic Net:  min ‖y − Xβ‖² + λ [ α Σ |βⱼ| + (1 − α) Σ βⱼ² ]

stages.name: Ridge: smooth shrinkage
stages.html:
• Circle-shaped constraint: loss contours touch it at a point generally off the axes, so no exact zeros.
  • Closed form: β = (XᵀX + λI)⁻¹Xᵀy; the λI term also fixes singular XᵀX.
  • Correlated features share weight instead of one hogging it.

stages.name: Lasso: exact zeros from corners
stages.html:
• Diamond corners lie on the axes; contours usually first touch at a corner.
  • Result: sparse β, automatic selection, easier explanation.
  • No closed form; solved by coordinate descent.

stages.name: Lasso's weakness
stages.html:
• Picks one of a correlated group arbitrarily; which one changes across resamples.
  • With p > n, selects at most n features.
  • Selection instability is a problem when "which features matter" is the deliverable.

stages.name: Elastic Net
stages.html:
• L1 part gives sparsity; L2 part groups correlated features so they enter or leave together.
  • Two hyperparameters (λ, α), both by CV.
Truth / data Pick
Many small correlated effects Ridge
Few strong drivers, low correlation Lasso
Sparse but correlated groups, p ≫ n Elastic Net

stages.name: Practicalities
stages.html:
• Standardise features, or the penalty shrinks by units rather than importance.
  • Tune λ on a log grid with CV (LassoCV, ElasticNetCV).
  • Bayesian view: Ridge = Gaussian prior, Lasso = Laplace prior on β.

followUps.question: Why exactly does L1 produce zeros and L2 doesn't?
followUps.html:
It's in the penalty's gradient.

L2: d/dβ (λβ²)  = 2λβ          ← shrinks as β shrinks, so it never pushes all the way
L1: d/dβ (λ|β|) = λ·sign(β)    ← constant push, whatever the size

So L1 pushes small coefficients to exactly zero and holds them there (soft-thresholding).

followUps.question: Should you trust Lasso's selected features as "the drivers"?
followUps.html:
Cautiously. With correlated features the choice is arbitrary and unstable.

Before calling them causes:Elastic Netstability selectionreport the stable ones

Stability selection asks how often a feature is chosen across bootstraps. And it's still association.

followUps.question: Is regularisation relevant for gradient boosting?
followUps.html:
Yes, in its own form.

XGBoost control Kind
alpha L1 on leaf weights
lambda L2 on leaf weights
Depth, learning rate, subsampling structural regularisation

Same principle: constrain complexity to reduce variance.

followUps.question: How do you pick λ?
followUps.html:
Cross-validation over a log-spaced grid.

One-standard-error rule:find the λ with minimum CV errortake the largest λ within one SE of ita simpler model with statistically equivalent performance

followUps.question: Where does weight decay in neural nets fit?
followUps.html:
Weight decay is L2 regularisation applied to the network's weights.

Optimiser Weight decay
SGD equals L2 shrinkage
Adam mixed into the gradient, so the effective penalty varies by parameter
AdamW decoupled from the gradient: true shrinkage again

dontSay: "Lasso is always better because it selects features." — depends on the truth's structure.
"Ridge sets unimportant coefficients to zero." — it never reaches zero.
"No need to scale for regularisation." — the penalty is scale-sensitive.

spine: Three ways to estimate the gradient
Problem 2: one step size for all
What still dominates: the learning rate
ml-dl-q39.testing: whether you can name the two problems optimizers solve and which feature fixes which.
ml-dl-q39.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Three ways to estimate the gradient "The three variants differ in how much data each gradient estimate uses."
2 · Problem 1: noisy direction "Batch gradient descent uses the whole dataset per step: exact gradient, deterministic, but one slow step per pass and memory-bound. Stochastic gradient descent uses one example: very cheap, very noisy. The noise helps escape shallow minima but makes convergence jittery. Mini-batch is the production compromise: vectorised on GPUs and less noisy, with batch size trading gradient noise against steps per second."
3 · Problem 2: one step size for all "Vanilla SGD then has two separate problems. The direction is noisy and oscillates across narrow valleys; momentum fixes that by following an exponential moving average of gradients, which damps the zigzag and speeds up consistent directions."
4 · Adam = both fixes "The second problem: one learning rate for every parameter. AdaGrad and RMSProp fix that by dividing each parameter's step by a running magnitude of its past gradients, so rarely updated parameters get bigger steps. RMSProp's moving average stops AdaGrad's step size shrinking to zero."
5 · What still dominates: the learning rate "Adam is momentum plus RMSProp, with bias correction for the first steps, so it solves both at once, which is why it's the default."
Close "The caveats: tuned SGD with momentum sometimes generalises slightly better, AdamW is the modern variant, and the learning-rate schedule still matters more than the choice between good optimizers."

stages.name: Three ways to estimate the gradient
stages.html:
Variant Data per step Pros Cons
Batch all n exact, deterministic slow per step, memory
Stochastic 1 cheap, noise escapes shallow minima noisy, poor hardware use
Mini-batch 32–4096 GPU-efficient, moderate noise batch size is a hyperparameter

stages.name: Problem 1: noisy direction
stages.html:
v ← β v + (1 − β) g          (β ≈ 0.9)
θ ← θ − η v
  • Averages out zigzags across steep, narrow valleys; accelerates along consistent slopes.
  • Nesterov: evaluate the gradient at the look-ahead position for slightly better corrections.

stages.name: Problem 2: one step size for all
stages.html:
s ← β₂ s + (1 − β₂) g²       RMSProp (AdaGrad sums instead: s ← s + g²)
θ ← θ − η g / (√s + ε)
  • Parameters with large gradients take smaller steps; rare features get larger ones.
  • AdaGrad's sum only grows, so its step size decays to zero; RMSProp's moving average avoids that.

stages.name: Adam = both fixes
stages.html:
m ← β₁ m + (1 − β₁) g        direction (momentum)
v ← β₂ v + (1 − β₂) g²       scale (RMSProp)
m̂ = m / (1 − β₁ᵗ),  v̂ = v / (1 − β₂ᵗ)      correct the zero-initialised start
θ ← θ − η m̂ / (√v̂ + ε)
  • AdamW: apply weight decay directly to θ, not through the gradient (see Q62).

stages.name: What still dominates: the learning rate
stages.html:
• A bad LR ruins any optimizer; a good schedule (warmup, then cosine or step decay) matters more than SGD vs Adam.
  • Batch size and LR interact: larger batches often need proportionally larger LR (linear scaling rule) plus warmup.

followUps.question: Why does SGD sometimes generalise better than Adam?
followUps.html:
One common explanation: SGD's noise steers it to flatter minima.

SGD Adam
Step size uniform, noisy scaled per parameter
Tends towards flatter minima, which generalise better can settle into sharper ones

It's task-dependent; for transformers, AdamW is the standard anyway.

followUps.question: What does bias correction fix?
followUps.html:
The moving averages start at zero, so early on they are biased toward zero.

m̂ = m / (1 − β₁ᵗ)      v̂ = v / (1 − β₂ᵗ)     ← v is worst hit, with β₂ = 0.999

Without it the first steps would be the wrong size. The effect fades after a few thousand steps.

followUps.question: How does batch size affect training?
followUps.html:
Bigger batches trade noise for fewer updates.

Bigger batch
Gain less noisy gradients, better hardware utilisation
Cost fewer updates per epoch
Past a point diminishing returns, sometimes worse generalisation

Scale the learning rate with batch size and use warmup when going large.

followUps.question: Is Adam's memory cost relevant?
followUps.html:
Yes, at scale.

Adam state = 2 fp32 values per parameter = 8 bytes per parameter
7B parameters × 8 bytes ≈ 56 GB           ← on top of weights and gradients

That's why sharded optimisers (ZeRO) and 8-bit optimisers exist.

followUps.question: When would you still use plain SGD with momentum?
followUps.html:
In three places.

Case Why
CNN training in computer vision still common, with a well-tuned schedule
Tight memory avoids Adam's extra state
Linear models on huge sparse data SGD-based solvers are common

dontSay: "Adam is always better." — it solves two specific problems; the LR schedule still dominates.
"Mini-batch is just faster SGD." — it's a variance-throughput trade-off.
"Momentum adapts the learning rate." — that's the second moment's job.

spine: The loss is where business cost enters
ml-dl-q40.testing: whether you derive the loss from the cost structure.
ml-dl-q40.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Two requirements in one sentence "The sentence hides two requirements: robustness to a heavy tail, and asymmetry, because under-forecasting costs more than over-forecasting."
2 · Why MSE and MAE fail "MSE fails both. It squares errors, so the occasional huge order dominates training, and it's symmetric. MAE fixes robustness, since it predicts the median and grows linearly, but it's still symmetric and its constant gradient makes optimisation cruder."
3 · Huber for the tail "Huber blends the two: squared near zero, linear in the tails, with delta setting the crossover. That gives robustness with clean gradients, but it's still symmetric."
4 · Quantile loss for the asymmetry "The direct answer is quantile, or pinball, loss. Training at, say, the 0.8 quantile penalises under-prediction four times as much as over-prediction, so the business asymmetry lives in the objective instead of a fudge added afterwards. Gradient boosting libraries support it natively."
5 · Log target as an alternative "An alternative for the tail is modelling log of order value, but you then need to correct the retransformation bias, and it's still symmetric in log space."
6 · The loss is where business cost enters "The meta-point I'd say out loud: the loss function is where business cost enters the model."
Close "Choosing it by convention instead of by the cost structure is the actual mistake."

stages.name: Two requirements in one sentence
stages.html:
Requirement Needs
"occasionally huge" a loss robust to large errors
"under-forecasting costs more" a loss whose penalty depends on the error's sign

stages.name: Why MSE and MAE fail
stages.html:
Loss Tail-robust Asymmetric Predicts
MSE mean
MAE median
Huber between mean and median
Quantile (τ) τ-quantile

stages.name: Huber for the tail
stages.html:
• Quadratic for |error| < δ, linear beyond.
  • δ chosen relative to the typical error scale; tune by CV.
  • Good when the tail is noise you don't want to chase.

stages.name: Quantile loss for the asymmetry
stages.html:
• Pick τ from the cost ratio: if under costs c_u and over costs c_o per unit, τ = c_u / (c_u + c_o). Under 4× over → τ = 0.8.
  • LightGBM / XGBoost: objective="quantile", alpha=0.8.

stages.name: Log target as an alternative
stages.html:
• Train on log(value): compresses whales, errors become roughly multiplicative.
  • Retransformation: exp(prediction) estimates the median, not the mean; apply a smearing correction if you need the mean.
  • Still symmetric in log space; combine with a quantile objective if asymmetry matters.

stages.name: The loss is where business cost enters
stages.html: Evaluate with the same cost: report expected business cost (asymmetric) on a holdout, not RMSE.

followUps.question: How do you get the quantile from the cost ratio?
followUps.html:
The pinball loss at τ is minimised by the τ-quantile, and the costs fix τ.

τ = c_u / (c_u + c_o)        ← c_u = cost of under-forecasting, c_o = cost of over
c_u = 4, c_o = 1  →  τ = 4 / 5 = 0.8

Expected cost is lowest where the probability of being under equals c_o / (c_u + c_o).

followUps.question: Why not train MSE and add a safety margin afterwards?
followUps.html:
Because a constant margin ignores that uncertainty varies by order.

MSE plus a fixed margin Quantile regression
Buffer the same for every order conditional on the input
Small, predictable orders over-buffered little buffer
Volatile orders under-buffered a large buffer

Cheaper on average for the same protection.

followUps.question: Can you get prediction intervals this way?
followUps.html:
Yes: train one quantile model per bound.

80% interval:model at τ = 0.1model at τ = 0.9check coverage: about 80% of holdout actuals fall inside

Watch for quantile crossing, where the lower bound lands above the upper.

followUps.question: What metric do you report?
followUps.html:
The business cost with the real asymmetry, plus quantile coverage.

cost = 4 × under-units + 1 × over-units     ← in money

RMSE on a quantile model is meaningless, because it rewards predicting the mean.

followUps.question: When would you use Tweedie or Poisson loss instead?
followUps.html:
When many orders are zero and the rest are positive and skewed, like spend per visitor.

Part of the target Tweedie models it as
The zeros a point mass at zero
The positive orders a continuous, skewed tail

You can still add the asymmetry with a quantile-based decision on top.

dontSay: "MSE because it's the standard regression loss." — fails both requirements.
"Log the target and it's handled." — fixes the tail, not the asymmetry.
"We'll add 20% to every forecast." — ignores varying uncertainty.

spine: Why it's first: it prices the problem
ml-dl-q41.testing: the mechanism, plus judgement about baselines and production value.
ml-dl-q41.trap: "it squashes a linear output through a sigmoid."
ml-dl-q41.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · What it models: linear log-odds "Mechanically, it models the log-odds of the positive class as a linear function of the features. The sigmoid isn't the model; it's just the function that turns log-odds back into a probability. It's trained by maximum likelihood, which is the same as minimising cross-entropy, and each coefficient is a log-odds ratio: a directly interpretable effect size."
3 · Why it's first: it prices the problem "I train it first because it prices the problem. If gradient boosting only beats it by a hair, the signal is mostly linear and I ship the simple thing. If there's a big gap, that tells me the problem needs interactions and non-linearity, and by how much."
4 · Operational virtues "It also has operational virtues that keep it in production at serious companies. Its probabilities are reasonably calibrated out of the box, which trees' aren't. It scores in microseconds on any hardware, the artifact is tiny, it's stable across retrains, and it's easy to explain to model-risk teams and regulators."
5 · Making it competitive "And with regularisation and good feature engineering, interactions, binning or weight-of-evidence encoding, it stays genuinely competitive on wide, sparse data."
Close "Ads and credit-risk stacks relied on it for decades for exactly that reason."

stages.name: What it models: linear log-odds
stages.html:
log( p / (1 − p) ) = β₀ + β·x          the model
p = 1 / (1 + e^−(β₀ + β·x))            inverse link back to probability
  • A one-unit increase in xⱼ multiplies the odds by e^βⱼ.

stages.name: How it's trained: maximum likelihood
stages.html:
• Maximise Π p^y (1 − p)^(1−y) ⇔ minimise binary cross-entropy.
  • Convex: one global optimum, solved with L-BFGS, Newton or SGD.
  • Regularisation (L2 default in sklearn, C = 1/λ) prevents blow-up on separable data.

stages.name: Why it's first: it prices the problem
stages.html:
Logistic vs boosting gap Reading
tiny signal mostly linear; ship logistic
moderate interactions matter; boosting may be worth its cost
huge strongly non-linear, or check for leakage in the complex model

stages.name: Operational virtues
stages.html:
• Calibrated probabilities (with a well-specified model), good for thresholds and expected value.
  • Microsecond scoring, kilobyte artifact, CPU or edge.
  • Explainable coefficients and reason codes; auditors understand it.
  • Stable across retrains; small, reviewable changes.

stages.name: Making it competitive
stages.html:
• Interactions and polynomial terms for known effects.
  • Binning / weight-of-evidence for non-linear numeric effects (credit scorecards).
  • One-hot or hashed high-cardinality categoricals on sparse data, with L1/L2.
  • Multiclass: softmax (multinomial) or one-vs-rest.

followUps.question: Why cross-entropy and not MSE for logistic regression?
followUps.html:
Cross-entropy is its likelihood, and it's convex in the coefficients.

Cross-entropy MSE through a sigmoid
Principled? yes: the likelihood no
Surface convex non-convex
Confidently wrong large gradient vanishing gradient

Q19 has the gradient argument.

followUps.question: What happens with perfectly separable data?
followUps.html:
Unregularised, the coefficients diverge.

Chain:perfect separationlikelihood keeps improving as coefficients growcoefficients → ∞probabilities become 0 or 1

Regularisation keeps them finite, which is one reason sklearn regularises by default.

followUps.question: Is it really calibrated out of the box?
followUps.html:
Typically close, when it's well specified and left alone.

Distorts calibration
Strong regularisation
Class weights
Resampling

Always check a reliability curve before using the probabilities in a decision.

followUps.question: How do you interpret a coefficient of 0.7 on a standardised feature?
followUps.html:
One standard deviation up multiplies the odds by about 2, holding the other features fixed.

odds ratio = e^0.7 ≈ 2

It's association, not causation, and correlated features make individual coefficients less stable.

followUps.question: When would you ship logistic over a better-scoring GBM?
followUps.html:
Price the gap, then decide.

Ship logistic when
The gain is small within noise, or small in business terms
Regulators need transparent reasons
Latency or hardware is tight
Operations stability and easy monitoring outweigh a small accuracy win

dontSay: "It squashes a linear score with a sigmoid." — that's the link, not the model.
"It's outdated." — it's the baseline and still a production workhorse.
"It can't model non-linearity." — with feature engineering it can.

ml-dl-q42.testing: breadth under time pressure, with a structural reason for each weakness.
ml-dl-q42.trap: long answers per model; this is rapid fire.
ml-dl-q42.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Decision tree "Decision tree. Killer property: human-readable rules, handles mixed types and missing values, and needs no preprocessing. Weakness: high variance. Small changes in the data restructure the whole tree, so a single tree is almost always beaten by its own ensemble. Depth and minimum leaf size are its bias-variance dials."
2 · kNN "kNN. Killer property: zero training and arbitrarily complex decision boundaries, which makes it a strong lazy baseline. Weakness: inference cost and the curse of dimensionality. It stores and searches the data at query time, distances lose meaning as dimensions grow, and it needs scaling. In production it becomes an approximate-nearest-neighbour index, at which point it's really a retrieval system."
3 · Naive Bayes "Naive Bayes. Killer property: absurdly fast, works with tiny data and huge sparse vocabularies like text, and updates online. Weakness: the conditional-independence assumption makes its probabilities badly calibrated and overconfident, even when the ranking is decent. Fine as a filter, wrong as a probability source."
4 · The pattern: regime specialists "The pattern: each is a regime specialist. Trees for interpretable tabular rules, kNN when data is small and local structure is everything, naive Bayes for sparse counts."
Close "And all three are baselines that price the problem before boosting."

stages.name: Decision tree
stages.html:
Point What it means
Killer if-then rules anyone can audit; mixed types, missing values, no scaling.
Weakness high variance; greedy splits change drastically with small data changes.
Dials max_depth, min_samples_leaf, cost-complexity pruning.
Usually superseded by Random Forest (variance) or boosting (bias).

stages.name: kNN
stages.html:
Point What it means
Killer instant "training", flexible boundaries, intuitive.
Weakness O(n·d) per query, memory = the dataset, distance concentration in high d, needs scaling.
Production form ANN index (FAISS/HNSW); recommendation and semantic search.

stages.name: Naive Bayes
stages.html:
Point What it means
Killer trains in one pass, tiny data, huge sparse features, online updates.
Weakness assumes features independent given the class; correlated features double-count evidence → extreme probabilities.
Variants Multinomial (counts, text), Bernoulli (binary), Gaussian (continuous).

stages.name: The pattern: regime specialists
stages.html:
Model Best regime Avoid when
Decision tree need readable rules accuracy matters more than readability
kNN small data, local structure high d, tight latency, huge n
Naive Bayes sparse text/counts, very little data calibrated probabilities needed

stages.name: Where each still ships
stages.html:
• Tree: policy rules, compliance-friendly models, surrogate explanations.
  • kNN: similarity search, recommendation candidates, embedding lookups.
  • Naive Bayes: spam and text triage, very-low-latency first-pass filters.

followUps.question: How do you fix naive Bayes calibration?
followUps.html:
Post-hoc calibration on held-out data, or fewer correlated features.

Use Fix
Probabilities needed Platt or isotonic
Ranking only (spam filter with a tuned threshold) maybe none

followUps.question: Why does Random Forest fix the tree's weakness but not boosting's style?
followUps.html:
Because they attack different errors.

Random Forest Boosting
Trees deep, decorrelated shallow
Combines by averaging adding corrections
Removes variance, the single tree's problem bias

Both beat one tree, for different reasons (Q11).

followUps.question: How do you choose k in kNN?
followUps.html:
Cross-validate.

k Behaviour
Small low bias, high variance
Large smooths
  • Odd k for binary classification, to avoid ties.
  • Distance-weighted voting.
  • Scale features first, always.

followUps.question: Why does naive Bayes work well for text despite a false assumption?
followUps.html:
Because classification only needs the right class to score highest, not correct probabilities.

  • Violated independence: distorts magnitudes, but often preserves the ranking.
  • Huge sparse vocabularies: its low variance beats more flexible models on small data.

followUps.question: Would you ship a single decision tree?
followUps.html:
Yes, when the requirement is auditable rules: a compliance policy, or a triage rule set humans must follow.

Conditions:constrain depthvalidate stability across resamplescompare accuracy with an ensemble

The comparison makes the trade-off explicit.

dontSay: "Naive Bayes probabilities are good because it's Bayesian." — independence breaks calibration.
"kNN is cheap." — cheap to train, expensive to serve.
"Decision trees are the best because interpretable." — high variance alone.

ml-dl-q43.testing: whether you verify before debating, and price accuracy against operational cost.
ml-dl-q43.trap: debating ship-or-not before checking the 0.4 is real.
ml-dl-q43.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · First, is the gain real? "Before arguing either side, I'd check the gain is real. The meta-learner must be trained on out-of-fold predictions from the base models; training it on in-sample predictions is leakage and the 0.4 could be fiction. Then I'd re-measure on a time-split holdout with a confidence interval, because 0.4 points is often inside the noise."
2 · The case for shipping "If it's real, the case for shipping: at high volume in ads, risk or pricing, 0.4 AUC can translate into real money that dwarfs the infrastructure cost. And genuinely diverse base models, say linear plus trees plus a neural net, hedge each other's failure modes."
3 · The case against "The case against is an operations list. You now version, retrain, monitor and keep consistent several models instead of one. Inference latency and cost multiply. Debugging drift becomes 'which of five models moved?'. Explainability gets harder. And stacking gains often shrink under drift, because the meta-weights were fit to one period's error structure."
4 · Middle paths "Middle paths: a simple weighted blend of two diverse models often captures most of the gain, or distil the ensemble into a single student model for serving."
5 · Decide in money "The deciding move is to price the 0.4 in money and let the ops cost argue against it honestly."

stages.name: First, is the gain real?
stages.html:
• Out-of-fold meta-training: base models predict on folds they didn't train on; the meta-learner trains on those predictions.
  • Time-split holdout with a bootstrap CI on the AUC difference.
  • Keep the meta-learner simple (logistic, ridge); the diversity of bases does the work.

stages.name: The case for shipping
stages.html:
• High-volume decisions: small ranking gains compound (ads, credit, fraud, pricing).
  • Diverse bases reduce correlated failure modes.
  • The value is measurable in an A/B test.

stages.name: The case against
stages.html:
Cost Why it hurts
N models to retrain, version, monitor N× failure surface
Latency and compute sequential or parallel inference of all bases
Drift debugging which component moved?
Explainability reason codes across a blend
Gain decay meta-weights fit to one era

stages.name: Middle paths
stages.claim: most of the gain, less cost
stages.html:
Experiment 1

Weighted blend

Average two genuinely different models (e.g. GBM + logistic) with a weight tuned on validation.

Why? Most stacking gain comes from diversity, not a clever meta-learner.

Best suited when two diverse models are already in production or cheap to run.

Experiment 2

Distillation

Train one student model on the ensemble's predictions.

Why? Serve one model with most of the ensemble's accuracy.

Best suited when latency or ops cost is the main objection.

stages.name: Decide in money
stages.html: Convert 0.4 AUC into expected profit or loss at the operating point, subtract the added infra and team cost, and confirm with an A/B test. If it doesn't clear a pre-agreed bar, ship the single model.

followUps.question: Why must the meta-learner train on out-of-fold predictions?
followUps.html:
Because in-sample predictions are overconfident: the bases saw those rows.

Meta-learner trained on Learns
In-sample predictions to trust whichever base overfits most; that won't hold on new data
Out-of-fold predictions what the bases actually produce at serving time

followUps.question: The bases are three GBMs with different seeds. Worth stacking?
followUps.html:
Rarely. Their errors are highly correlated, so there's little to combine.

Bases Do
Same family, different seeds simple averaging: it captures the small variance cut
Different model families or feature views stacking pays off

followUps.question: How would you monitor a stacked model in production?
followUps.html:
Watch the parts, not only the final score.

  • Each base's score distribution.
  • The meta-model's inputs.
  • The meta-weights, re-checked periodically on recent data.

A shift in one base explains most incidents, so it has to be visible separately.

followUps.question: Is 0.4 AUC points large?
followUps.html:
It depends on the operating point and the volume.

Where the gain sits Verdict
Top of a fraud queue could be meaningful
Below the threshold, in cases nobody looks at worthless

Measure precision and recall at the actual operating point.

followUps.question: When is stacking clearly worth it?
followUps.html:
Where each point of accuracy is worth money and the team can maintain several models.

  • Competitions.
  • High-stakes, high-volume systems with strong MLOps.

Even then, check that a blend or distillation doesn't get there cheaper.

dontSay: "Ship it, it's higher." — verify, then price.
"Never use ensembles in production." — sometimes worth it.
"The meta-learner should be a GBM too." — keep it simple.

ml-dl-q44.testing: whether you know what each importance measures and its biases.
ml-dl-q44.trap: picking one as "the truth" without saying what it measures.
ml-dl-q44.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · What gain importance counts "I'd trust SHAP more, but first say what each one measures, because they answer different questions."
2 · Its biases "XGBoost's default importance, gain or split count, measures how much each feature was used during training. It's biased toward high-cardinality and continuous features, which offer more split points; correlated features split the credit unpredictably; and it describes the training set, not generalisation."
3 · Permutation importance "Permutation importance shuffles a feature on validation data and measures the drop in performance. That's closer to what the model actually relies on, but correlated features mask each other: shuffle one and its twin covers for it."
4 · SHAP "SHAP allocates each prediction's difference from the baseline across features, with consistency guarantees from Shapley values, and gives both local and global views. TreeSHAP computes it exactly and fast for trees. It's generally the most trustworthy of the three, though it also spreads credit across correlated features rather than resolving them."
5 · None is causal "None of them is causal. They all describe the model, not the world, and a leaky feature will top all three charts."
6 · Use disagreements as a diagnostic "In practice I use SHAP for rankings and explanations, permutation as a cross-check, and treat disagreements as a diagnostic: they usually point to correlated clusters or leakage."

stages.name: What gain importance counts
stages.html:
Point What it means
Gain total loss reduction from splits on the feature.
Weight / split count how often the feature is used.
Cover how many samples those splits affected.
  • All measured on training data, inside the fitting process.

stages.name: Its biases
stages.html:
Bias Effect
High cardinality / continuous more candidate splits → inflated importance
Correlated features arbitrary credit split between twins
Training-set based rewards features the model overfit on
Metric choice gain, weight, cover can rank differently from each other

stages.name: Permutation importance
stages.html:
• Shuffle one column in validation data; importance = metric drop.
  • Model-agnostic, generalisation-aware.
  • Weakness: correlated features cover for each other; shuffling creates unrealistic rows.

stages.name: SHAP
stages.html:
• Local: each prediction's deviation from the baseline, split across features, summing exactly.
  • Global: mean |SHAP| per feature; beeswarm shows direction and spread.
  • TreeSHAP: exact and fast for tree ensembles.
  • Still shares credit among correlated features.

stages.name: None is causal
stages.html: Every method explains the model's behaviour. A leaked feature, or a proxy for something else, can top every chart. Importance ≠ cause ≠ acceptable-to-use.

stages.name: Use disagreements as a diagnostic
stages.html:
Pattern Likely reason
High gain, low permutation/SHAP high-cardinality feature used for noisy splits
High SHAP, low permutation correlated twin covers when shuffled
One feature tops all three by far check for leakage

followUps.question: How do you handle correlated features in importance?
followUps.html:
Group them, and report group importance.

Option A:shuffle the whole correlated cluster togetherpermutation or SHAP importance for the group
Option B:cluster features by correlationkeep one representative each

That's more honest than pretending to split credit precisely.

followUps.question: Why is a random ID feature sometimes "important"?
followUps.html:
Because high cardinality gives many split options, and trees use them to memorise rows.

Check:permutation importance on validation datait was memorisationdoes the ID encode time, or leak?

followUps.question: Which would you show a regulator?
followUps.html:
SHAP-based reason codes per decision. Never gain importance.

With the reason codes
Method documented
Stability checked across retrains
Top features reviewed for whether they're legitimate to use

Gain importance is unstable and isn't tied to individual decisions.

followUps.question: Is permutation importance on training data useful?
followUps.html:
No: on training data it measures what the model memorised.

Computed on Shows
Training data what was memorised
Held-out data what the model relies on for new cases

followUps.question: How do importances help with drift monitoring?
followUps.html:
Track mean |SHAP| per feature over time.

Signal:a feature's contribution changes suddenlya data or pipeline changeflagged before labels arrive

dontSay: "Gain importance shows what matters most." — it shows training usage, with biases.
"SHAP tells us the causes." — it explains the model.
"They disagree, so I'll average them." — investigate the disagreement.
