links.target: 01-ML/12-Interpretability & Responsible ML/04-SHAP — Values, Math Intuition & Plots

ml-dl-q45.testing: whether you read assumptions off the objective and resist the elbow heuristic.
ml-dl-q45.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The objective "K-Means minimises the within-cluster sum of squared distances to centroids, and that objective hides its assumptions. It prefers spherical clusters of similar size and similar density, separable by Euclidean distance. Give it a crescent, or one big and one small cluster, and it will carve them wrongly while the loss looks fine. It also always returns exactly K clusters, whether or not structure exists."
3 · Mechanics that matter "Mechanics worth saying: Lloyd's algorithm only reaches a local optimum, so use K-Means++ initialisation and several restarts. Scaling is mandatory, because it's distance-based. And for large data, mini-batch K-Means trades a little quality for a lot of speed."
4 · Choosing K honestly "For choosing K, the elbow method reads a bend off a curve that always decreases, and often there's no clean bend. Silhouette, which compares separation to cohesion per point, is more honest. Stronger still is stability: do the clusters survive resampling and different seeds?"
5 · Validate outside the geometry "The real validation is external: do the clusters differ on business variables they weren't built from, and do they stay stable over time? A clustering nobody can act on is a scatter plot with extra steps."
6 · Alternatives when shapes are wrong "If shapes or densities are the problem, I'd switch: Gaussian mixtures for elliptical clusters and soft assignment, HDBSCAN for arbitrary shapes and noise."

stages.name: The objective
stages.html:
minimise  Σₖ Σ_{x ∈ Cₖ} ‖x − μₖ‖²

Lloyd's algorithm: assign points to the nearest centroid, move centroids to their cluster means, repeat.

stages.name: The assumptions it hides
stages.html:
Assumption When it fails
Spherical clusters elongated or curved shapes
Similar sizes one large and one small group get split or merged
Similar densities sparse clusters absorbed by dense ones
Euclidean geometry categorical or mixed data
K clusters exist returns K groups from structureless data

stages.name: Mechanics that matter
stages.html:
• K-Means++ initialisation, n_init ≥ 10 restarts.
  • Standardise features; consider PCA first in high dimensions.
  • Mini-batch K-Means for millions of rows.

stages.name: Choosing K honestly
stages.html:
Method Honest?
Elbow (inertia vs K) weak: inertia always drops; elbows are often ambiguous
Silhouette better: cohesion vs separation per point
Stability (ARI across seeds/bootstraps) strongest internal evidence
Gap statistic compares to a null reference distribution

stages.name: Validate outside the geometry
stages.html:
• Clusters differ significantly on variables not used to build them (revenue, churn).
  • Stable month over month.
  • Each can be named in one actionable sentence.

stages.name: Alternatives when shapes are wrong
stages.html:
Structure Use
Elliptical, overlapping, soft membership Gaussian Mixture Models
Arbitrary shapes, noise, unknown K DBSCAN / HDBSCAN
Nested groupings, dendrogram hierarchical clustering
Categorical data K-modes / K-prototypes

followUps.question: Why does K-Means need scaling?
followUps.html:
Because it uses Euclidean distance, so a feature in large units dominates the assignment.

d(x, c) = √ Σⱼ (xⱼ − cⱼ)²      ← the largest-scale feature dominates the sum

After scaling, each feature contributes comparably, unless you weight some deliberately.

followUps.question: The silhouette peaks at K = 2 but the business wants 6 segments. Now what?
followUps.html:
Tell them the data supports 2 strong groups; 6 would be partly arbitrary.

Option How
Sub-segment hierarchical clustering inside each of the 2
Business-rule segments define the 6 by rules, informed by the clustering

Don't present forced clusters as natural.

followUps.question: Can K-Means work on categorical data?
followUps.html:
Not directly.

  • Why: the mean of one-hot vectors isn't a meaningful category, and Euclidean distance on them is crude.
  • Use instead: K-modes or K-prototypes, or embed the categories first.

followUps.question: How do you check the clusters aren't just noise?
followUps.html:
Compare against a null.

Null test:shuffle each feature independently (structure destroyed)run the same pipelineis your silhouette or stability clearly better?

The gap statistic formalises this.

followUps.question: How do you assign new customers to segments?
followUps.html:
Same scaler, nearest centroid.

Assign:new customerthe fitted scalernearest stored centroidsegment

Monitor the distribution of assignments and of distances over time; drift in either means the segmentation needs refitting.

dontSay: "The elbow method gives K." — often ambiguous; use silhouette and stability.
"K-Means finds natural groups." — it always returns K spherical-ish groups.
"No need to scale." — distance-based.

spine: Not a bug: a density verdict
Where DBSCAN still earns its place
ml-dl-q46.testing: whether you understand density-based clustering well enough to read its output as information.
ml-dl-q46.trap: "lower the threshold until noise goes away."
ml-dl-q46.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Not a bug: a density verdict "It's not a bug; it's a verdict and a diagnostic."
2 · What eps and minPts control "DBSCAN grows clusters from core points: a point with at least minPts neighbours within radius eps. Points reachable from a core point join its cluster; points reachable from none are labelled noise. So 40% noise means 40% of the data doesn't sit in any region as dense as I specified. Either that's true, the data is sparse and noisy, or my eps is too tight for how the features are scaled."
3 · Check scaling and eps "Eps is the neighbourhood radius, best chosen from the knee of a k-distance plot. MinPts is the density bar, roughly the dimensionality plus a margin. Both are meaningless without scaled features, and eps degrades in high dimensions because distances concentrate."
4 · The one-global-eps weakness "The structural weakness is one global eps. If clusters have different densities, no single eps is right: the dense cluster merges with neighbours while the sparse one shatters into noise."
5 · Switch to HDBSCAN "That's exactly what HDBSCAN fixes: it builds a density hierarchy and extracts clusters at different densities, with essentially one parameter, the minimum cluster size."
6 · Where DBSCAN still earns its place "So my steps: check scaling, redo the k-distance plot, and if densities visibly vary, switch to HDBSCAN rather than tuning DBSCAN harder."

stages.name: Not a bug: a density verdict
stages.html:
Point type Rule
Core ≥ minPts points within eps
Border within eps of a core point, not core itself
Noise neither

stages.name: What eps and minPts control
stages.html:
Parameter Controls Too small Too large
eps how far a neighbourhood reaches everything is noise clusters merge
minPts how many neighbours make a region dense (≥ dimensions + 1, often 2×) noise points form tiny clusters sparse clusters become noise
  • eps: how far a neighbourhood reaches. Too small → everything is noise; too large → clusters merge.
  • minPts: how many neighbours make a region dense. Rule of thumb ≥ dimensions + 1, often 2× dimensions.

stages.name: Check scaling and eps
stages.html:
Step What I do Why
1 scale the features unscaled units make one eps meaningless across dimensions
2 k-distance plot, k = minPts: sort each point's distance to its k-th neighbour, take eps at the knee picks eps from the data
3 reduce dimensions (PCA or UMAP) first distances concentrate in high dimensions

Step 1 — Scale features. Unscaled units make eps meaningless in some dimensions.

Step 2 — k-distance plot. Sort each point's distance to its k-th neighbour (k = minPts); choose eps at the knee.

Step 3 — Reduce dimensions. In high dimensions distances concentrate; PCA or UMAP first can help.

stages.name: The one-global-eps weakness
stages.html:
• A single eps can't fit both a tight cluster and a diffuse one.
  • Symptom: tuning eps trades "sparse cluster becomes noise" for "dense clusters merge".

stages.name: Switch to HDBSCAN
stages.html:
• Builds clusters across all densities; keeps the most persistent ones.
  • Main parameter: min_cluster_size; also gives membership probabilities and outlier scores.
  • Usually the better default for exploratory clustering.

stages.name: Where DBSCAN still earns its place
stages.html:
• Arbitrary shapes; no need to choose K.
  • The noise label is useful for anomaly triage.
  • Deterministic for core points; simple to explain.

followUps.question: Could 40% noise be the right answer?
followUps.html:
Yes. A large noise fraction can be a finding, not a failure.

  • Where: fraud logs or sensor data, where most points are isolated and only a few dense patterns exist.
  • Condition: the clusters that were found are meaningful and stable.

followUps.question: How does DBSCAN handle new points?
followUps.html:
It has no native predict.

Workaround:new pointnearest core point within eps?that point's clusternoise

HDBSCAN offers approximate_predict for this.

followUps.question: Why not just increase eps until noise drops to 5%?
followUps.html:
Because noise percentage isn't an objective; cluster quality and stability are.

What raising eps does: wider neighbourhoodsdistinct clusters merge"dense" is redefined to fit a target number, not the data

followUps.question: DBSCAN on 50 million points?
followUps.html:
Standard implementations are too heavy: the neighbourhood queries cost memory and time.

Option How
Spatial index faster neighbourhood queries
Subsample find the structure, then assign the rest
GPU cuML
HDBSCAN on a sample approximate prediction for the remainder

followUps.question: DBSCAN vs K-Means in one line?
followUps.html:
K-Means partitions; DBSCAN finds dense regions.

K-Means DBSCAN
Shape spherical arbitrary, by density
Number of clusters you set K discovered
Every point assigned? yes no: low-density points are noise

dontSay: "It's a bug; I'll raise eps." — noise is information.
"DBSCAN doesn't need parameter tuning." — eps and minPts are everything.
"It works fine without scaling." — eps depends on units.

ml-dl-q47.testing: whether you can build evidence without labels, in layers a stakeholder trusts.
ml-dl-q47.trap: "the silhouette score is 0.6, so it's good."
ml-dl-q47.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Internal metrics: consistency, not truth "I'd build the case in layers, from weakest to strongest evidence. Internal metrics first: silhouette, Davies-Bouldin, Calinski-Harabasz. They measure cohesion against separation, but they share the same geometric prejudices as the algorithms, favouring compact round clusters. So they're consistency checks, not truth."
2 · Stability under resampling "Stability is stronger evidence. Re-run the clustering under bootstrap resampling, different seeds and small feature perturbations, and measure agreement between runs with something like the adjusted Rand index. Structure that evaporates under resampling was noise wearing a costume."
3 · External validation on unseen variables "External validation is what convinces a sceptic: the clusters differ significantly on variables they weren't built from, revenue, churn, support tickets, and they persist over time. That's the difference between 'the algorithm returned groups' and 'these segments exist'."
4 · Actionability "The final test is actionability. Name each cluster in one sentence a marketer or product manager can act on. If a cluster can't be described, it's a mathematical artifact."
5 · Guard against p-hacking geometry "And I'd guard against the meta-risk: try enough algorithms and values of K and you'll find clusters in anything."
Close "So I'd fix the pipeline, features, algorithm and selection metric, before looking, rather than p-hacking geometry."

stages.name: Internal metrics: consistency, not truth
stages.html:
Metric Measures Bias
Silhouette per-point cohesion vs nearest other cluster favours convex, well-separated clusters
Davies-Bouldin average similarity of each cluster to its closest same
Calinski-Harabasz between- vs within-cluster dispersion favours spherical, more clusters

stages.name: Stability under resampling
stages.html:
Perturb Measure agreement with Reading
bootstrap samples adjusted Rand index between runs high and steady: structure is real
different seeds Jaccard per cluster some clusters solid, others not: report per cluster
small feature noise adjusted Rand index collapses: the clusters were an artefact
  • Bootstrap samples, different seeds, small feature noise.
  • Agreement: adjusted Rand index or Jaccard per cluster between runs.
  • Report per-cluster stability: some clusters may be solid, others not.

stages.name: External validation on unseen variables
stages.html:
Test How Convincing when
Held-out variables keep business variables out of the clustering features clusters differ on them anyway
Significance and size ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis, with effect sizes differences are large, not just significant
Persistence re-cluster next month the same segments reappear
  • Hold out business variables from the clustering features.
  • Test differences between clusters (ANOVA / Kruskal-Wallis, effect sizes).
  • Check persistence: re-cluster next month; do the segments reappear?

stages.name: Actionability
stages.html:
• "Price-sensitive weekend shoppers who churn after promotions end."
  • If a cluster has no crisp description or distinct action, merge or drop it.

stages.name: Guard against p-hacking geometry
stages.html:
• Decide features, algorithm and selection metric up front.
  • Compare to a null (shuffled features) to show structure beats chance.
  • Report the choices tried, not only the winner.

followUps.question: How do you present this to a sceptical VP?
followUps.html:
Lead with the external evidence. Business differences persuade; silhouette scores don't.

Order of slides:external differencesstabilityone slide on method

For example: "segment A has 3× the churn and half the order value of segment B, stable for three months."

followUps.question: Silhouette is low but segments differ strongly on revenue. Which wins?
followUps.html:
The external evidence, if it's stable.

Signal What it really says
Low silhouette clusters touch or aren't spherical; not that they're useless
Strong revenue difference the segments capture something real

Report both honestly.

followUps.question: How do you compare two clusterings?
followUps.html:
On agreement and on usefulness.

Question Measure
Do they agree? adjusted Rand index or normalised mutual information between the label assignments
Which is more useful? stronger external differences, more actionable segments

followUps.question: Isn't using business variables for validation circular?
followUps.html:
Only if they were used as clustering features.

Honest design:hold the business variables outcluster on the restcompare segments on the held-out variables

Differences there are independent evidence that the clusters capture real structure.

followUps.question: What if the segments change every month?
followUps.html:
Either behaviour is genuinely shifting, or the clustering is unstable. Check within a month first.

Within a month Across months Verdict
unstable — the clustering is unstable
stable unstable the population is changing

For a changing population: a refresh cadence, and a mapping between old and new segments.

dontSay: "Silhouette 0.6, done." — internal metrics share the algorithm's biases.
"The clusters look clear on the plot." — plots aren't evidence (see Q36).
"I tried 12 algorithms and picked the best-looking." — that's p-hacking.

spine: Two axes: trial cost and important dimensions
ml-dl-q48.testing: whether you choose search strategy by budget structure.
ml-dl-q48.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Two axes: trial cost and important dimensions "I choose along two axes: how expensive one trial is, and how many hyperparameters actually matter."
2 · Grid "Grid search grows exponentially with dimensions and wastes budget on parameters that don't matter. It's defensible for one or two parameters, or when you need an exhaustive, auditable sweep."
3 · Random "Random search beats grid because usually only a few hyperparameters matter. Random sampling covers each important dimension densely instead of repeating the same few values. It's the right default when trials are cheap."
4 · Bayesian "Bayesian optimisation, like Optuna's TPE or a Gaussian-process approach, builds a model of score versus configuration and spends each trial where improvement is likely. It earns its overhead when a single trial is expensive and the budget is tens of trials, not thousands. It's sequential by nature, though batched versions exist."
5 · Hyperband "Hyperband and successive halving attack a different axis: cheap partial evaluations. Start many configurations, kill the losers early at increasing budgets. It wins when learning curves are informative early, epochs or boosting rounds. Combine it with Bayesian sampling, BOHB or Optuna with pruning, and you get both."
6 · Discipline for any method "Whatever the method: search rates and regularisation on log scales, repeat top configurations across seeds, keep the test set out, and remember tuning gains are usually smaller than one good feature."

stages.name: Two axes: trial cost and important dimensions
stages.html:
Few params matter Many params matter
Cheap trials random search random search, large budget
Expensive trials Bayesian optimisation Bayesian + early stopping (BOHB)
Informative early curves Hyperband / pruning BOHB / Optuna with pruning

stages.name: Grid
stages.html:
grid cost = Π (values per parameter)
5 parameters × 4 values each = 4⁵ = 1,024 configurations   ← × 5 folds = 5,120 fits
  • Cost = product of values per parameter.
  • Fine for 1–2 params or a required audit sweep.

stages.name: Random
stages.html:
P(at least one of n random trials lands in the top 5%) = 1 − 0.95ⁿ
n = 60  →  1 − 0.95⁶⁰ ≈ 0.954                              ← 60 trials, about a 95% chance
  • With 60 random trials, there's a 95% chance of hitting the top 5% of a single important dimension.
  • Each trial explores new values on every dimension.

stages.name: Bayesian
stages.html:
• Surrogate model (TPE, GP) + acquisition function (expected improvement).
  • Worth the overhead for hour-long trainings with a budget of 20–100 trials.
  • Sequential; parallelism needs batched suggestions.

stages.name: Hyperband
stages.html:
• Successive halving: train many configs briefly, keep the best fraction, give them more budget, repeat.
  • Hyperband runs several halving brackets to hedge against early curves being misleading.
  • Needs a meaningful "partial budget": epochs, rounds, data subset.

stages.name: Discipline for any method
stages.html:
• Log-scale search for learning rate, regularisation.
  • Re-run top configs across seeds; differences within noise are ties.
  • Tune on validation/CV only; test once at the end (nested CV if data is small).
  • Features and data usually beat tuning.

followUps.question: Why does random search beat grid with the same budget?
followUps.html:
Random search spends the budget on the parameter that matters.

grid 5 × 5 × 5 = 125 trials  →    5 distinct values of each parameter
random,          125 trials  →  125 distinct values of each parameter

If only one of the three parameters matters, the grid has tested just 5 values of it.

followUps.question: When is Hyperband misleading?
followUps.html:
When early performance doesn't predict final performance.

Configuration Early Final
Small learning rate slow start wins
Strong regularisation looks bad fine

Use a sensible minimum budget and Hyperband's multiple brackets.

followUps.question: How do you tune a model that takes 8 hours to train?
followUps.html:
Shrink the problem, then confirm at full scale.

Plan:tune on a data subset or fewer epochs to narrow the rangesBayesian optimisation with pruning, parallel across GPUsconfirm the final few configurations at full scale

Settings transferred from similar past models give a head start.

followUps.question: Your tuned model beats the baseline by 0.2%. Ship it?
followUps.html:
Not yet. Check it's outside noise and not selection bias from many trials.

  • Noise: repeat seeds, compute a confidence interval.
  • Selection bias: the best of many trials is optimistic.
  • Perspective: small tuning gains often vanish on new data; a better feature or more data usually matters more.

followUps.question: Which hyperparameters matter most for gradient boosting?
followUps.html:
Four groups, in this order.

Rank Hyperparameter
1 learning rate, with the number of rounds set by early stopping
2 tree depth or number of leaves
3 min child weight / min samples per leaf
4 row and column subsampling

Regularisation terms are secondary.

dontSay: "Grid search to be thorough." — exponential waste.
"Bayesian is always best." — overhead isn't worth it for cheap trials.
"I tuned on the test set." — no.

ml-dl-q49.testing: statistical judgement plus business sense, delivered constructively to a PM.
ml-dl-q49.trap: "B is higher, ship it" or a flat "no".
ml-dl-q49.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Is 0.004 inside the noise? "I'd say: maybe, but first let's check the difference is real and worth something. First, is 0.004 inside the noise? A single test-set score has sampling variance. I'd bootstrap the test set to get a confidence interval on the difference, or run a paired test on per-example results, like McNemar's for classification, since both models saw the same examples. With typical test sizes, 0.004 is very often a tie."
2 · Selection bias "Second, selection effects. If B was the best of many candidates evaluated on this same test set, part of its edge is the winner's curse."
3 · Does it move the business? "Third, translate it to the business metric. Does 0.004 change revenue or cost at our operating threshold? Offline differences this small often vanish online."
4 · Settle it online "If it might matter, settle it with an A/B test on the business KPI. If we can't A/B test, the offline gain should clear a practical-significance bar agreed in advance, not just statistical significance."
5 · Weigh what the metric hides "And I'd weigh what the metric hides: latency, cost, calibration and per-segment performance. B can win on average and lose on the segment that matters most."
Close "If B is no worse on those and the gain survives, ship it."

stages.name: Is 0.004 inside the noise?
stages.html:
Method Use for Reading
Bootstrap the test set 1,000+ times a confidence interval of (B − A) interval includes 0: a tie
McNemar's test paired per-example correctness are the disagreements one-sided?
DeLong's test a difference in AUC significance of the AUC gap
  • Bootstrap the test set 1,000+ times; CI of (B − A).
  • Paired tests: McNemar's on per-example correctness; for AUC, DeLong's test.
  • If the CI includes 0, it's a tie.

stages.name: Selection bias
stages.html:
What happened Why the score is inflated Remedy
many candidates were compared on one test set the best of many noisy scores is partly luck refresh the test set, or keep a final one nobody selects on
  • Many candidates compared on one test set → the best one's score is inflated.
  • The test set is now partly a validation set; refresh it or hold back a final one.

stages.name: Does it move the business?
stages.html:
• Recompute the business outcome at the actual threshold for both models: approvals, fraud caught, revenue.
  • A metric gain spread below the threshold changes nothing users see.

stages.name: Settle it online
stages.html:
• A/B test on the business KPI with a pre-registered duration and metric.
  • If not possible: require a pre-agreed practical-significance bar offline.

stages.name: Weigh what the metric hides
stages.html:
Dimension Question
Latency / cost is B slower or pricier?
Calibration do B's probabilities still mean what they say?
Segments does B lose on a key segment?
Robustness stable across time slices?

followUps.question: How big should the test set be to detect 0.004?
followUps.html:
Often tens or hundreds of thousands of examples.

SE(accuracy) = √( p(1−p) / n )     ← the difference must clear this noise

It depends on the metric's variance and the base rate, so run a power analysis before claiming a difference. With a few thousand examples, 0.004 is almost never detectable.

followUps.question: The PM says "higher is higher, why not?"
followUps.html:
Because switching has costs, and if the difference is noise we pay them for nothing.

  • Costs: validation, deployment, monitoring, risk.
  • Worst case: we ship a slightly worse model.
Fast path I'd offer:a quick paired test todayan A/B test

followUps.question: What if B is statistically better but only by 0.004?
followUps.html:
Statistical significance isn't practical significance.

Question Answered by
Is the difference real? the test; with a huge test set, tiny differences become "significant"
Is it worth it? business impact against the switching cost

followUps.question: Is McNemar's test right for AUC?
followUps.html:
No. Pick the test that matches the metric.

Metric Test
Accuracy at a threshold McNemar's: paired correct/incorrect predictions
AUC DeLong's test, or a paired bootstrap of AUC

followUps.question: How would you avoid this situation next time?
followUps.html:
Agree three things in advance.

Agreed up front
Decision metric the one number that decides
Minimum meaningful improvement below it, don't switch
Evaluation protocol repeated CV or a fresh holdout, with a paired test

Then shipping decisions are mechanical, not negotiated.

dontSay: "B is better, ship it." — no uncertainty estimate.
"The difference is too small, never." — test it; it might be real.
"Statistically significant, so it matters." — practical significance is separate.

spine: It's a theorem, not a bug
Choose the definition that matches the harm
ml-dl-q50.testing: whether you know the impossibility result and treat fairness as a governed trade-off.
ml-dl-q50.trap: "we'll tune the model until all metrics pass," or "we removed the protected attribute."
ml-dl-q50.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · It's a theorem, not a bug "It's a theorem, not an engineering failure. When base rates differ between groups, demographic parity, which is equal approval rates, equalised odds, which is equal true- and false-positive rates, and predictive parity, which is equal precision or calibration, can't all hold at once, except with a perfect predictor. Any calibrated model with unequal base rates violates the others."
2 · Choose the definition that matches the harm "So the job isn't to satisfy every metric. It's to choose the definition that matches the harm in this domain. Equal opportunity among qualified applicants, equal true-positive rates, means something different from equal approval rates, and that choice encodes values and law, not statistics."
3 · Make it a governance decision "That makes it a governance decision. Legal, compliance and product own it, and it's documented, for example in a model card. My role as architect is to give them the quantified trade-off: what each definition costs in the others and in accuracy."
4 · Apply technical levers "Once chosen, there are technical levers: reweighting data before training, constrained optimisation during training, or group-specific thresholds after training, which is simple and auditable. Removing the protected attribute alone doesn't work, because proxies like postcode carry it back in."
5 · Monitor in production "And fairness is monitored per segment in production, not audited once, because drift breaks fairness just like it breaks accuracy."

stages.name: It's a theorem, not a bug
stages.html:
Definition Requires equal across groups
Demographic parity approval rate P(ŷ=1)
Equalised odds TPR and FPR
Equal opportunity TPR only
Predictive parity / calibration precision / P(y=1 | score)

With different base rates P(y=1), calibration and equalised odds can't both hold (Kleinberg et al., Chouldechova), and demographic parity conflicts with both.

stages.name: Choose the definition that matches the harm
stages.html:
Setting Definition usually chosen Why
Lending equal opportunity: qualified applicants approved at equal rates the harm is denying someone who would repay; regulation may also bar disparate impact
Risk scores read by people calibration within groups a score must mean the same thing for everyone
Any setting an ethical and legal choice first statistics only shows the trade-off
  • Lending: equal opportunity (qualified applicants approved equally) is common; regulation may prohibit disparate impact.
  • Risk scoring used by humans: calibration within groups often matters most.
  • The choice is ethical and legal first, statistical second.

stages.name: Make it a governance decision
stages.html:
• Present the trade-off curve: accuracy and each fairness metric under different constraints/thresholds.
  • Decision owners: legal, compliance, product, with documentation (model card, decision log).
  • Record who decided, which definition, and why.

stages.name: Apply technical levers
stages.html:
Stage Lever Trade-off
Pre-processing reweighing, resampling simple; indirect control
In-processing constrained optimisation, adversarial debiasing precise; complex
Post-processing group-specific thresholds simple, auditable; may need legal review

Dropping the protected attribute ("fairness through unawareness") fails: proxies (postcode, name, school) reintroduce it, and you lose the ability to measure disparity.

stages.name: Monitor in production
stages.html:
• Track chosen metric per group on live decisions and delayed outcomes.
  • Alert on divergence; include in model reviews and retraining gates.

followUps.question: Isn't using the protected attribute for thresholds illegal?
followUps.html:
It depends on jurisdiction and domain, which is why legal must own the choice.

  • Restriction: some lending rules bar protected attributes from decisions, even to correct bias.
  • Common compromise: the attribute is used only for measurement, and for choosing mitigations that don't use it directly.

followUps.question: Why does removing the protected attribute fail?
followUps.html:
Because other features correlate with it, so the model reconstructs it.

Result:attribute droppedproxies remainthe model rebuilds it implicitlyand you can no longer measure the disparity

The problem becomes invisible, not solved.

followUps.question: How much accuracy does fairness cost?
followUps.html:
It varies: often less than people fear, sometimes significant. So measure it.

Method:plot the frontier of accuracy against the chosen fairness metricdecision-makers pick a point on it

followUps.question: What goes in the model card?
followUps.html:
Whatever makes the decision reviewable and auditable.

Section Content
Intended use and what it isn't for
Training data description
Metrics performance and fairness, per group
Fairness definition the one chosen, and why
Limitations known ones
Monitoring plan what is tracked

followUps.question: Can labels themselves be biased?
followUps.html:
Yes.

Mechanism:past approvalsrepayment is observed only for approved applicantslabels reflect past decisions

Equalising metrics on biased labels can entrench the bias. Consider reject inference, the outcome definition, and data audits.

dontSay: "We'll satisfy all fairness metrics." — mathematically impossible with different base rates.
"We removed race, so it's fair." — proxies.
"The data scientists decide the fairness definition." — governance decides.

links.label: Fairness — Demographic Parity, Equalized Odds, Equal Opportunity
links.target: 01-ML/12-Interpretability & Responsible ML/06-Fairness — Demographic Parity, Equalized Odds, Equal Opportunity

spine: Honest scheme: walk-forward with a gap
ml-dl-q51.testing: both leaks (folds and features) and a concrete honest scheme.
ml-dl-q51.trap: fixing the split but not the feature engineering.
ml-dl-q51.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Leak 1: the fold structure "There are two leaks."
2 · Leak 2: the features "The first is the fold structure. Random K-fold trains on the future to predict the past. With autocorrelation, neighbouring time points are near-duplicates, and they land in different folds, so the score measures interpolation, not forecasting. The inflation can be dramatic."
3 · Honest scheme: walk-forward with a gap "The second leak hides in the features. Rolling means, lags or normalisation computed over the whole series before splitting carry future information into past rows, even if the split itself is correct."
4 · Report over time "The honest scheme is walk-forward validation: train on an expanding or rolling window, test on the next block, step forward, and aggregate across several origins. Add a gap, an embargo, between train and test when features look back over a window, so no training row overlaps the test period through its features. Use a rolling window when old regimes actively mislead."
5 · Beat the naive baselines "I'd report performance per fold over time rather than pooled: decay across folds tells you how fast things drift and sets the retraining cadence."
Close "And I'd always compare against naive baselines, last value and seasonal naive, which forecasting models embarrassingly often fail to beat."

stages.name: Leak 1: the fold structure
stages.html:
Random K-fold:   train ■□■■□■■□■   test □ scattered through time → interpolation
Walk-forward:    train ■■■■■|gap|test ■  → next origin: train ■■■■■■■|gap|test ■

stages.name: Leak 2: the features
stages.html:
• A 30-day rolling mean at day t computed centred, or normalisation using full-series statistics.
  • Fix: compute features using only data ≤ t, inside each fold's training window.
  • Target-derived features (lagged target) need the same care at the fold boundary.

stages.name: Honest scheme: walk-forward with a gap
stages.html:
fold 1:  [ train ████████         ] gap [ test ██ ]
fold 2:  [ train ████████████     ] gap [ test ██ ]
fold 3:  [ train ████████████████ ] gap [ test ██ ]        ← expanding window; time runs left to right
gap ≥ forecast horizon and feature lookback                 ← nothing from the test period leaks back
  • Expanding window: more data each step; rolling window: fixed length, forgets old regimes.
  • Gap ≥ forecast horizon and feature lookback.
  • TimeSeriesSplit(gap=…) in sklearn, or a custom backtest loop.

stages.name: Report over time
stages.html:
• Metric per fold, in time order: a downward trend is drift speed.
  • Horizon-specific errors: 1-step vs 7-step ahead.

stages.name: Beat the naive baselines
stages.html:
Baseline Forecast
Naive last observed value
Seasonal naive value one season ago
Moving average mean of recent window

A model that can't beat seasonal naive isn't ready. Use scale-free metrics like MASE to compare.

followUps.question: How big should the gap be?
followUps.html:
At least the forecast horizon plus the longest feature lookback.

gap ≥ forecast horizon + longest feature lookback

No training row's features or labels may overlap the test period. For a label over the next 7 days, the last training row is 7 days before the test starts.

followUps.question: Expanding or rolling window?
followUps.html:
Compare both in the backtest.

Window Use when
Expanding older data is still relevant and more data helps
Rolling the process changes and old regimes mislead (post-pandemic demand, a pricing change)

followUps.question: Is K-fold ever OK for time-series models?
followUps.html:
Rarely.

Case Verdict
Purely autoregressive model, stationary series some research shows blocked or purged CV can be acceptable
Production forecasting with features walk-forward: the safe default, because it mirrors deployment

followUps.question: How many origins?
followUps.html:
Enough to cover the seasonal patterns and some regime variety: often 5–12.

Origins Estimate of
Few the average error only, and noisily
More both the average error and its variance

followUps.question: How do you tune hyperparameters with walk-forward?
followUps.html:
Tune on the earlier origins; keep the most recent window untouched.

Order:earlier originspick settingsmost recent window(s)report

Tuning across all folds reuses the latest period for both selection and reporting.

dontSay: "Shuffle and 5-fold." — trains on the future.
"I computed rolling features on the full series first." — feature leak.
"Our MAPE is 8%." (without a naive baseline) — meaningless alone.

links.target: 01-ML/11-Model Selection, Validation & Tuning/02-Time-Series Cross-Validation — Walk-Forward, Expanding, Rolling

spine: Sort by what each is structurally good at
ml-dl-q52.testing: whether you match method to problem shape, not fashion.
ml-dl-q52.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Sort by what each is structurally good at "I'd sort them by what they're structurally good at."
2 · ARIMA "ARIMA and SARIMA are principled for a single, well-behaved series: explicit autoregressive and moving-average structure on a stationary series, interpretable orders from ACF and PACF, and proper prediction intervals. The cost is per-series care, stationarity work, and weakness with covariates and with many series."
3 · Prophet "Prophet decomposes trend, seasonality and holidays, is robust to missing data and outliers, and was built for many business series with strong calendar effects, run by analysts who aren't statisticians. The cost is a rigid functional form: it underperforms when dynamics aren't calendar-driven, and it isn't a magic upgrade over naive baselines."
4 · Global GBM "Gradient boosting with engineered features, lags, rolling statistics, calendar, promotions and price, wins when external drivers matter and you have many related series: one global model learns across all of them. The cost is that you own the feature engineering, the temporal validation discipline, and the multi-step strategy, and trees can't extrapolate a trend beyond what they've seen."
5 · The decision shape "So: one well-understood series, ARIMA. Hundreds of calendar-driven series and speed, Prophet or seasonal-naive. Drivers plus cross-series signal, a global GBM, today's industry default."
6 · Always against seasonal-naive "And everything is judged walk-forward against seasonal-naive."

stages.name: Sort by what each is structurally good at
stages.html:
Problem shape Lean toward
One series, clear structure, need intervals ARIMA / SARIMA / ETS
Many series, strong calendar/holiday effects, little tuning Prophet (or ETS), seasonal-naive
Many related series, exogenous drivers (price, promo, weather) global GBM with lags
Very long histories, complex patterns, lots of series consider deep models (N-BEATS, TFT)

stages.name: ARIMA
stages.claim: explicit structure, one series at a time
stages.html:
ARIMA(p, d, q):   (1 − φ₁L − … − φₚLᵖ)(1 − L)ᵈ yₜ = (1 + θ₁L + … + θ_qL^q) εₜ
                   ↑ autoregressive    ↑ differencing        ↑ moving average of past errors
  • Make stationary (differencing, ADF test), choose p, d, q from ACF/PACF or auto-ARIMA.
  • SARIMA adds seasonal terms; ARIMAX adds regressors (awkwardly).
  • Strengths: interpretable, calibrated intervals. Weakness: scale to thousands of series, non-linear drivers.

stages.name: Prophet
stages.html:
Prophet:   y(t) = g(t) + s(t) + h(t) + εₜ
                  ↑ trend   ↑ seasonality  ↑ holidays      ← a curve fitted to time, no autoregression
  • y = trend + seasonality + holidays + error, fitted as a curve.
  • Handles gaps, outliers, changepoints.
  • Weakness: fixed form; doesn't use autoregressive dynamics well; often matched by simple baselines.

stages.name: Global GBM
stages.html:
• One model across all series: shares patterns, handles cold-start series via similarity.
  • Features: lags, rolling means/std, calendar, holidays, price, promotions, series ID/attributes.
  • Multi-step: recursive (feed predictions back) vs direct (one model per horizon).
  • Weakness: can't extrapolate trends; detrend or add trend features.

stages.name: The decision shape
stages.html: Start with seasonal-naive and ETS as baselines, try a global GBM, and keep whichever wins walk-forward by a meaningful margin on MASE.

stages.name: Always against seasonal-naive
stages.html: Many production forecasts don't beat seasonal-naive. Prove yours does, per series segment, walk-forward.

followUps.question: Why can't GBMs extrapolate trends?
followUps.html:
Because a tree's prediction is an average of training targets in a leaf.

Consequence:leaf value = mean of training targetsit can never exceed what training sawa rising series flattens

Fixes: forecast differences or detrended values, or add a linear trend component.

followUps.question: Recursive or direct multi-step forecasting?
followUps.html:
Recursive compounds errors; direct multiplies models.

Recursive Direct
Models one one per horizon
Lags its own predictions fed back real values only
Risk errors compound more to train and maintain

Many teams use direct for short horizons, or one model with the horizon as a feature.

followUps.question: When would you pick deep learning?
followUps.html:
Only when three things hold together.

  • Many long, related series with complex patterns.
  • Enough data.
  • A team to maintain it.

Otherwise global GBMs and statistical baselines usually match it at far lower cost.

followUps.question: How do you forecast a new product with no history?
followUps.html:
Borrow from similar products.

Approach How
Global model with product attributes learns from similar products
Analogous-product curves reuse a launch curve
Hierarchical priors start from the category

Update quickly as early sales arrive.

followUps.question: How do you get prediction intervals from a GBM?
followUps.html:
Three ways, all checked for coverage in the walk-forward backtest.

Method How
Quantile models train at, say, 0.1 and 0.9
Conformal prediction on backtest residuals
Bootstrap resample the residuals

dontSay: "Prophet is the best forecasting tool." — often matched by naive baselines.
"ARIMA for our 10,000 SKUs." — per-series care doesn't scale.
"Our model has low error." (no baseline) — beat seasonal-naive first.

ml-dl-q53.testing: mechanism per method and which cold-start case kills each.
ml-dl-q53.trap: treating cold start as one problem.
ml-dl-q53.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Content-based "For each, what does it learn from and which cold start kills it? Content-based matches item features to a profile built from the user's own history. It doesn't need other users, so it handles new items natively, because they have features. It fails for new users with no history, and it over-specialises, recommending more of the same."
2 · Collaborative filtering "Collaborative filtering, user-based or item-based neighbourhoods, learns only from the interaction matrix. It captures taste patterns content can't, 'people who liked X also liked Y', but it fails for both new users and new items, since neither has interactions, and it struggles with sparsity. Item-based aged better because item similarities are more stable and cacheable."
3 · Matrix factorisation "Matrix factorisation, SVD-style or ALS, decomposes the interaction matrix into latent user and item factors, generalising better from the same sparse data. It was the classic quality winner. ALS fits the implicit-feedback formulation. It has the same cold-start weakness as CF."
4 · Cold-start playbook "So production systems are hybrids. New users get onboarding signals, popularity or context priors, and exploration; new items get content features plus an exposure boost."
5 · Implicit feedback is confidence "And implicit feedback, clicks and views, is confidence, not preference: no click isn't dislike."
Close "That changes the loss, how you sample negatives, and how you evaluate."

stages.name: Content-based
stages.html:
• Represent items by features (genre, text embeddings, attributes); build a user profile from items they engaged with.
  • new items; new users; filter bubble, limited serendipity.

stages.name: Collaborative filtering
stages.html:
• User-based: similar users' items. Item-based: items similar by co-interaction.
  • captures taste beyond features; new users and new items; sparsity, popularity bias.

stages.name: Matrix factorisation
stages.html:
R (users × items) ≈ U · Vᵀ     each user and item gets a k-dim vector
  • SVD / SGD for explicit ratings; ALS with confidence weights for implicit feedback.
  • best classic quality on sparse data; same cold start as CF.

stages.name: Cold-start playbook
stages.html:
Case Answer
New user onboarding choices, popularity / trending, context (location, device), bandits for exploration
New item content features / embeddings, exposure boost, similar-item mapping
New platform content-based + popularity until interactions accumulate

Hybrids: feed content features into factorisation (e.g. LightFM) or two-tower models.

stages.name: Implicit feedback is confidence
stages.html:
• Clicks, views, dwell time: positive signal with varying confidence; absence is ambiguous.
  • Loss: weighted (ALS-WR), BPR pairwise ranking, or sampled softmax.
  • Evaluation: ranking metrics (NDCG, recall@k) and online tests.

followUps.question: Why did item-based CF age better than user-based?
followUps.html:
Because items are fewer and their similarity is more stable than users' tastes.

Item-based User-based
Count fewer items many users
Similarity stable shifts quickly as users interact
Serving precomputed and cached recomputed

followUps.question: What's a two-tower model and why is it common now?
followUps.html:
Two encoders, one embedding space, and relevance as a dot product.

User side:history and featuresuser toweruser vector
Item side:features and contentitem toweritem vector
score(u, i) = u · i
  • New items: handled through content features.
  • Serving: ANN retrieval over item embeddings, scaling to millions of items.

followUps.question: How do you avoid a filter bubble?
followUps.html:
Design for it and measure it.

Lever Where
Diversity and novelty in re-ranking
Exploration traffic reserved
Popularity-balanced candidates in retrieval
Coverage and diversity metrics alongside relevance

followUps.question: Does "no click" mean the user disliked it?
followUps.html:
No. They may not have seen it, or seen it and been busy.

From exposure logs Treat as
Shown and ignored a weak negative
Never shown unknown

followUps.question: How do you evaluate offline?
followUps.html:
With a time-based split and ranking metrics, then an A/B test.

Protocol:train on past interactionstest on future onesrecall@k and NDCG, per segment (new vs heavy users)confirm with an A/B test

Offline numbers carry the old policy's bias (Q16).

dontSay: "Matrix factorisation solves cold start." — it doesn't.
"No click means dislike." — implicit feedback is confidence.
"Pick the best algorithm." — production uses hybrids.

Matrix Factorization — SVD, ALS; implicit vs explicit feedback
