ml-dl-q54.testing: whether you anchor a technology decision on economics and operations.
ml-dl-q54.trap: comparing vendor feature lists before knowing the cost of a mistake.
ml-dl-q54.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Price the two errors first "Before comparing vendors, I'd price the two errors. A missed fraud costs the loss amount plus chargeback fees. A false positive costs a blocked good customer, support time and maybe churn. Those two numbers set the operating point, the size of the review queue, and the accuracy bar any option has to clear."
2 · When to buy "Buy when fraud isn't our differentiator and vendors have network effects we can't replicate, like fraud signals shared across thousands of merchants. I'd evaluate them on our own data with a backtest at our operating point, not their marketing metrics, and price integration and per-transaction fees against our loss rate."
3 · When to build "Build when our fraud patterns are proprietary, we have enough labelled data, and at our scale the economics beat vendor pricing. And cost the full lifecycle, the team, serving, monitoring, retraining, compliance, not just the notebook."
4 · Hybrid is usual "In practice the answer is usually a hybrid: the vendor score becomes one feature inside our own model, plus a rules layer for known patterns and instant response. We keep control of the operating point, and the vendor covers our cold start."
5 · Own the ongoing loop "Whoever supplies the model, fraud drifts adversarially: fraudsters adapt to what you deploy."
Close "So we own monitoring, retraining cadence and the human-review loop, and that ongoing cost usually decides the question."

stages.name: Price the two errors first
stages.html:
Error Cost components
False negative (missed fraud) loss amount, chargeback fees, scheme penalties
False positive (blocked good customer) lost sale, support cost, churn, reputation
  • Combined with review capacity, these set the threshold and the precision/recall needed at it.

stages.name: When to buy
stages.html:
Buy a vendor Build in-house
Data advantage consortium signals across merchants you can't collect alone patterns specific to your product (promo abuse, account takeover)
Time to value fast; the vendor maintains the model slow; you own the lifecycle
Cost shape per-transaction fees engineers, pipelines, real-time serving, monitoring, compliance
Pick when fraud is generic and volume is modest fraud is yours alone and volume makes fees exceed a team
  • Consortium data across merchants (device, email, card signals) you can't collect alone.
  • Faster time to value; vendor handles model upkeep.
  • Evaluate: backtest on your labelled history, at your threshold, with cost per decision.
  • Watch: per-transaction fees, latency, data-sharing terms, explainability for disputes.

stages.name: When to build
stages.html:
• Your fraud is specific to your product (promo abuse, account takeover in your app).
  • Enough labels and volume; costs at scale beat vendor pricing.
  • Full lifecycle cost: engineers, feature pipelines, real-time serving, monitoring, model risk, compliance.

stages.name: Hybrid is usual
stages.html:
transaction → rules layer (hard blocks, known patterns)
            → model (own features + vendor score) → threshold → approve / review / decline
            → human review queue → labels back into training
  • "Fine-tune" here usually means adapting a vendor or foundation model to your data where the vendor allows it; check what's actually tunable.

stages.name: Own the ongoing loop
stages.html:
• Fraudsters probe and adapt; performance decays faster than in normal drift.
  • Needed regardless of source: monitoring by segment, delayed-label evaluation, fast retraining, rule updates, feedback from investigators.

followUps.question: How do you evaluate a vendor fairly?
followUps.html:
On your data, at your operating point.

Evaluation:historical, time-split dataset with known outcomesthey score it, or you score locallycompare
Compare on
Precision at review capacity, dollar loss caught
Latency and cost per call
Stability across segments

Their headline AUC on other clients' data doesn't transfer.

followUps.question: Labels arrive after 60 days (chargebacks). How does that affect the choice?
followUps.html:
Slow labels make decay hard to detect and retraining slow.

Response How
Faster signals favours a partner who has them
Proxy labels investigator decisions, customer confirmations
Label-free monitoring score and feature distributions; needed either way

followUps.question: Why keep a rules layer if you have a model?
followUps.html:
Three reasons.

Rules give you
Speed minutes to respond to a new attack; the model needs retraining
Hard policy sanctions, velocity limits
Auditability each rule is readable

The model handles the nuanced cases.

followUps.question: What does it cost to build, roughly?
followUps.html:
Don't invent numbers; estimate by component for your context, over at least a year.

Component
Engineers and data scientists
Real-time feature infrastructure, serving, monitoring
Investigator tooling
Compliance reviews

Then compare the total with vendor fees × volume.

followUps.question: How do you handle explainability for declined customers?
followUps.html:
Reason codes, whoever built the model.

Source Explanation
Your model SHAP-based reason codes
Your rules clear rule descriptions
A black-box vendor confirm before signing that they provide reasons for disputes and regulatory requests

dontSay: "We'll build because we have data scientists." — cost the lifecycle.
"Vendor X has 0.98 AUC." — on whose data, at what threshold?
"Once deployed, it'll keep working." — fraud adapts.

links.label: Build vs Buy vs Fine tune

ml-dl-q55.testing: numerical stability reasoning and the free fix.
ml-dl-q55.trap: "clip the logits" or "lower the learning rate."
ml-dl-q55.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Overflow and underflow "exp of a large logit overflows the float range to infinity, so you get infinity divided by infinity, which is NaN. Very negative logits underflow to zero, and if they all do, the denominator collapses."
2 · Softmax is shift-invariant "The fix is free because softmax is shift-invariant: subtracting the same constant from every logit doesn't change the output. So subtract the maximum logit first. The largest exponent becomes exp of zero, which is one, and nothing overflows."
4 · Log-sum-exp and fused losses "The same idea in log space is the log-sum-exp trick for log-probabilities. In practice you use the fused log_softmax or cross-entropy functions that take raw logits, instead of composing log of softmax yourself."
5 · Where it reappears "And this pressure comes back in attention at long context, with many logits and growing magnitudes, which is why fused attention kernels compute softmax with a running maximum and sum."

stages.name: Overflow and underflow
stages.html:
• float32 exp overflows above ~88.7 (float16 above ~11): exp(1000) = inf → inf/inf = NaN.
  • Very negative logits: exp → 0; if all underflow, 0/0 = NaN; log(0) = −inf in log-softmax.

stages.name: Softmax is shift-invariant
stages.html: softmax(z)ᵢ = e^{zᵢ} / Σⱼ e^{zⱼ} = e^{zᵢ − c} / Σⱼ e^{zⱼ − c}   for any c

stages.name: Subtract the max
stages.html:
z = z - z.max(dim=-1, keepdim=True).values
p = z.exp() / z.exp().sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
  • Largest term becomes e⁰ = 1; denominator ≥ 1, never 0.

stages.name: Log-sum-exp and fused losses
stages.html:
log Σ e^{zⱼ} = m + log Σ e^{zⱼ − m},   m = max z
  • F.log_softmax, F.cross_entropy(logits, y), BCEWithLogitsLoss: stable internally.
  • Never torch.log(torch.softmax(z)).

stages.name: Where it reappears
stages.html:
• Attention scores QKᵀ/√d over thousands of keys; FlashAttention-style kernels use an online softmax with running max and sum.
  • Growing logits during training also cause instability (z-loss, QK-norm as mitigations; see Q69).

followUps.question: Why does fp16 hit this sooner?
followUps.html:
Because fp16's largest value is tiny.

fp16 max ≈ 65,504
exp(x) > 65,504  when  x > ln(65,504) ≈ 11      ← overflow for logits above about 11

That's why softmax and reductions are usually computed in fp32 even in mixed-precision training.

followUps.question: Why divide attention scores by √d?
followUps.html:
Because dot products of d-dimensional vectors grow with d.

scores = QKᵀ / √d      ← keeps the variance of the logits roughly constant
Without it:large logitssoftmax saturates towards one-hotgradients vanish

followUps.question: Would clipping logits fix it?
followUps.html:
It avoids NaN, but it changes the answer.

Clipping logits Subtracting the max
NaN avoided avoided
Output distribution and gradients distorted exact
Cost free free

There's no reason to distort the values.

followUps.question: The NaN appears only after thousands of steps. Is it still softmax?
followUps.html:
Possibly, if logits grow as the weights drift large. It may also be somewhere else.

Other suspects
log of zero
Division by a zero norm
fp16 gradient overflow
Find it:anomaly detectionthe first op that produced inf or NaNlogit magnitudes over time

followUps.question: What does temperature do numerically?
followUps.html:
It rescales the logits before softmax.

p = softmax(z / T)
T < 1  → larger logits, sharper distribution, more overflow risk without max-subtraction
T > 1  → flatter distribution

The max-subtraction trick still applies after scaling.

dontSay: "Lower the learning rate." — may delay it, doesn't fix the arithmetic.
"Compute log(softmax(x))." — unstable.
"Clip the logits." — distorts outputs when an exact fix exists.

links.label: Attention Numerics at Long Context
links.target: 02-DL/03-Transformer Architecture Core/06-Attention Numerics at Long Context

ml-dl-q56.testing: the collapse argument, plus a practical default.
ml-dl-q56.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Linear layers collapse "Without a nonlinearity, any stack of linear layers collapses into a single linear map, because a product of matrices is just another matrix. Depth would buy nothing."
2 · Saturating activations "Which one: sigmoid and tanh saturate. Their derivatives go to near zero in the tails, so gradients vanish in deep stacks. I keep sigmoid for gates and output probabilities only."
3 · ReLU "ReLU is the cheap default: no saturation for positive inputs and sparse activations. Its failure is dead units, stuck at zero with zero gradient after a bad initialisation or learning rate."
4 · GELU/SiLU "GELU and SiLU are the transformer-era defaults: smooth, with a small leak for negative inputs, and empirically better at scale."
5 · The picking rule "So my rule: hidden layers get ReLU-family or GELU; the output layer is dictated by the task and loss: linear for regression, sigmoid for binary or multi-label probabilities, softmax for multiclass."
Close "A sigmoid in a deep hidden stack is a vanishing-gradient bug."

stages.name: Linear layers collapse
stages.html:
W₃(W₂(W₁x)) = (W₃W₂W₁)x = W x

Adding a nonlinearity σ between layers breaks the collapse and lets networks approximate non-linear functions.

stages.name: Saturating activations
stages.html:
• σ'(z) ≤ 0.25; tanh' ≤ 1 but → 0 at the tails.
  • Deep stacks multiply these → vanishing gradients (Q18).
  • Still right for gates (LSTM) and output probabilities.

stages.name: ReLU
stages.html:
• max(0, x): derivative 1 for positive inputs.
  • Dead ReLUs: permanently negative pre-activations get no gradient. Mitigations: Leaky ReLU, careful init (He), sane LR.

stages.name: GELU/SiLU
stages.html:
• GELU ≈ x·Φ(x); SiLU/Swish = x·σ(x).
  • Smooth near zero, small negative outputs → fewer dead units, better optimisation at scale.
  • Gated variants (SwiGLU) in modern LLM FFNs (Q64).

stages.name: The picking rule
stages.html:
Layer Choice
Hidden, CNN/MLP ReLU (or Leaky ReLU)
Hidden, transformer GELU / SwiGLU
Output, regression linear (identity)
Output, binary / multi-label sigmoid (+ BCE)
Output, multiclass softmax (+ cross-entropy)

followUps.question: Why not use the same activation for output layers?
followUps.html:
Because the output activation defines what the output means, and it must match the loss.

Output means Activation Loss
An unbounded value none (linear) MSE
A probability sigmoid BCE
A distribution over classes softmax cross-entropy

The pairing keeps the likelihood interpretation and the gradients correct.

followUps.question: How do you detect dead ReLUs?
followUps.html:
Track, per layer, the fraction of units that are zero for every input in a batch.

Signal:that fraction keeps growingunits are dying
  • Fixes: lower the learning rate, use He init, or switch to Leaky ReLU or GELU.

followUps.question: Is ReLU differentiable at 0?
followUps.html:
Not strictly, and it doesn't matter.

  • Convention: frameworks define the gradient there as 0 (or 1).
  • Why it's harmless: exact zeros are rare with real-valued inputs.

followUps.question: Why did transformers move to GELU?
followUps.html:
Empirically better results in BERT- and GPT-style models.

Property Effect
Smooth helps optimisation
Small negative region keeps gradients flowing

Later, gated variants (SwiGLU) improved further per FLOP.

followUps.question: Does the activation affect initialisation?
followUps.html:
Yes.

Init Assumes
He ReLU, which zeroes half its inputs
Xavier a symmetric activation such as tanh

A mismatch changes the activation variance across depth (Q20).

dontSay: "We add activations to make it non-linear." (without the collapse argument) — circular.
"Sigmoid in hidden layers is fine." — vanishing gradients in depth.
"Softmax for multi-label." — use independent sigmoids.

links.label: Activation Family
links.target: 02-DL/05-Training Mechanics that make transformers work/04-Activation Family

links.label: ReLU & Variants
links.target: 02-DL/05-Training Mechanics that make transformers work/03-ReLU & Variants

ml-dl-q57.testing: that you can demystify embeddings and argue against one-hot concretely.
ml-dl-q57.trap: "a vector that captures meaning" with no mechanism.
ml-dl-q57.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · A learned lookup table "An embedding is a learned dense vector: a row of a matrix selected by a token or item ID, trained by backpropagation like any other weight. It's a lookup table with gradients; nothing mystical."
2 · Why the geometry means something "Its geometry becomes meaningful because training pushes things used in similar contexts toward similar vectors. Similarity in that space means 'useful for the same predictions'."
3 · What one-hot can't do "One-hot vectors can't do that. Every pair is orthogonal and equally far apart, so related words share no statistical strength, and the dimension equals the vocabulary size, which is huge and sparse."
4 · Tokenisation decides the units "Upstream, tokenisation decides the units. Subword schemes like BPE give a bounded vocabulary with no true out-of-vocabulary words, at the cost of splitting rare words into pieces."
5 · Where embeddings go next "A detail that lands well: in many language models the input embedding matrix and the output projection are weight-tied, sharing parameters. And the same idea is everywhere beyond text: user and item embeddings in recommenders, categorical embeddings for tabular data, and embedding search for retrieval."

stages.name: A learned lookup table
stages.html:
E ∈ ℝ^{V × d}          V = vocabulary size, d = embedding dim (e.g. 768)
embed(token_id) = E[token_id]     ≡ one_hot(token_id) · E

Gradients update only the rows used in a batch.

stages.name: Why the geometry means something
stages.html:
• Tokens that predict similar next tokens, or appear in similar contexts, get similar gradients → similar vectors.
  • Distance/cosine reflects usefulness for the model's objective, not a dictionary definition.

stages.name: What one-hot can't do
stages.html:
One-hot Embedding
dimension = V (50k+) d (hundreds)
all tokens equidistant related tokens close
no sharing between related tokens statistical strength shared
sparse, memory-heavy input layer dense, efficient

stages.name: Tokenisation decides the units
stages.html:
• Word-level: huge vocab, out-of-vocabulary words.
  • Character-level: tiny vocab, long sequences.
  • Subword (BPE, WordPiece, SentencePiece): bounded vocab, rare words split into pieces.

stages.name: Where embeddings go next
stages.html:
• Weight tying: output logits = h · Eᵀ, saving parameters.
  • Sentence/document embeddings for retrieval (contrastive training).
  • Categorical embeddings in tabular and recommender models.

followUps.question: How do you choose the embedding dimension?
followUps.html:
Trade capacity against memory and overfitting, and tune by validation.

d ≈ cardinality^(1/4)      ← a common starting heuristic for categorical features

For LLMs it isn't a free choice: it's tied to the model width.

followUps.question: Is an embedding the same as word2vec?
followUps.html:
No: word2vec is one way to train embeddings.

word2vec Modern models
Trained by predicting context words end-to-end with the task
Vector per word one, fixed contextual: different in different sentences

followUps.question: Why can't embeddings from two models be compared directly?
followUps.html:
Because each model's space has its own arbitrary basis and scale.

  • Meaningful: distances within one space.
  • Meaningless: distances across two.
  • To mix them: align the spaces, or re-embed everything with one model.

followUps.question: How do embeddings help a tabular model with a 1M-level categorical?
followUps.html:
One-hot is infeasible; an embedding table is not.

Lookup:level IDa row of the embedding tablea small dense vector learned from the task
  • Gain: similar levels share strength.
  • Rare and unseen levels: a shared "other" embedding, or hashing.

followUps.question: What does weight tying buy?
followUps.html:
Fewer parameters, and often better generalisation.

input embedding  E   (V × d)
output layer     Eᵀ           ← the same matrix, used twice

The input and output representations of a token are forced to agree.

dontSay: "Embeddings capture the meaning of words." (only) — say how.
"One-hot works fine for big vocabularies." — size and no sharing.
"Embeddings are pre-computed." — usually learned with the task.

links.label: Encoder only vs Decoder only vs Encoder Decoder
links.target: 02-DL/03-Transformer Architecture Core/01-Encoder-only vs Decoder-only vs Encoder-Decoder

ml-dl-q58.trap: "deeper is more powerful" without saying in what sense.
ml-dl-q58.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · What UAT actually says "The universal approximation theorem is an existence result: for any continuous function on a bounded domain, some single hidden layer that's wide enough can approximate it arbitrarily well."
2 · What it doesn't: size "It's silent on three things that matter in practice. How wide: the required width can grow exponentially with the input dimension. Depth buys compositionality: hierarchical functions, features built on features, can be expressed with exponentially fewer units when stacked."
3 · What it doesn't: findability "Whether gradient descent finds it: existence says nothing about training. Deep networks with residuals and normalisation turn out to be trainable in practice."
4 · What it doesn't: generalisation "Whether it generalises: fitting the training data isn't learning the function. Depth is an inductive bias that matches the compositional structure of real data, edges into textures into objects, characters into words into meaning, so deep models learn more from less data."
5 · Depth as inductive bias "So the one-liner: approximation isn't optimisation isn't generalisation."
Close "The theorem only covers the first."

stages.name: What UAT actually says
stages.html:
for any continuous f on a compact set and any ε > 0, there exist N, aᵢ, wᵢ, bᵢ with
sup over x of | Σᵢ₌₁ᴺ aᵢ·σ(wᵢ·x + bᵢ) − f(x) | < ε          ← one hidden layer, N units
it says such a network EXISTS                               ← not how big N is, nor how to find it

For continuous f on a compact set and any ε > 0, there exists a one-hidden-layer network with enough units such that |network(x) − f(x)| < ε everywhere.

stages.name: What it doesn't: size
stages.html:
One wide layer Several layers
Units needed for some functions exponential in input dimension polynomial
Why every feature is built from scratch composition reuses intermediate features
  • Some functions need exponentially many units in one layer but polynomially many across several layers (depth-separation results).
  • Composition reuses intermediate features instead of re-deriving them.

stages.name: What it doesn't: findability
stages.html:
• UAT guarantees parameters exist, not that SGD reaches them.
  • Practical trainability comes from residuals, normalisation, good init and optimisers.

stages.name: What it doesn't: generalisation
stages.html:
• A huge shallow net could memorise training data without learning the underlying function.
  • Generalisation depends on inductive bias, data and regularisation.

stages.name: Depth as inductive bias
stages.html:
Domain Hierarchy depth exploits
Vision pixels → edges → textures → parts → objects
Language characters → words → phrases → meaning
Audio samples → phonemes → words

followUps.question: Is deeper always better then?
followUps.html:
No.

  • Trainability: without residuals and normalisation, very deep plain networks train poorly (vanishing gradients).
  • Returns: past a point they diminish relative to width, data and compute.

Scaling laws treat depth, width and data together.

followUps.question: Does UAT apply to ReLU networks?
followUps.html:
Yes. The condition is only that the activation isn't a polynomial.

Version of the theorem Covers
Non-polynomial activations ReLU and others
Bounded width deep networks of limited width

followUps.question: Why do wide shallow networks sometimes do well?
followUps.html:
Because for simple or smooth targets, width is enough.

Target Winner
Simple or smooth wide and shallow; easier to optimise in some regimes (neural tangent kernel)
Compositional: vision, language depth, clearly

followUps.question: How does this connect to CNNs vs ViTs?
followUps.html:
Both show that inductive bias, not representational power, decides what gets learned.

CNN ViT
Built-in prior locality, translation equivariance weaker
Little data helped by the prior needs more
Scale saturates sooner scales further (Q71)

UAT says both can represent the function; bias decides which learns it from your data.

followUps.question: What's the one sentence to remember?
followUps.html:
"UAT is about representation; depth matters for efficiency, trainability and generalisation, which the theorem doesn't address."

UAT covers UAT is silent on
Can a network represent it? how many units, whether training finds it, whether it generalises

dontSay: "One layer is enough, so depth is just fashion." — ignores size and learnability.
"Deeper networks can represent more functions." — both can represent; efficiency differs.
"UAT guarantees we can train it." — existence ≠ findability.

spine: The cell state is an additive highway
ml-dl-q59.testing: the arithmetic of the cell state, then one job per gate.
ml-dl-q59.trap: listing gates without explaining why the design fixes vanishing gradients.
ml-dl-q59.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The cell state is an additive highway "The core trick is the cell state: an additive highway through time. The new cell state is the old one, scaled by a gate, plus new information. Addition instead of repeated matrix multiplication is what lets gradients survive over long sequences; it's the same insight residual connections use across layers."
2 · Forget gate "Each gate has one job. The forget gate decides what fraction of the old cell state to keep. The input gate decides what new information to write. The output gate decides how much of the cell to expose as the hidden state at this step."
5 · GRU and the honest limit "A GRU merges this into two gates, update and reset, with fewer parameters and usually comparable results; it's the pragmatic default if you must use a recurrent model. The honest limit: gating fixed vanishing gradients, but not the sequential bottleneck."
Close "An LSTM still processes one step at a time and can't be parallelised across the sequence, which is why attention won anyway."

stages.name: The cell state is an additive highway
stages.html:
c_t = f_t ⊙ c_{t−1} + i_t ⊙ g_t
h_t = o_t ⊙ tanh(c_t)

∂c_t/∂c_{t−1} = f_t: when the forget gate is near 1, gradients pass through almost unchanged.

stages.name: Forget gate
stages.html:
• f_t = σ(W_f [h_{t−1}, x_t] + b_f), per dimension in (0, 1).
  • Initialise its bias positive (e.g. 1) so the cell remembers by default early in training.

stages.name: Input gate
stages.html:
• i_t = σ(…) chooses how much of the candidate g_t = tanh(…) enters the cell.
  • Separating "write" from "keep" lets the cell hold values unchanged for many steps.

stages.name: Output gate
stages.html:
• o_t = σ(…) controls what the next layer and next step see as h_t.
  • The cell can store information that isn't shown yet.

stages.name: GRU and the honest limit
stages.html:
LSTM GRU
Gates forget, input, output update, reset
Separate cell state yes no
Parameters more ~25% fewer
Quality similar on most tasks similar

Both still compute step t after t−1: no parallelism over time.

followUps.question: Why does the additive update help gradients?
followUps.html:
Because the gradient through the cell is a product of forget-gate values, not of weight-matrix Jacobians.

cₜ = fₜ ⊙ cₜ₋₁ + iₜ ⊙ c̃ₜ
∂cₜ/∂cₜ₋₁ = fₜ          ← with f ≈ 1 it stays near 1 over many steps

A vanilla RNN's product shrinks exponentially instead (Q23).

followUps.question: Why sigmoid for gates and tanh for candidates?
followUps.html:
Because gates are switches and candidates are content.

Activation Range Role
Gates sigmoid 0 to 1 a soft switch: a fraction to let through
Candidates tanh −1 to 1 signed content, centred on 0

The tanh range keeps the cell state bounded and balanced.

followUps.question: Do LSTMs have infinite memory?
followUps.html:
No. A longer leash than a vanilla RNN, but finite.

Why:forget gates are rarely exactly 1a little is lost every stepinformation decays over hundreds of steps

followUps.question: Where are LSTMs still used?
followUps.html:
Where memory per step must be constant, and on small data.

  • Streaming or on-device: keyword spotting, some time series.
  • Small-data sequence tasks.
  • Successor: state-space models (Mamba) revive recurrent inference with parallel training.

followUps.question: What's peephole LSTM?
followUps.html:
A variant where the gates also see the cell state directly.

  • Helps: precise timing tasks, slightly.
  • In practice: rarely used; standard LSTM or GRU are the defaults.

dontSay: "Gates let the LSTM remember everything." — decays, just slower.
"LSTMs solved long sequences, so why transformers?" — the sequential bottleneck remained.
Listing gates without the additive cell update.

spine: The reframe: the retrofit became the model
ml-dl-q60.testing: the origin story with mechanism, and the conceptual leap to transformers.
ml-dl-q60.trap: "attention lets the model focus on important words" with no mechanism.
ml-dl-q60.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The fixed-vector bottleneck "Vanilla sequence-to-sequence models squeezed the whole source sentence into one fixed-size vector, the encoder's final hidden state. That was an information bottleneck: translation quality visibly dropped as sentences got longer."
2 · Bahdanau: soft lookup per step "Bahdanau attention fixed it. At every decoder step, compute a relevance score between the decoder's state and every encoder state, softmax those scores into weights, and feed the weighted sum of encoder states, a context vector, into the decoder. It's content-based addressing over the source, and the alignment between source and target words is learned jointly with translation."
3 · Luong: simpler scoring "Luong attention simplified the scoring, dot-product or a bilinear form instead of a small MLP, and changed where the context vector enters the decoder. Worth naming to show you know the lineage."
4 · The reframe: the retrofit became the model "The reframe that matters: attention started as a retrofit to fix an RNN's memory."
Close "The transformer's move was to delete the RNN and keep only the retrofit."

stages.name: The fixed-vector bottleneck
stages.claim: one vector for a whole sentence
stages.html:
encoder: x₁ … x_T → h_T  (single vector)  → decoder generates y₁ … y_U

Long sentences lose detail; BLEU dropped with length.

stages.name: Bahdanau: soft lookup per step
stages.html:
score(s_{t−1}, h_i) = vᵀ tanh(W s_{t−1} + U h_i)
α_{t,i} = softmax_i(score)
c_t = Σ_i α_{t,i} h_i        → fed into decoder step t
  • Differentiable, learned alignment; attention maps looked like word alignments.

stages.name: Luong: simpler scoring
stages.html:
Bahdanau Luong
Score small MLP (additive) dot / general (bilinear)
Decoder state used previous step current step
Cost higher cheaper, matmul-friendly

stages.name: The reframe: the retrofit became the model
stages.html:
• Attention gave every output direct access to every input.
  • The transformer removed recurrence: self-attention within encoder and decoder, plus cross-attention between them, all parallel.

followUps.question: What's the difference between attention and self-attention?
followUps.html:
It's about which sequence the query looks at.

Seq2seq (cross) attention Self-attention
Query from the decoder state a token
Keys from the encoder states every token in the same sequence
Sequences two one

Transformers use both.

followUps.question: Are attention weights explanations?
followUps.html:
Not reliably: a hint, not proof.

  • What they show: where information was pulled from in one layer.
  • What they miss: other paths (residuals, other heads) matter too.
  • The catch: different weightings can produce the same output.

followUps.question: Why did dot-product scoring win?
followUps.html:
Because it's a matrix multiplication.

Chain:all scores as one matmulGPUs do it fast and in parallelscaled by √d it trains stablythe basis of transformer attention

followUps.question: Did attention fix the RNN's sequential training?
followUps.html:
No.

Problem Fixed by
Information bottleneck attention
Step-by-step training the transformer, by removing recurrence (Q61)

With attention added, the encoder and decoder were still RNNs.

followUps.question: What does the context vector represent?
followUps.html:
A weighted summary of the source, specific to the current output step.

cₜ = Σᵢ αₜᵢ · hᵢ      ← αₜᵢ = how much encoder state i matters at step t

Mostly the parts of the input relevant to what the decoder is generating now.

dontSay: "Attention was invented for transformers." — it came from seq2seq RNNs.
"Attention focuses on important words." (alone) — give the scoring and weighted sum.
"Attention made RNNs parallel." — it didn't.

ml-dl-q61.testing: hardware, optimisation and economic reasons, plus the costs.
ml-dl-q61.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Reason 1: parallel training "Three real reasons. One, parallelism. Training computes every position at once as dense matrix multiplications, exactly what GPUs and TPUs are built for. An RNN's step-by-step chain leaves most of the hardware idle."
2 · Reason 2: constant path length "Two, path length. Any two tokens are one attention step apart, versus a number of hops proportional to their distance through a recurrent chain. Credit assignment over long ranges stops decaying with distance."
3 · Reason 3: scaling economics "Three, the economics those two unlock. More tokens and more parameters trained per dollar, which let transformers ride scaling laws that recurrent networks couldn't reach in practice."
4 · The price paid "And the price: attention costs grow quadratically with sequence length, and the architecture has no built-in sense of order, so position has to be injected explicitly with positional encodings."
Close "Long-context inference also needs a KV cache that grows with the sequence."

stages.name: Reason 1: parallel training
stages.html:
• Self-attention for all positions = a few large matmuls per layer.
  • RNNs: step t waits for step t−1 → poor GPU utilisation during training.
  • Teacher forcing plus causal masking lets decoder training run in parallel too.

stages.name: Reason 2: constant path length
stages.html:
RNN / LSTM Transformer
Max path between tokens O(n) O(1)
Gradient over long range decays with distance direct
Sequential ops per layer O(n) O(1)

stages.name: Reason 3: scaling economics
stages.html:
• Efficient training at scale → bigger models on more data.
  • Performance improves predictably with compute (scaling laws), which justified the investment.

stages.name: The price paid
stages.html:
Cost Mitigations
O(n²) attention compute/memory FlashAttention, sparse/sliding attention, linear attention
No inherent order positional encodings (sinusoidal, learned, RoPE, ALiBi)
KV cache grows with context at inference GQA/MQA, paged attention, quantised caches
Weak inductive bias needs more data (Q71)

followUps.question: Isn't inference still sequential for transformers?
followUps.html:
Generation is, yes. Training isn't, and that's what mattered.

Phase Transformer
Training parallel across positions
Prompt processing parallel
Generation token by token; the KV cache avoids recomputing past tokens

The training speed-up is what drove the scaling advantage.

followUps.question: Why do transformers need positional encodings?
followUps.html:
Because self-attention is permutation-equivariant.

Without position:shuffle the inputsthe outputs shuffle identicallyword order is invisible

Positional encodings inject the order.

followUps.question: Are RNNs coming back?
followUps.html:
Partly.

  • What's new: state-space models (Mamba) and linear-attention RNNs train in parallel and run inference recurrently with constant memory.
  • Where it appeals: long contexts.
  • Status: competitive in some settings; transformers remain dominant, often hybridised with them.

followUps.question: "Transformers understand context better." Fair?
followUps.html:
Too vague.

Causal chain:direct token-to-token paths + parallel trainingscale becomes affordablebetter "understanding"

Understanding is the result; those two properties are the cause.

followUps.question: When would an LSTM still be the right choice?
followUps.html:
In three cases.

Case Why
Small data fewer parameters to fit
Strict streaming or on-device constant memory per step
Very long streams quadratic attention is prohibitive, and a small recurrent model is enough

dontSay: "Attention is all you need." — a slogan, not a reason.
"Transformers are more accurate." — explain why.
Forgetting the costs (quadratic attention, positional encodings).

links.label: Why Attention Beats Recurrence at Scale
links.target: 02-DL/03-Transformer Architecture Core/03-Why Attention Beats Recurrence at Scale

ml-dl-q62.testing: the mechanism of the coupling, not just "AdamW is better".
ml-dl-q62.trap: "AdamW adds weight decay to Adam." Adam with L2 already had it; the difference is where it's applied.
ml-dl-q62.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · First moment steers "Adam keeps two moving averages per parameter. The first moment is an average of recent gradients, which is momentum: it steers and smooths the direction. The second moment is an average of squared gradients, which acts as a per-parameter step-size scaler: parameters with large recent gradients take smaller steps. Bias correction fixes both averages being underestimated in the first steps, since they start at zero."
4 · The coupling bug "The problem with classic Adam plus L2 regularisation is where the decay goes. Adding λ times the weights to the loss puts the decay term into the gradient, and then it gets divided by the square root of the second moment like everything else. So parameters with a large gradient history get less decay. The regularisation strength becomes tangled with the gradient scale."
5 · AdamW's fix "AdamW decouples it: weight decay is applied directly to the weights at the update step, outside the adaptive scaling. Decay then means what it says, uniformly. That changed results enough that it's the default for transformer training, hence the new name."
6 · The memory cost "One cost worth naming: those two extra states per parameter mean optimizer memory is about twice the model size in fp32, a big part of the training-memory budget."

stages.name: First moment steers
stages.html:
m_t = β₁ m_{t−1} + (1 − β₁) g_t        β₁ ≈ 0.9

Smooths noisy gradients; direction of travel.

stages.name: Second moment scales
stages.html:
v_t = β₂ v_{t−1} + (1 − β₂) g_t²       β₂ ≈ 0.95–0.999
step ∝ m̂ / (√v̂ + ε)

Large, frequent gradients → smaller effective steps; rare ones → larger.

stages.name: Bias correction
stages.html: m̂ = m / (1 − β₁ᵗ), v̂ = v / (1 − β₂ᵗ); matters most in early steps (and interacts with warmup, Q63).

stages.name: The coupling bug
stages.html:
Adam + L2:  g ← g + λθ ;  θ ← θ − η m̂ / (√v̂ + ε)
            → decay term also divided by √v̂: parameters with big gradients decay less

stages.name: AdamW's fix
stages.html:
AdamW:  θ ← θ − η ( m̂ / (√v̂ + ε) + λθ )
            → uniform shrinkage regardless of gradient history
  • Typical: weight decay ~0.01–0.1, often excluded for biases and norm parameters.

stages.name: The memory cost
stages.html:
• Two fp32 states per parameter: 8 bytes/param.
  • 7B parameters → ~56 GB of optimizer state alone (see Q65); motivates ZeRO sharding and 8-bit optimizers.

followUps.question: Isn't L2 regularisation the same as weight decay?
followUps.html:
For plain SGD, yes. For adaptive optimisers, no.

Optimiser L2 vs weight decay
SGD equivalent, up to a scaling of λ
Adam different: the adaptive denominator rescales the L2 gradient per parameter

That difference is exactly what AdamW fixes.

followUps.question: Why exclude LayerNorm and bias parameters from weight decay?
followUps.html:
Because decay there costs more than it gives.

  • They're few.
  • They don't cause overfitting in the same way.
  • Shrinking norm gains toward zero can hurt training.

Common recipes apply decay only to weight matrices.

followUps.question: Why β₂ = 0.95 in LLM training instead of 0.999?
followUps.html:
A shorter memory for the second moment.

β₂ = 0.999 → averages over about 1,000 steps
β₂ = 0.95  → averages over about 20 steps      ← 1 / (1 − β₂)

It reacts faster when gradient scales shift, which improves stability and reduces loss spikes in large-scale training.

followUps.question: How do you reduce Adam's memory?
followUps.html:
Three ways, each trading some fidelity or communication for memory.

Option How
ZeRO stage 1+ shard optimiser state across GPUs
8-bit optimiser states lower precision
Adafactor factorises the second moment

followUps.question: What does ε do?
followUps.html:
It prevents division by zero and caps the step for parameters with tiny v.

step = lr · m̂ / (√v̂ + ε)

Too small an ε can cause instability with tiny gradients in low precision, so it's occasionally tuned (1e-8 vs 1e-6).

dontSay: "AdamW adds weight decay to Adam." — the point is decoupling.
"Both moments are momentum." — the second one scales.
"Adam has no memory overhead." — 2× parameters in fp32.

links.target: 02-DL/05-Training Mechanics that make transformers work/08-Optimizer Family

links.label: Regularization — L1, L2 & Weight Decay
links.target: 02-DL/05-Training Mechanics that make transformers work/07-Regularization — L1, L2 & Weight Decay

links.label: GPU Memory Budget & the Levers
links.target: 02-DL/06-Training at scale/01-GPU Memory Budget & the Levers

ml-dl-q63.testing: the mechanism behind a recipe step everyone copies.
ml-dl-q63.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Culprit 1: Adam's noisy second moment "Two things are wrong at step ten."
2 · Culprit 2: an unformed network "First, Adam's second-moment estimate. It's an average of squared gradients built from only a handful of noisy samples, so the adaptive denominator is unreliable. Some parameters with tiny early estimates get enormous effective steps."
3 · What warmup does "Second, the network itself is raw. Attention distributions and output logits are unformed, gradients are large and badly conditioned. A full-size learning rate at that moment can push weights into divergence or saturation you never recover from. The original post-norm transformers were notoriously dependent on warmup; pre-norm reduced the need but didn't remove it."
4 · Then decay "Warmup ramps the learning rate from near zero to its peak over the first few hundred or thousand steps, so the optimizer statistics and the network settle before full-size steps land. Then a decay schedule, cosine or linear, takes over: large steps to cover ground, small steps to converge."
5 · Pair it with clipping "And I'd pair it with gradient clipping: warmup prevents the early blow-ups, clipping insures against a rare bad batch later in training."

stages.name: Culprit 1: Adam's noisy second moment
stages.html:
Adam step:  Δθ = − η · m̂ / ( √v̂ + ε )
early on, v̂ comes from only a few gradients     ← bias correction fixes its mean, not its noise
a parameter with a small early v̂ gets a huge step ← warmup keeps η tiny until v̂ settles
  • v̂ estimated from very few gradients early; bias correction fixes its mean but not its noise.
  • Parameters with small early v̂ get step ≈ η·m̂/√v̂ that's far too large.

stages.name: Culprit 2: an unformed network
stages.html:
• Random init: attention nearly uniform, logits poorly scaled, residual stream statistics unsettled.
  • Large early updates can blow up activations, saturate softmax, or create dead units.
  • Post-norm (norm after residual add) amplifies this; pre-norm is more stable.

stages.name: What warmup does
Then decay
stages.html:
• Cosine or linear decay to ~10% of peak (or lower).
  • Alternatives: inverse square root (original transformer), warmup-stable-decay schedules for continued training.

stages.name: Pair it with clipping
stages.html:
• Global-norm clipping (e.g. 1.0) caps any single catastrophic step.
  • Log the pre-clip norm: frequent clipping late in training means the LR is too hot (Q67, Q69).

followUps.question: How long should warmup be?
followUps.html:
Commonly a few hundred to a few thousand steps, or about 1–5% of training.

Make it longer for
Larger learning rates
Larger batches
Deeper models

Too short risks early instability; too long wastes training at a low rate.

followUps.question: Does warmup matter with SGD?
followUps.html:
Less for the second-moment reason, but it's still useful.

  • When: large batches and large learning rates; the "linear scaling rule" pairs with warmup.
  • Why: early gradients are large and the network is fragile.

followUps.question: Why does pre-norm need less warmup?
followUps.html:
Because in pre-norm the residual path is a pure identity.

pre-norm:   x + f(Norm(x))      ← gradients flow straight through the identity
post-norm:  Norm(x + f(x))      ← normalisation sits on the residual path

Post-norm makes early gradients to the lower layers larger and less stable.

followUps.question: Can you skip warmup by lowering the peak LR?
followUps.html:
You can stay stable, but you give up the high learning rate later.

Low peak, no warmup Warmup to a high peak
Early steps stable stable
Later trains slower or ends worse fast

followUps.question: Your loss explodes at step 300 during warmup. What do you check?
followUps.html:
Five suspects.

Suspect Action
Peak LR too high for this model and batch lower the peak
Warmup too short lengthen it
fp16 overflow without proper loss scaling check the numerics
Bad init find the first NaN layer
A data problem inspect the batch

dontSay: "Warmup helps the model converge." (only) — give the two mechanisms.
"It's needed because the LR is too high." — the point is safely using a high LR.
"Clipping replaces warmup." — they solve different problems.

ml-dl-q64.testing: what "smooth" and "gated" buy, and honesty about the cost.
ml-dl-q64.trap: "GELU is just better" with no mechanism.
ml-dl-q64.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · ReLU's hard zero "ReLU is cheap and sparse, but it has a hard zero: any unit with negative input gets no gradient at all, so units can die, and the kink makes the loss surface less smooth."
2 · GELU: smooth gating "GELU is roughly x times the probability that a standard normal is below x. It gates each input smoothly by its own magnitude, and it lets small negative inputs through with a small gradient, so units don't fully die. Empirically it trains better at transformer scale."
3 · SwiGLU: a learned gate "SwiGLU goes further: the feed-forward layer becomes a gated product of two projections, one passed through SiLU and multiplied element-wise by the other. So the gate is learned and input-dependent for every hidden unit. It's consistently better quality per FLOP and standard in Llama-style models, usually with the hidden dimension trimmed to keep the parameter count comparable."
4 · The costs "What's worse: slightly more compute, and for gated FFNs an extra projection matrix. That's negligible next to the matmuls, which is why everyone pays it."
5 · The init tie-in "One tie-in: activation choice interacts with initialisation assumptions; He initialisation was derived for ReLU."

stages.name: ReLU's hard zero
GELU: smooth gating
stages.html:
• GELU(x) = x · Φ(x); negative inputs produce small negative outputs with non-zero gradient.
  • Smoothness helps optimisation in deep, wide networks.

stages.name: SwiGLU: a learned gate
stages.html:
FFN_ReLU(x)   = W₂ · ReLU(W₁ x)
FFN_SwiGLU(x) = W₂ · ( SiLU(W₁ x) ⊙ (W₃ x) )      three matrices
  • Hidden size often set to ~⅔ of 4d so total parameters match the ReLU FFN.
  • The gate W₃x decides, per input, which hidden features pass.

stages.name: The costs
stages.html:
Cost Size
Extra projection (W₃) offset by smaller hidden dim
Activation compute (erf/sigmoid) tiny vs matmuls
Kernel support universal in modern frameworks

stages.name: The init tie-in
stages.html: He init assumes ReLU's halving of variance; smooth or gated activations change activation statistics slightly, and deep recipes also scale residual projections at init.

followUps.question: Why not Leaky ReLU instead of GELU?
followUps.html:
Leaky ReLU fixes dead units but keeps the kink.

Leaky ReLU GELU / SiLU Gated (SwiGLU)
Dead units fixed fixed fixed
Smooth everywhere no yes; empirically optimises better in transformers yes
Input-dependent gating no no yes

followUps.question: Is the SwiGLU gain large?
followUps.html:
Modest but consistent.

  • Size: a better loss at the same compute, reported across several studies.
  • Why it's adopted: the cost is negligible, not because the gain is dramatic.

followUps.question: What's SiLU?
followUps.html:
The input multiplied by its own sigmoid.

SiLU(x) = Swish(x) = x · σ(x)

Smooth, with a non-monotonic dip below zero. A similar shape to GELU, and cheaper to compute exactly.

followUps.question: Why doesn't activation choice matter much for inference latency?
followUps.html:
Because the matrix multiplications dominate.

Part of the FFN Share of time
Matmuls and memory bandwidth almost all
Element-wise activation a small fraction, often fused into the matmul kernel

followUps.question: Would you switch an existing ReLU model to GELU?
followUps.html:
Not by swapping it into a trained model: the weights were learned for ReLU.

Situation Decision
Existing trained model leave it
New training run yes, as the modern default; validate on your task, since the gains are empirical

dontSay: "GELU is better." (no mechanism) — smoothness and non-zero negative gradients.
"SwiGLU is free." — an extra projection; small cost, compensated by hidden size.
"ReLU is obsolete." — still the default in many CNNs.

ml-dl-q65.testing: fluency with memory arithmetic and what it implies for infrastructure.
ml-dl-q65.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Count bytes per parameter "Before activations, count bytes per parameter. In mixed-precision AdamW you keep the working weights in bf16, 2 bytes; an fp32 master copy of the weights, 4 bytes; two fp32 Adam moments, 8 bytes; and the gradients, 2 to 4 bytes. That's about 16 bytes per parameter, the standard figure from the ZeRO paper."
2 · Multiply "Seven billion times 16 bytes is about 112 gigabytes of state, already more than a single 80-gigabyte GPU before a single activation."
3 · Add activations "Activations come on top and scale with batch size times sequence length times depth times width. They're attacked with activation checkpointing: store only some activations and recompute the rest during the backward pass, trading roughly a third more compute for much less memory."
4 · Contrast with inference "For contrast, inference needs about 2 bytes per parameter in bf16, less when quantised, plus the KV cache. So training and serving memory are almost an order of magnitude apart."
5 · What the arithmetic justifies "And this arithmetic is the reason sharded optimizers like ZeRO and FSDP exist: in plain data parallelism most of those 16 bytes are duplicated on every GPU."

stages.name: Count bytes per parameter
Multiply
stages.html:
Item Bytes/param 7B total
bf16 weights 2 14 GB
fp32 master weights 4 28 GB
Adam moments (fp32) 8 56 GB
Gradients (bf16) 2 14 GB
Total state 16 ~112 GB

stages.name: Add activations
stages.html:
• Scale with batch × sequence length × layers × hidden size (attention adds more at long context).
  • Activation checkpointing: recompute in backward; ~⅓ extra compute for large savings.
  • Micro-batching with gradient accumulation keeps activations bounded (Q67).

stages.name: Contrast with inference
stages.html:
• bf16 inference: ~14 GB weights; int8 ~7 GB; int4 ~3.5 GB.
  • Plus KV cache, growing with batch × context length.

stages.name: What the arithmetic justifies
stages.html:
• ZeRO-1/2/3 / FSDP: shard optimizer states, gradients, then parameters across data-parallel GPUs (Q68).
  • 8-bit optimizers, CPU/NVMe offload, LoRA for fine-tuning (only adapter weights get optimizer state).

followUps.question: Why keep fp32 master weights at all?
followUps.html:
Because updates are tiny relative to the weights.

In bf16 only:weight + tiny updaterounds back to the same weightthe update is lost
With masters:update accumulates in fp32copy to bf16 for compute

followUps.question: How does LoRA change the budget for fine-tuning?
followUps.html:
The base is frozen, so almost all the training state disappears.

Full fine-tune LoRA
Base weights master, gradient and Adam state for each frozen: 2 bytes/param, less if quantised (QLoRA)
Gradients and Adam state every parameter the small adapter matrices only

A 7B model then fine-tunes on a single 24–48 GB GPU.

followUps.question: With ZeRO-3 on 8 GPUs, what's per-GPU state?
followUps.html:
About 14 GB of sharded state per GPU, plus working memory.

112 GB / 8 GPUs ≈ 14 GB per GPU      ← sharded weights, gradients, optimiser state

On top: activations, the temporarily gathered parameters of the layer being computed, and communication buffers.

followUps.question: What dominates memory at long context?
followUps.html:
Activations, especially attention intermediates.

Growth:longer sequenceactivations grow with lengthquadratically for naive attention
Remedy Effect
FlashAttention never stores the full attention matrix
Checkpointing, sequence parallelism cut activation memory further

followUps.question: "7B × 2 bytes = 14 GB, so one GPU is fine." Response?
followUps.html:
That's inference weights only.

inference: 7B × 2 bytes  = 14 GB
training:  7B × 16 bytes = 112 GB     ← master weights + optimiser state + gradients
                         ≈ 8× more, before activations

dontSay: "14 GB for a 7B model." (for training) — that's inference weights.
"Activations are negligible." — they often dominate at long context.
"Just use a bigger GPU." — 112 GB of state exceeds any single one today.

ml-dl-q66.testing: number formats and the practical fix, not just "use bf16".
ml-dl-q66.trap: "fp16 is less precise." It's the range, not the precision, that bites.
ml-dl-q66.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Same 16 bits, different split "The two formats spend their 16 bits differently."
2 · fp16's narrow range "fp16 has more mantissa bits, so better precision, but a narrow exponent range. Small gradients underflow to zero, and large intermediate values overflow to infinity, and one infinity cascades into NaNs."
3 · Loss scaling "Loss scaling is the fp16 patch. Multiply the loss by a large factor, which scales all gradients up into the representable range, then unscale them before the optimizer step. Dynamic loss scaling lowers the factor automatically when it sees infinities, skipping that step, and slowly raises it again."
4 · bf16 keeps fp32's range "bf16 keeps fp32's exponent range with fewer mantissa bits. No underflow drama, no loss scaling needed, it's essentially drop-in, and it's the default on modern accelerators. The lost precision is tolerable because stochastic gradient descent is noise-tolerant anyway."
5 · What stays in fp32 "Both schemes still keep fp32 master weights, and numerically sensitive operations like softmax, normalisation and large reductions typically run in fp32 regardless."

stages.name: Same 16 bits, different split
stages.html:
Format Exponent bits Mantissa bits Max value Smallest normal
fp32 8 23 ~3.4e38 ~1.2e−38
fp16 5 10 ~65,504 ~6.1e−5
bf16 8 7 ~3.4e38 ~1.2e−38

stages.name: fp16's narrow range
stages.html:
Format Exponent bits Mantissa bits Largest value Smallest normal value
fp16 5 10 65,504 about 6 × 10⁻⁵
bf16 8 7 about 3 × 10³⁸ about 1 × 10⁻³⁸
fp32 8 23 about 3 × 10³⁸ about 1 × 10⁻³⁸

fp16 trades range for precision; bf16 keeps fp32's range and gives up precision.

  • Gradients smaller than ~6e−5 (subnormals down to ~6e−8) become zero: silent loss of learning signal.
  • Activations or logits above 65,504 → inf → NaN downstream.
  • "Mid-training" failures often come from gradually growing activations or logits.

stages.name: Loss scaling
stages.html:
loss_scaled = loss × S            (e.g. S = 2¹⁶)
grads_scaled = ∇ loss_scaled       stays representable
grads = grads_scaled / S           before clipping and the optimizer step
if inf/NaN in grads: skip step, S ← S/2 ;  else occasionally S ← S×2

stages.name: bf16 keeps fp32's range
stages.html:
• Same exponent range as fp32: underflow/overflow behave like fp32.
  • Coarser precision (~3 significant digits) is acceptable for gradients and activations.
  • Supported on A100/H100, TPUs; the default for LLM training.

stages.name: What stays in fp32
stages.html:
• Master weights and optimizer states.
  • Softmax, LayerNorm/RMSNorm statistics, loss computation, large reductions.
  • Autocast handles this per op.

followUps.question: Why unscale before clipping?
followUps.html:
Because the clipping threshold refers to the true gradient norm.

Order:unscaleclipstep

Clipping the scaled gradients would use a threshold S times too large, which effectively disables clipping (Q67).

followUps.question: If bf16 is so easy, why did anyone use fp16?
followUps.html:
Hardware.

fp16 bf16
Older GPUs (V100 and earlier) fast not supported
Extra precision yes; can matter for some inference workloads no
Current hardware, training — the default

followUps.question: Could bf16's lower precision hurt?
followUps.html:
Occasionally, when many small values are accumulated.

  • Guard: accumulations and master weights stay in fp32.
  • In practice: a non-issue for standard training.

followUps.question: Where does fp8 fit?
followUps.html:
One step further down the same road.

  • What: fp8 formats (E4M3, E5M2) for matmuls on newer GPUs, with per-tensor scaling factors.
  • Gain: more throughput.
  • Cost: careful scaling recipes; used for large-scale training and inference with library support (e.g. Transformer Engine).

followUps.question: How do you find which op produced the first inf?
followUps.html:
The first non-finite output localises it.

Hunt:anomaly detection or forward hookslog the max activation per layerreplay the failing batchthe first module with inf

dontSay: "fp16 is less precise, that's why it NaNs." — fp16 is more precise; range is the issue.
"bf16 needs loss scaling too." — it doesn't.
"Mixed precision means everything is 16-bit." — masters and sensitive ops stay fp32.

links.target: 02-DL/06-Training at scale/01-GPU Memory Budget & the Levers

ml-dl-q67.testing: both knobs and the subtle interaction: when clipping is applied.
ml-dl-q67.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Gradient accumulation fakes the batch "Two knobs. Gradient accumulation fakes the bigger batch: run eight micro-batches, add up their gradients, and take one optimizer step. Mathematically that's the large batch, as long as the loss is averaged correctly over all micro-batches. It's safe in transformers because LayerNorm has no statistics across examples, unlike BatchNorm."
2 · Clipping caps the bad step "Gradient clipping handles the spikes: compute the global gradient norm, and if it exceeds a threshold, scale the whole gradient down. It caps the size of any single step, turning a catastrophic batch into a survivable one."
3 · Order of operations "The interaction is timing. Clip once, after accumulation is complete, and after unscaling any fp16 loss scale. Clipping each micro-batch clips a different quantity and changes what the large batch means."
4 · Log the pre-clip norm "And one habit that reads senior: log the gradient norm before clipping."
Close "It's the vital sign that shows whether spikes are building, or whether the clip is doing work every step, which usually means the learning rate is too high."

stages.name: Gradient accumulation fakes the batch
stages.html:
opt.zero_grad()
for micro in micro_batches:                 # 8 × 512k tokens
    loss = model(micro).loss / len(micro_batches)
    loss.backward()                          # gradients add up
# one step for the full 4M-token batch
  • Scale the loss (or average) so the accumulated gradient equals the large-batch mean.
  • BatchNorm would see only micro-batch statistics; LayerNorm is per-example, so it's unaffected.

stages.name: Clipping caps the bad step
stages.html:
‖g‖ = sqrt(Σ over all params of ‖gᵢ‖²)
if ‖g‖ > c:  g ← g · c / ‖g‖            (e.g. c = 1.0)
  • Keeps the direction, limits the magnitude.
  • Insurance against rare outlier batches; not a fix for a bad LR.

stages.name: Order of operations
stages.html:
1. Accumulate all micro-batch gradients.
  2. Unscale (if using fp16 loss scaling).
  3. Compute the global norm and clip.
  4. Optimizer step; zero gradients.

stages.name: Log the pre-clip norm
stages.html:
Pre-clip norm pattern Reading
Rare spikes clipping doing its job
Clipped most steps LR too high or instability building
Steady rise before a spike growing logits / numerics (Q69)

followUps.question: Is accumulation exactly equal to a large batch?
followUps.html:
For the gradient maths, yes, with correct averaging.

Differs How
BatchNorm statistics computed per micro-batch
Dropout masks differ, which is fine
Data ordering small effects
Throughput lower: micro-batches run one after another

followUps.question: Why clip by global norm instead of per value?
followUps.html:
Because it keeps the gradient's direction.

g ← g · min(1, c / ‖g‖)      ← one scale factor for the whole model
Per-value clipping Global-norm clipping
Direction changed kept
Scope each value alone the model as one vector, so one exploding layer triggers the cap

followUps.question: Should you retune the LR when changing batch size?
followUps.html:
Only if the effective batch changes.

Change Learning rate
Effective batch larger usually larger too (roughly linear or square-root scaling), with warmup
Accumulation reproducing the recipe's batch keep the recipe's value

followUps.question: What's a sensible clip threshold?
followUps.html:
1.0 is a common default for transformers; then set it from the data.

Method:log the pre-clip norm distributionthreshold high enough that normal steps aren't clippedlow enough to cap the outliers

followUps.question: Clipping each micro-batch "for safety" — harmless?
followUps.html:
No.

Wrong:clip each micro-batchaccumulatestep
Right:accumulateclip oncestep

Clipping partial gradients, whose norms differ from the full batch's, biases the combined update and makes the result depend on how the batch was split.

dontSay: "Just use a smaller batch." — changes the recipe's dynamics.
"Clip every micro-batch." — wrong quantity.
"Clipping fixes a too-high learning rate." — it hides it.
