ml-dl-q68.testing: whether you pick parallelism by the specific bottleneck and know each cost.
ml-dl-q68.trap: listing the three types without saying when to use each.
ml-dl-q68.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Ask what stopped fitting "I'd organise it by what exactly stopped fitting."
2 · Data parallel "Data parallelism replicates the model on every GPU, splits the batch, and all-reduces gradients. It scales throughput, but every GPU holds the full training state, about 16 bytes per parameter. It dies when the model plus state doesn't fit on one device."
3 · ZeRO/FSDP "ZeRO or FSDP is still data parallelism, but it shards the redundancy: first the optimizer state, then gradients, then the parameters themselves, gathering each shard only when it's needed. Same maths, far less memory per GPU. It's the first thing I'd reach for."
4 · Tensor parallel "Tensor parallelism splits individual weight matrices across GPUs. Activations must be synchronised inside every layer, so it needs NVLink-class bandwidth and stays within a node. Use it when a single layer is too big or too slow."
5 · Pipeline parallel "Pipeline parallelism assigns blocks of consecutive layers to different GPUs and feeds micro-batches through so stages stay busy, but the ramp-up and ramp-down 'bubble' is idle time. It's for spreading depth across nodes."
6 · Compose: 3D "Frontier training composes all three, so-called 3D parallelism."
Close "The design rule is to pick the cheapest parallelism that fixes what specifically doesn't fit."

stages.name: Ask what stopped fitting
stages.html:
What doesn't fit / too slow Reach for
Throughput (model fits) data parallel
Training state (optimizer, grads, params) ZeRO / FSDP
One layer's weights or compute tensor parallel
Total depth across nodes pipeline parallel
Very long sequences sequence / context parallel

stages.name: Data parallel
stages.html:
Data parallel
What is split the batch; every GPU holds a full replica
Communication all-reduce of gradients once per step
Memory per GPU full model + full optimizer state
Stops working when one replica no longer fits on one GPU
  • All-reduce gradients each step; scales well with good interconnect.
  • Memory per GPU: full model + full optimizer state.

stages.name: ZeRO/FSDP
stages.html:
Stage Sharded Memory per GPU (N GPUs)
ZeRO-1 optimizer state ~ (4 + 12/N) bytes/param
ZeRO-2 + gradients smaller
ZeRO-3 / FSDP + parameters ~16/N bytes/param + working set

Cost: more communication (all-gather params per layer, reduce-scatter grads).

stages.name: Tensor parallel
stages.html:
• Column/row splits of attention and FFN weights (Megatron-style).
  • Communication inside every layer → needs NVLink/NVSwitch; usually ≤ 8 GPUs in a node.

stages.name: Pipeline parallel
stages.html:
• Layers grouped into stages on different GPUs/nodes; activations passed between stages.
  • Micro-batching (GPipe, 1F1B schedules) reduces the bubble; bubble fraction ≈ (stages − 1) / (micro-batches + stages − 1).

stages.name: Compose: 3D
stages.html:
• Tensor parallel within a node, pipeline across nodes, data parallel (often FSDP/ZeRO) across replicas.
  • Plus activation checkpointing and mixed precision throughout.

followUps.question: Why is tensor parallelism kept inside a node?
followUps.html:
Because it communicates activations in every layer, forward and backward.

Link Bandwidth and latency Tensor parallelism
NVLink inside a node very high, low latency works
Cross-node network usually not enough too slow

followUps.question: You're fine-tuning a 13B model on 8 GPUs in one node. What do you use?
followUps.html:
FSDP (or ZeRO-3) with activation checkpointing and bf16: likely enough on its own.

If it still doesn't fit:add LoRACPU offloadonly then tensor or pipeline parallelism

The last step adds complexity, so it comes last.

followUps.question: Does ZeRO change the training maths?
followUps.html:
No. It's the same data-parallel algorithm.

Changes?
Where state lives yes: sharded
Communication yes: added, to gather state
The maths no: results match plain data parallelism up to numerical noise

followUps.question: How do you shrink the pipeline bubble?
followUps.html:
Three levers.

  • More micro-batches per step.
  • Interleaved schedules (virtual stages).
  • Balanced stages, so each takes similar time.

followUps.question: What's sequence parallelism?
followUps.html:
Splitting the sequence dimension across GPUs.

  • Applied to: operations like LayerNorm and dropout, or attention itself (ring attention).
  • Gain: less activation memory for very long contexts.

dontSay: "Use data parallel." (for a model that doesn't fit) — it replicates everything.
"Tensor parallel across nodes." — bandwidth-bound.
"Pipeline parallel has no cost." — the bubble.

links.label: GPU Memory Budget & the Levers
links.target: 02-DL/06-Training at scale/01-GPU Memory Budget & the Levers

spine: Look first: grad norms and the first NaN
ml-dl-q69.testing: an ordered incident response for training, not a guess.
ml-dl-q69.trap: "lower the learning rate and keep training."
ml-dl-q69.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Look first: grad norms and the first NaN "First I look, before changing anything. The gradient-norm history around the spike: a sudden wall suggests a bad batch, a slow build suggests numerics or logit growth. And which layer produced the first infinity or NaN. That split alone separates a data problem from a numerics problem."
2 · Four usual suspects "The four usual suspects: a bad data shard, corrupt, duplicated or adversarial, which I confirm by replaying that exact batch; a learning rate too hot for this phase of training, or a schedule bug; fp16 numerics overflowing; and growing logits, attention or output logits drifting upward until softmax breaks, which is what z-loss and QK-normalisation mitigate."
3 · Recover from a checkpoint "To recover: restore a checkpoint from before the spike, skip or reshuffle the offending data window, and resume with a lower learning rate or tighter clipping. 'Never recovers' usually means the weights are poisoned, so continuing forward throws good compute after bad."
4 · Prevent the next one "To prevent the next one: checkpoint often enough that losing work is acceptable, keep data ordering deterministic so the bad batch can be bisected, and put pre-clip gradient norms on a dashboard as the early warning."

stages.name: Look first: grad norms and the first NaN
stages.html:
• Grad-norm history: sudden jump vs gradual build.
  • First non-finite tensor: which layer and op.

stages.name: Four usual suspects
stages.html:
Suspect Evidence Confirm
Bad data shard sudden spike at a specific step replay that batch; inspect samples
LR too hot / schedule bug spikes cluster after LR changes check schedule logs
fp16 numerics inf in activations or grads loss-scale history, switch to bf16
Growing logits slow rise in logit magnitudes log max attention/output logits per layer

stages.name: Recover from a checkpoint
stages.html:
Experiment 1

Restore and skip

Reload the last checkpoint before the spike and skip or reshuffle the offending data window.

Why? Weights after the spike are damaged; continuing wastes compute.

Best suited when the spike aligns with a specific batch.

Experiment 2

Restore and cool down

Resume with a lower LR (or longer warmup back to it) and tighter clipping.

Why? Gives the model a stable path through the region that destabilised it.

Best suited when spikes aren't tied to one batch.

Experiment 3

Fix the numerics

Switch to bf16, add z-loss on output logits, add QK-norm.

Why? Removes the mechanism, not just the symptom.

Best suited when logits or activations were growing before the spike.

stages.name: Prevent the next one
stages.html:
• Checkpoint cadence sized to acceptable lost work.
  • Deterministic data order and logged batch indices, so batches can be bisected.
  • Dashboards: pre-clip grad norm, loss-scale, max logits per layer, per-shard loss.
  • Automatic rollback on non-finite loss.

followUps.question: Why not just keep training? Loss sometimes recovers.
followUps.html:
Sometimes it does, but "never recovers" means it hasn't.

Choice Cost
Keep training compute burned on damaged weights
Restore only the steps since the last checkpoint

followUps.question: What's z-loss?
followUps.html:
A small penalty that keeps output logits from drifting large.

z-loss = λ · ( log Σ eᶻ )²      ← the log of the softmax normaliser, squared

It improves stability in large-scale training.

followUps.question: How do you find the bad batch?
followUps.html:
Replay and bisect, which a deterministic data order makes possible.

Hunt:list the samples in the steps before the spikereplay them on the pre-spike checkpointbisect until one reproduces the gradient explosioninspect it

Typical finds: corrupted text, extreme lengths, duplicates.

followUps.question: How often should you checkpoint?
followUps.html:
Trade storage and write time against lost work.

  • At scale: every few hundred to a few thousand steps.
  • Set by: how much GPU-time you're willing to lose, and how fast you can write.
  • Helps: async or sharded saves.

followUps.question: Spikes keep happening at random points. What's structural?
followUps.html:
The recipe, not bad luck.

Likely cause Fix
LR too high for this model and batch lower the peak
β₂ too high for Adam β₂ ≈ 0.95
Missing stabilisers pre-norm, QK-norm, z-loss
Data check the quality filters

dontSay: "Lower the LR and continue." — the weights are already damaged.
"Probably a random fluctuation." — spikes have causes.
"We don't know which data it saw." — make data order deterministic.

links.label: Attention Numerics at Long Context
links.target: 02-DL/03-Transformer Architecture Core/06-Attention Numerics at Long Context

spine: Diff the request path against the eval path
Fix: replay a golden set through production
ml-dl-q70.testing: whether you know the model you evaluated isn't the system you deployed.
ml-dl-q70.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Diff the request path against the eval path "I'd walk the production request path and diff it against the evaluation path, because the model you evaluated is rarely exactly the system you deployed."
2 · Tokeniser and template "Suspect number one in the LLM era is tokenisation and formatting: different chat templates, missing special tokens, a different truncation side or padding. The eval harness and the serving stack silently disagree."
3 · Numerics "Second, numerics. It was trained and evaluated in bf16 but served quantised, int8, int4 or fp8, so offline eval scored a different model than the one in production. Re-run the eval on the deployed artifact."
4 · Decoding settings "Third, decoding. Eval used greedy decoding or a fixed seed; production uses temperature and top-p, different maximum lengths and stop conditions. That's a different generation policy."
5 · Real traffic and mode flags "Fourth, the data and the mode. Real prompts don't look like the benchmark, and custom serving paths can leave dropout or normalisation in training mode."
6 · Fix: replay a golden set through production "The fix pattern: a golden set replayed end-to-end through the real production stack as a release gate, plus regular re-evaluation of sampled live traffic."

stages.name: Diff the request path against the eval path
stages.html:
Stage Eval harness Production
Input formatting ? ?
Tokeniser + version ? ?
Precision / quantisation ? ?
Decoding params ? ?
Inputs benchmark real users

Every difference is a suspect.

stages.name: Tokeniser and template
stages.html:
Check Mismatch to look for
Chat template roles, system prompt, BOS and EOS tokens
Tokeniser a different version or normalisation
Truncation left vs right; a shorter max context cutting the instructions
  • Chat template mismatch (roles, system prompt, BOS/EOS tokens).
  • Different tokeniser version or normalisation.
  • Truncation from the left vs right; max context differences cutting instructions.

stages.name: Numerics
stages.html:
• Quantisation (int8/int4/fp8) and kernel differences change outputs, sometimes a lot on specific tasks.
  • Evaluate the exact deployed artifact, not the training checkpoint.

stages.name: Decoding settings
stages.html:
Setting Training-time evaluation Serving Effect of a mismatch
temperature, top-p, top-k often greedy product defaults different outputs from the same weights
repetition penalty, max tokens, stop sequences unset set truncated or altered answers
batching and padding fixed engine-dependent small numerical differences
  • Temperature, top-p/top-k, repetition penalties, max tokens, stop sequences.
  • Batch-dependent effects in some serving engines (padding, speculative decoding settings).

stages.name: Real traffic and mode flags
stages.html:
• Distribution shift: longer, messier, multilingual or adversarial inputs.
  • Mode bugs: dropout active or BatchNorm using batch statistics in a custom path (Q21).
  • Preprocessing differences for images/audio (resizing, normalisation constants).

stages.name: Fix: replay a golden set through production
stages.html:
• Golden set with expected outputs/grades run through the full serving stack before each release.
  • Log production inputs/outputs (with privacy controls); sample and grade regularly.
  • Pin tokeniser, template and decoding config with the model version.

followUps.question: How do you catch a template mismatch quickly?
followUps.html:
Compare token IDs, not text.

Check:log the exact token IDs production sends for a few requestsrun the same prompts through the eval harnessdiff the IDs

Any difference in special tokens or ordering shows immediately.

followUps.question: Quantisation dropped quality on one task only. Why?
followUps.html:
Because some capabilities are more sensitive to precision loss.

  • Sensitive: arithmetic, long-context retrieval, rare languages.
  • So: evaluate a quantised model per task.
  • Options: higher precision, or quantisation-aware methods, for the sensitive layers.

followUps.question: Is it ever the model after all?
followUps.html:
Yes, when the benchmark doesn't represent real usage.

Order:rule out pipeline differencesthen question the model

Pipeline differences are cheaper to fix and more common in the first weeks after launch.

followUps.question: How do you evaluate production quality without labels?
followUps.html:
With four signals that don't need labels.

Signal What
LLM-as-judge a calibrated rubric on sampled traffic
User feedback implicit and explicit
Task-specific checks format validity, tool-call success
Periodic human review keeps the judge honest

followUps.question: Who owns the serving config?
followUps.html:
It should be versioned with the model.

One release artifact:tokeniser + template + decoding parameters + quantisation recipereviewed like codeeval and prod read the same config

dontSay: "Retrain the model." (first) — check the pipeline.
"Benchmarks are just different from real life." — find the specific skew.
"We evaluated the checkpoint, so prod is the same." — not after quantisation and templates.

ml-dl-q71.testing: inductive bias as a data-budget trade-off.
ml-dl-q71.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Convolution's two built-in assumptions "Convolution hard-codes two assumptions that happen to be true of images. Locality: nearby pixels relate more than distant ones. And translation equivariance through weight sharing: a cat detector works anywhere in the image. Because those are baked in, a CNN doesn't spend data learning them."
2 · What a ViT must learn "A vision transformer has almost no spatial prior: image patches plus positional encodings, and attention between everything. It has to learn locality from data. With enough data that flexibility wins, and it can learn things convolution can't express. With little data, it loses to the CNN's head start."
3 · The general law "That's the general law: a stronger inductive bias gives better sample efficiency but a lower ceiling; a weaker bias is data-hungry but has a higher ceiling. Match the prior to your data budget."
4 · What to do in practice "In practice, with a small dataset, I'd fine-tune a pretrained model, CNN or ViT, rather than train from scratch, because pretraining supplies the missing data."
Close "And hybrid designs like ConvNeXt or convolutional stems for ViTs borrow the CNN's bias where it helps."

stages.name: Convolution's two built-in assumptions
stages.html:
Assumption Mechanism
Locality small kernels see neighbourhoods; receptive field grows with depth
Translation equivariance the same kernel weights slide over every position
(Plus) hierarchy pooling and stacking build parts into objects

stages.name: What a ViT must learn
stages.html:
• Image → 16×16 patches → linear embeddings + positions → transformer.
  • Every patch can attend to every other from layer 1; locality isn't given.
  • With little data it overfits or learns poor spatial structure.

stages.name: The general law
stages.html:
Strong bias (CNN) Weak bias (ViT)
Small data better worse
Huge data good often better, higher ceiling
Long-range relations limited by receptive field native

stages.name: What to do in practice
stages.html:
• Small dataset: fine-tune a pretrained backbone; data augmentation; freeze early layers.
  • ViT from scratch on small data: use strong augmentation/distillation (DeiT) or hybrid stems.
  • Latency-sensitive edge deployment: efficient CNNs often still win.

followUps.question: Is translation equivariance the same as invariance?
followUps.html:
No.

equivariance: f(shift(x)) = shift(f(x))     ← the feature map moves with the input
invariance:   f(shift(x)) = f(x)            ← the output doesn't change

Convolutions are equivariant; pooling and global aggregation add approximate invariance for classification.

followUps.question: With a pretrained ViT, does the small-data problem go away?
followUps.html:
Largely, for fine-tuning.

From scratch Pretrained
ViT on small data struggles fine-tunes very well: pretraining already taught spatial structure
CNN advantage here mostly gone

followUps.question: Why not always use the higher-ceiling model?
followUps.html:
Because the ceiling only matters if you can reach it.

  • To reach it: you need the data and the compute.
  • Below that: the stronger prior gives better results for your actual budget.

followUps.question: Where else does this bias-vs-data law show up?
followUps.html:
Everywhere.

Stronger prior Weaker prior
GBMs on tabular data deep nets
Graph networks on graphs generic transformers
Physics-informed models pure data-driven ones

When data is scarce, pick the prior that's true of your data.

followUps.question: Name the generative lineage in one breath.
followUps.html:
Each one fixes the previous one's failure.

Lineage:autoencoder (no sampling)VAE (blurry samples)GAN (sharp, but unstable; mode collapse)diffusion (stable, high quality, slower sampling)

dontSay: "CNNs are just better for images." — only with limited data.
"ViTs don't work on small data." — pretrained ones do.
"More flexibility is always better." — only with enough data.

spine: The working picture: MLPs store, attention moves
ml-dl-q72.testing: mechanistic interpretability tools, and judgement about using them in production.
ml-dl-q72.trap: presenting model editing as a routine fix.
ml-dl-q72.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Localise in depth: logit lens "I'd localise it in two steps. First, the logit lens: project the residual stream at each layer onto the vocabulary and watch where in depth the wrong answer starts to dominate. Fact recall tends to emerge in a band of layers, not everywhere."
2 · Localise causally: activation patching "Second, causal localisation with activation patching, also called causal tracing. Run a clean prompt and a corrupted one, swap activations component by component, and see which swap restores or flips the answer. That tells you which layers, heads and MLPs are causally responsible, not just correlated."
3 · The working picture: MLPs store, attention moves "The working picture from this research: mid-layer MLPs behave like key-value memories that store associations, and attention heads move information between token positions. Factual recall lives disproportionately in those MLPs."
4 · Editing as surgery "Model editing methods like ROME rewrite the located MLP weights directly. They work impressively on the target fact but are brittle: side effects on related facts and paraphrases. So I'd verify with a neighbourhood evaluation, not a single prompt."
5 · Caveats "Two caveats: attention maps aren't explanations, and superposition, features sharing neurons, is why current work uses sparse autoencoders to find interpretable features."
6 · What you'd actually ship "Would I ship an edit for one fact? No."
Close "I'd fix it with data, retrieval or the system prompt first; editing is a research tool until side-effect evaluation matures."

stages.name: Localise in depth: logit lens
stages.html:
logitsₗ = W_U · LayerNorm( hₗ )        ← decode the residual stream at layer ℓ as if it were the last
track P(false token) vs P(true token) across ℓ   ← the layers where it jumps are where the fact is retrieved
  • At each layer, apply the final unembedding (after norm) to the residual stream.
  • Track the probability of the false token vs the true one by layer.
  • A sharp rise over a few layers suggests where the association is retrieved.

stages.name: Localise causally: activation patching
stages.html:
Step Run Result
1 clean prompt: "The Eiffel Tower is in" the model's answer
2 corrupted prompt: subject tokens noised answer lost
3 restore one clean activation at a time (layer × position × MLP or attention) answer returns only for some components
4 read off those components they are causally involved
  1. Clean prompt ("The Eiffel Tower is in") → model's answer.
  2. Corrupted prompt (subject noised) → answer lost.
  3. Restore one component's clean activation at a time (layer × position × MLP/attention).
  4. Components whose restoration recovers the answer are causally involved.

stages.name: The working picture: MLPs store, attention moves
stages.html:
Component Role in factual recall
Early/mid MLPs at the subject token retrieve attributes (key → value)
Attention heads move retrieved attributes to the final position
Late layers shape the output token

stages.name: Editing as surgery
stages.html:
• Treat an MLP layer as a linear associative memory; compute a rank-one update mapping the subject key to a new value.
  • Evaluate: efficacy (target fact), generalisation (paraphrases), specificity (unrelated facts unchanged), fluency.

stages.name: Caveats
stages.html:
• Attention weights ≠ causal importance.
  • Superposition: many features share neurons; sparse autoencoders (SAEs) extract more interpretable features.
  • Localisation can be distributed; one fact may involve several layers.
  • Edits can ripple to related entities or break consistency.

stages.name: What you'd actually ship
stages.html:
• Short term: system prompt correction or retrieval (RAG) with an authoritative source.
  • Medium term: fix training/fine-tuning data; add the fact to evaluation suites.
  • Editing: research and diagnosis tool; if ever used, only with a large neighbourhood and regression eval.

followUps.question: Why not just fine-tune on the correct fact?
followUps.html:
You can, but one fact is a fragile thing to fine-tune on.

Risk
Overfit to that phrasing
Forgetting of other knowledge
No generalisation to paraphrases

It needs mixed data and regression evaluation. Retrieval is often simpler and more reliable for factual accuracy.

followUps.question: What's the difference between logit lens and patching?
followUps.html:
One observes, the other intervenes.

Logit lens Patching
Kind observational interventional
Shows what the representation encodes at each layer which components cause the output
Use to form hypotheses to confirm them

followUps.question: Would you ship a ROME edit to fix a customer complaint?
followUps.html:
No.

ROME edit System-prompt or retrieval fix
Side effects not well characterised auditable
Doesn't survive retraining survives
Slower faster

Editing is for understanding, and maybe for targeted fixes with extensive evaluation.

followUps.question: What are sparse autoencoders for?
followUps.html:
For turning mixed-up neurons into readable features.

Idea:model activationsan overcomplete, sparse dictionary of featureseach feature more interpretable than a neuron

Neurons mix many concepts because of superposition. With the features you can find and steer specific ones.

followUps.question: How do you know the false fact isn't from training data?
followUps.html:
Search the training corpus, or a proxy, for the claim.

Finding Meaning Fix
The claim is common the model learned it faithfully data or retrieval

Localisation tells you where a fact is stored, not why it's there.

dontSay: "Look at the attention maps to see where the fact is." — not causal.
"Just edit the weights with ROME." — side effects.
"Fine-tune on one example." — overfits, may not generalise.
